div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
Tim Hindon 4aw sari, "Strike note wen with a, blossom, thy wife, though she be giiilty of a thou- _
sand faults." A YOUNG lady who was reoently crut driving became alarmed when the horse began to kick, and naively repiested her bean to get out and hold the

animal's feet. A C,ORRESPONDENT wants to know "how skin can be tanned ?" lie must have been a remarkably good boy when he went to school not to have learned that among other branches. "Timx changes all things," said a lecturer, at -which an auditor cried out—" If that's so, boss, I'd like to have it change this 'era ten-dollar counter-

_ felt bill." THE{ death of Pope Adrian caused such joy at Rome that the night after hisiiecease they adorned ,the door of his chid physician's house with gar lands, adding this inscription—" To the deliverer of his country." A BOSTON EDITOR, deSiTOll3 Of paying a compli• -ment to a minister Who lateely officiated in one of the fashionable chapels, said of his prayers that they. were the best ever addressed to a

Boston audience. A SCHOOL of geotare has been formed. We presume the main pur-pose Tien is to make it possible for married people to settle their little differences wiikout disturbing the entire neigh-

bourhood. A JUDGR hats decided thst a man is in duty bound to tell his wife where he spends his evenings when he is away from house. This decision is all right to a certain extent, but suppose the man doesn't know! A NAT URALIST has discovered that crows hold a solemn court at which otierillers are tried—a sort of crow bar. It is said thafno bird is now tried without caws, and that a true bill is indispensable

in every case. THE discovery has been made that the world does not revolve with the same momentum it did a thousand years ago' but it still swings rouna fast enough to satisfy the man with a heavy bill coming due. A METHODL.4T in America bragging how well he had instructed some Indians in. religion, called up one of them, and after some questions, asked him if he had not found great comfort last Sunday after receiving the sacrament. "Ay, master,' replied the savage; "but I wish it had been brandy." COLERIDGE has a very striking metaphor, the touching emphasis of which ha doubtless felt him- self :—" Experience is like the stern light of a ship only illuminating the track that is left behind.' , Could his own path have been retraced, under the ' light of his sad experience, how different, we may well believe, would kayo been the remembrance it left !—Ecce EpivortP. THE Scotch phrase "Take tent is tak' heed." This being used onCe by a Scotch physician to an English lady who was his patient occasioned a mistake which had nearly proved fatal. The physician repeated to her, Madam, tak' tent" Unfortunately the lady understood him that she wa.2 to drink tent wine regularly after her meals, jt al she suffered materially from following literally ‘is supposed preseription. " ARTHUR. I fear, ah ! I fear—you have ceased to love me !" "Why, Emma, whatever makes you think so?" "Well, you see, Arthur, it used to take you so long to button my gloves, and now —you do it so quickly !" ONE of Charles Lamb's friends visiting him, with his wife and children, happened in the course of conversation to repeat the old saying, "One fool makes many." "Ay, indeed," said Lamb merrily, pointing to the children, "you have a fine family." Wllv, Harry," said a lady to a small boy who as crying in the street, "what's the matter?" "Mothls's whipped me," groaned the boy. " What"lor ?" " Cause I fell in the river and got wet." "Well, don't you think you deserved it ? " "so,• I don't. I came Tarty near gettin' drowned, and if I had then wouldn't s.he a cried her eyes out! and. just because I didn't, an' I come home a little wet, she gives me a whippin'. Next time I'll get drowned, and teach her how to treat a fellow— boo-boo !"

PUGSBY (conelnding story)—" Thus was I saved by mere presence of mind: Bolgertop (gloomily) Great thing— presence of mind. I might have been a rich man to-day if my presence of mind had not failed me one time. Pugsby—" Indeed When was that?" Bolgertop—" You remember my .uncle George—rich old duller ? Well, sir, I was with him one day when he was taken with a fit. I was so frightened that I lost my presence of mind and called in a doctor, and uncle George is living yet." - A SHERIFF-Mr/CFR had a notice to warn out an old watchmaker whom he did not know had died some days previous. While proceeding to the -watchmaker's house he was accosted by a young girl—" Fat's this ye're on the day, William?" Nae very muckle ; I'm jist gaze to summon cot Tay old acquaintance, Mr. B—." "Weel, yell no need; he's summoned oot already." "Fa in a' the earth cud a summoned him cot fan I ha.'e the principal copy ? " " Death, William.' After ,giving his head a scratch, he with a. sigh replied —" Aweel, awed, he's done me 00G o' ninepence." "You lived with the Huppersets a while, didn't you, Sarah?" " Oln yes, mum; I was with 'ern about a year." "They are quite a respectable family, I've heard." "'Deed they was, mum. They're dreadful respectable; they ate so. 'Deed, mum, they was the moat respectable set I ever _lived with, and it kep' me on the go constant." " You don't say see? "'Deed I do. You see, mum, they was too respectable to do a hand's turn, euad took an awful sight af 'waiting on."----C'hica-go .Ledger. AN old Methodist minister, on account of long acquaintance, was disposed to spend a great aeal of his time in the office of the publishing firm of the Harpers of New York. One day he said—" Brother Harper, I never could understand what your duties are here. I know that brother John is the cashier, -that brother Wesley is the correspondent, and -brother Fleteher is the editor; but I never could learn what -were the duties of brother James." "My duties," replied Mr. Harper, "are the hard- est of them all. My business is to entertain the bores." THE celebratal Lady Waflace, when a very young girl, was—'romping with some other little misses near a mill-dam, and was often very incau- tiously approachiug the brink of the water, when Lady Maxwell, her mother, called out to her, "For God's sake, girl, be more cautious, or you will most certainly tumble into the water. and be drowned." " be dammed if I do, mernma," • replied the young pimster 'Oh, child," remarked -the mother, "that wit of yours will one day prove your ruin." "I'm sure, then, it won't be mother- - wit," retorted the little minx. WILL BE RETIRED Ehnev. How innocently unfortunate is the utter frankness of childhood. Young Orotund Delsarte, the dramatic reader, was taking tea, on invitation with the family, and in the evening favoured the guests with a few of his most startling recitations. He was approached by 'the midget of the family, a fairy in looks, but with -an early development of speech. "Now. I know you talk so loud when you speak pieces," she id to him. " And why. my dear ?" with a little patronising stroke of the golden hair. ' 'Cause you-re a Bellowcutionist ;ma said so.' That child • will be put to bed early after this. DIGBY met a friend who is terribly eiven to fib- bing, and accosted him -thus :—" Been to church to-day, Jones ? " "No," was the quick response ; "I've been on the bed neaely all (lay." "Just as I expected," chimed in Digby ; "you are lways One of the neatest retorts ever made was a brief response given by a young lady to a young fellow who offered her, with some hesitation, his seat in the tram-car. She got in with an eider companion; the car was crowde-d, and two young men sat near. One gave his seat at once to the elder lady ; the other kept his place. His friend asked him—dis- guising ft, however, -in German—why he did not give his place to the :young lady, "Because she is not pretty enough." But after a little reflection he rose and surrendered his seat. The lady took it, and thanked him—in German: Never was an ex- inguisher more effectually dropped upon imperti- nent youth. " Do you think, counsellor, that this action viel lie?" said the Judge to the lawyer for the plaintiff in a dubious case. Yes, your honour," responded the lawyer, "if all the witnesses will lie too."

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DtAß.Rsa.' NELLIE,

I expect you will agree with me that it is rather too early to talk of spring costumes ere the frosts have left us; yet I would call your attention to the fact that skirts promise to be wondprfully full, and in ordering any new costumes at this season this should be considered. Some of our largest firms are now showing dress cloths of enormous width, which allow the entire skirt to be out in one—that is to say, it is fashioned from an Immense round, with a hole cut in the centre for the waist. This, of course, gives the fashionable fulness round the feet, while the hips are fitted to perfection, without line or seam of any description. Gauze and ball gowns cut in this manner are remarkably successful, as thin materials naturally lend themselves more easily to such an arrange- ment.

For evening wear, few inexpensive fabrics are prettier than crepon, which is quite elabocate, and yet may be carried out very economically. Salmon pink, with velvet of a vivid ruby tint, known as "Solferino," would be charming for a dark-haired wearer, or peachy heliotrope with petunia for a blonde. The edge of the flounces has a fancy galon or narrow gimp laid on, and they are gathered in lhtle clusters at intervals of seven to nine inches, and have a more dressy effect than when gathered all round.

Hair dressing has been attracting considerable attention Utterly, and amongst some very pretty WhinOs is the chignon " Cadogant" which falls on the nape of the neck. This is very becom- Ingto some heads, while the Greek coil suit others; he smartest is the "New Elongated Twist," 4.1 .11 shows just a trifle above the- fringe, and height to the wearer. There is an endless of fringes to chose from the newest being • P.. &dated bandeau, the hair slightly frizzed, aid falling low on the forehead in front. The liaifrisable fringe defies all weathers, and will be brand to be most useful to ladies who take much outdoor exercise, either in town or in the country.

A new Paris jacket is in nut-brown beige, double breasted, and enhanced with a top collar in black •• are silk and large embossed buttons. It has a •, • • collar and bib, with wristlets in either velvet kan, and a hat in black velvet, with brim smartly turned up under rosette bows In ribbon matching the pleated aigrettea.

A pretty model, which will, I fancy, command many admirers, and will be found admirably suited to all requirements is made in accordion. pleated net, gauza, crepe, or chiffon, in black or Dolour. The stripes, arranged perpendicularly on the skirt, are of satin ribbon in a darker shade than the material of the skirt itself. The bodice and sleeves are of silk or satin the same shade as the skirt, "banded and boned" with same coloured ribbons. The material of the skirt is repeated on the bodice by accordion-pleated revers and a cunningly-devised vest of the same. A broad band and large double bow finish the waist, while an aigrette and lace butterfly are worn in the hair. To wash silk, cashmere, fine woollen goods, delicate plaids, and so on, use tepid water and some good white soap; courrcn soap will destroy the colouring. Rub it on all spots and soiled places, then rub carefully letween the hands, rinse in clean tepid water, and squeeze out the water as you would from a sponge. Then pin each piece smoothly and carefully on to a clean white sheet, which is affixed t(4 a wall, and don't forget to 'stretch it evenly while pinning. It is`best always to unpick the article to be washed, so that you can pin down each piece without a wrinkle. If you are careful and painstaking, your goods will look like new.
Yours very lovingly, JENNIE.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 24, 1894. THE DOUBLE LIFE;

A youth in Newton, Kansas,who took a plain girl to a dance, had to pay the other boys twenty-five cents each to dance with her. This is chivalry in Mary Ellen Lease's State! A lady writer says that anyone who goes about Lon- don at all cannot fail to notice how much on the increase is the use of both powder and paint. A clear, natural complexion is becoming a rarity even with quite young girls. There is a custom among the daughters of the House of Hapsburg, whose bridal trains, instead of finishing an honourable career in the ballroom, are bestowed after the ceremony on the church whose sacred floor they have swept. Only the other day, during the centenary cele- bration at Rennweg, the altar floor was covered with a sheen of satin and silver,mellowed by the breath of age, that had once formed part of Marie Antoinette's wed- ding garment. Mrs. Langtry is an inveterate gambler, but Mao is an exceedingly wise one. She always leaves off when she has made a good coup, and she never continues to play at Monte Carlo if she finds she is losing. There is, says the " Princess." great excitement at tho tables when she enters the Casino there, for in the first place she dresses exquisitely, and commands immediate attention on this account alone, but she is also very lucky, and there is always a rush to follow her lead. This season she has been -wearing the plainest gowns in the south, but they have been beautiful in their simplicity, and have quite eclipsed the most elaborate Parisian confections seen during the Carnival time.
Children's Teeth.

For real health and comfort it is as well te have sound teeth as to have sound lungs or sound brain. Mr. Deni- son Pedley, dental surgeol to the Evelina Hospital for Sick Children, has recently undertaken a dental exa- mination of the children in three of the principal metro- politan Poor Law Schools. The number of the children examined amounted te 3,145, and the number of separ- ate teeth to 70,000. The statistics, therefore, cover a very considerable area of observation. It was found that, of the whole 3,145 children oxantined,only 707 had quite sound teeth. That is to say, rather less than one in every five of that particular class were blessed with teeth that were healthy. The point of greatest practical importance is that a great many teeth go wrong, and inflict permanent injury as well as disfigurement upon children, which might easily be prevented by frequent inspect 'sus of the mouth. For example, in 110 children examined at the age of four, there were found no fewer than 290 teeth which required filling or extracting. But many people imagine that the teeth of children so young being their .first teeth, require no attention of any kind. The:mistake is most serious, and may lead to a life-long injury, In 340 children, examined at the age of nine, there were found the extraordinary number of 1,143 un- sound teeth—more than three in the mouth of every child exambied. As many as 833 of these were found capable of cure by filling, while no more than 310 re- quired extraction, of which eight only were permanent teeth. These are but a sample of Mr. Denison Pedley's facts. But they are most instructive. There are reasons for believing that the teeth of the class of children exa- mined are rather above than below the average for all classes. Ills said, indeed, that as we ourselves ascend in the social scale or teeth descend in quality. The ob- vious conclusion is that our children's mouths ought to be periodically inspected by competent and honest den- tists. We ought no more to expose children to risks of dyspepsia, disfigurement,and other injurious consequen- ces of bad teeth than to bad drainage, or to a climate of consumption. —Hospital.

Or., THE HAMPTON MYSTERY.

respect for my wishes? Think of yourself. What would your-loved 'society' say of you if it knew that you are a mystery to your own father? I have strange suspicions, Beatrice—" " S'uspicions ! and of me ?" cried the Lady Bea- trice, in a startled tone, an angry flush illumining her cheeks, aud she looked at the earl with a won-

dering, half-frightened gaze. "I like not the word 'suspicion' coupled with the name of Beatrice Hampton," responded her father, with a troubled look. " Yet what other word so well conveys my meaning? I know not what other word so well conveys my meaning? I know not what to think of you, Beatrice. You are not what you seem," and the earl regarded her keenly. "When Lord Adlowe was here five years since, he told me that you were leading a double life. His words have been confirmed a hundred times since by my own observation. You do lead a double life. You are one thing and seem an- other." _

TheiLady Beatrice started, and drooped her mag- nificent head, lowering her gaze to the fire, as if she feared her soul might look from her eyes and play the traitor. " I—l do not understand you?" she murmured. "I will endeavour to explain," returned the earl gravely. "You are the nominal mistress of my household. You receive our visitors, preside at our balls and parties, and fulfill your duties to society ably and gracefully. But I have little of your companionship at home. Day after day, even- ing after evening, you mysteriously shut yourself u-p in your own apartments, seeing no one, reply- ing to no summons or message, giving no evidence of life. It is as if your chambers were your tomb. I have frequently knocked at your door without elicting a response. The last time I was attatked by the gout, I sent for you, and yet you did not come to me for hours, and did not even send to in quir after ray welfare. Whit is the explanatien of this m.y.sterlr, Beatrtce ?" The ea.rl's•daughter stood like a statue motionless and silent. "I have tried to answer the question Mr myself," said the earl, after waiting in vain for a reply. "If it were possible for you to leave the house so continually without my knowledge, I should believe that half your time was spent away from home. I have remarked that these seclusions do, not occur at our country-seat. Does society make too great a draft upon your strength? or do you spend these missing hours-in opium-eater's dreams? I. again ask you Beatrice, what is the meaning of these seasons of dumbness and silence ?" • _

The Lady Beatrice lifted her head, turning her face to the light. Her countenance was of marble whiteness, save that in her cheeks burned restlessly a scarld glow. Her splendid eyes were like glew- ing sun!. Her manner betrayed an intense sup- pressed agitation_ and inward excitement, showing that her whole nature was in commotion.

"I have no explanations to give, father," she said a tremor of passion underlying her cold tones. "Think what you will—suspect as you may—l have nothing to say. Believe me an opium-eater, a hasheeeh dreamer, anything that may seem pro- bable. But do not jot...et that lam your daughter, as proud ad,yourself. I believe that I have within me the pride of all the Hamptons. I know I would rather die than sully the grand old name I bear. Let that suffice 1" The Lady Beatrice did indeed seem at that moment the incarnation of family pride. She stood erect in her imperial beauty, like one without a trace of weakness in heart or soul. Her father looked on her and sighed. Whether he would have pressed the subject further, and tried other means of gaining his daughter's confidence, did not appear, for at that moment the heavy c-urtains were again lifted, and Ormond, Lord Adlowe, entered the apart- ment. There was a peculiar gleam in his eyes, ard a singular smile about his mouth, faintly percept- ible under his moustache, showing that he had been a listener to most of the conversation between the father and daughter, but the gleam and the smile faded as he came forward into the light, and before either had been noticed. Lord Adlowe was in the prime of manhood. He was considered handsome, and years of foreign travel, with strange adventures in far-off lands, had contributed a halo of romance to his character, making him in the eyes of his fashionable world a hero of the Lara and Corsair school. His origin- ally fair complexion had been darkened by exposure to wind and sun. His hair was light in hue, and his eyes were pale in colour, keen, cold, and cruel in expression. They were small, shaped like the eyes of a Chinaman, and had in them at times a wicked light that proved their owner to possess a scheming soul and unlicensed evil passions.

Such was Lord Adlowe, the suitor of the Lady Beatrice Hampton. That he loved her devotedly his weary years of waiting proved. His regard for her was a strong, wild passion, that had never despaired 'of fulfilment. He had returned to Eng- land, impoverished in purse, hampered by debts, worn out by dissipation, with the fixed resolve of urging to a happy consummation his chins upon the hand of the Lady Beatrice. At sight of her, so radiant in her beauty, so elegant in her costume, the love he had borne her during nearly a score of years received such an imnetous as to become the one crowning passion of his life. His face flashed with eagerness, and he came forward rapidly, extending both his

hands. Lord Hampton, surprised and delighted, sprang up to greet him. The Lady Beatrice permitted her returned suitor to clasp her cold, jewelled hands, greeting him politely, Courteously, oven kindly, her manner warming under his manifestations of extreme de- light. She welcomed him home to England and to his friends in appropriate terms, and colored slightly under his gaze of eager admiration. The earl, encouraged by her gracious manner, began to hope that his conlrersation had had a desired effect, and that his daughter might be per- suaded to gratify his dearest hopes. He Welcomed his guest warmly, as a father might have done, clasping his hand so heartily that he he almost winced under the strong pressure. "You must excuse my abrupt, unannounced en- trance," said Lord Adlowe, smiling when thegroet- ings were concluded, and he had followed the example of the Lady Beatrice, and taken possession of a chair. "I told the porter,. who knew me at once, that I would announce myself, as I used to ' do. I wanted to surprise you both, and I Batter myself that I was successful. Hampton House has always been a second home to me. The place is unchanged. I hope I may say to the contrary of her who makes Hampton House an Eden.'' He looked earnestly at his lovely hostess, whose manner had resumed its usual hauteur and reserve. "I never change, Lord Adlowe," she replied significantly, holding before her face an embroid- ered hand-screen, as much to avert her suitor's regard as to avoid the heat of the fire. "I have always been your friend and well-wisher. lam still the same." "Nothing more 1" whispered the guest, in a low and eager tone. The increasing coldness of the lady's manner was sufficient answer. Nothing daunted by this reception of his lover- like advances, Lord Adlowe exerted himself to please. In this he was eminently successful so far as his host wa,s concerned, and even the Lady Bea- trice unbent slightly as she became interested in his remarks. His lordship had changed somewhat during his long absence, his manners had acquired a polish and suavity naturally foreign to them, many of his former prominent •traits seemed subdued, and his hostess began to believe that she should find him an interesting study. In the midst of her musings and speculations dinner was announced. The Lady Beatrice took the arm of the guest, and the three descended to the dining-room, a handsome apartment, brilliant with lights and fire and flowers. The repast was seasoned with witty remarks from Lord Adlowe, who was anxious to make a favourable impression upon his hostess. The lady listened, smiled, and replied, but it was as if a statue were talking and smiling. There was no heart in her words or her mirth. The dinner over, the guest escorted the Lady Beatrice to the door, and then returned to his wine and the companionship of the earl, spending half an hour with him. "The Lady Beatrice is more beautiful than ever !" he finally sighed. "And she is scarcely less cold than when she drove me from her !" "Do not despair, my boy," responded the earl, "I don't pretend to understand Beatrice, but there is no ice that the sun cannot melt. I believe she will yet reward your long and unwaver- ing devotion—" "I know she will !" said Lord Adlowe, with a strange smile, and with a strange light leaping to his eyes. " I can find my way to her heart at last, my lord. In less than six months I shall he your son-in-law. I will so up to the Lady Beatrice and endeavour to win her favour, while you are occu- pied with your wine and cigars." He excused himself gracefully, and hastened back to the drawing-room. The Lady Beatrice sat Oefose the fire alone. She looked up at his entra?l".

div.head: Orange Marmalade.
div.p: Orange Marmalade.

Choose the largest Seville oranges, as they usually con- tain the greatest quantity of juice, and choose them with clean skins, as the skins form the largest part of the marmalade. Weigh the oranges, and weigh also an equal quantity of loaf sugar. Peel the oranges, divid- ing the peel into quarters, and put them into a preserv- ing pan ; cover them well with water and set them on the fire to boil. In the meantime prepare your oranges; divide them into gores, then scrape with a teaspoon all the pulp from the white skin; or, instead of peeling the oranges, cut a hole in the orange and scoop out the pulp ; remove carefully all the pips, of which there are innumerable small ones in a Seville orange, which will escape observation unless they are very minutely ex- amined. Have a large basin near you with some cold water in it to throw the pips into—a pint is sufficient for a dozen oranges. A. great deal of glutinous matter adheres to them which, when strained through a sieve, should be boiled with the other parts. When the peels have boiled until they are sufficiently tender to admit a fork being stuck into them, strain them ; some of which may be boiled with the other parts ; scrape clean, all the pith, or inside, from them ; lay them in folds, and cut them into slices of about an inch long. Clarify your sugar, then throw your peels and pulp into it, stir it well, and let it boil about half an hour. If the sugar is broken into small pieces, and boiled with the fruit, it will answer the purpose of clarifying, but it'must be well skimmed when it boils. Marmalade should be made at the end of Mardi or ,the beginning of April, as Seville oranges are then at their beet.

div.head: DO ACTRESSES PROVIDE THEIR OWN
div.p: DO ACTRESSES PROVIDE THEIR OWN
PRESENTS?

A representative of " Cassell's Saturday Journal" recently bad a conversation with a male member of the dramatic profession on theatrical things in general, and the art of self-pufling in particular. "Many of the bouquets handed to actresses are genuine marks of pleasure and approval, I suppose ?" "Yes, and some are not," replied the actor candidly. " You don't surely mean that the lady herself "and I stopped short, scarcely daring to give utterance to the thought. But the actor went on—" Yes some ladies (it actually provide their own floral tributes, and some have been known to make the same bouquet—slightly altered—do double duty in one night." "And what is the idea ?" "Simply to get themaelves talked about and written about. Some provincial papers often refer to this kind '3 f thing, and—it's very significant this—these bouquets are generally knocking about the night the critics are present." "Do you think that reporters are ever bribed into noticing these occurrences in their critiques ?" " Well," returned the actor, shrugging his shoulders, " if a lady is capable of the one she is surely , capable of attempting the other." " And what about the presents of jewellery that are sometimes made to actresses ?" "It is a very discreditable practice, I know, and I'm glad to think not often carried on ; but still it does occasionally happen that a lady provides her own presents, and I have known the same article to be presented twice in the same evening. Satires and burlesques have been written anent the practice, so you may be sure the evil is existent. You read sometimes of organised applause : this, let me say, seldom takes place outside fiction. You will see that ladies are the , worst offenders in thie matter of stage puffery; perhaps we actors are only less sinners because we lack the opportunities. Taking the will for the deed, perhaps we are quite as guilty."

div.head: WONDERS OF ELECTRICITY.
div.p: THE WONDERS OF ELECTRICITY.
SIGNALIANG TO MARS.

Mr. W. H. Preece, engineer to the Telegraphic De- partment of the Pest Office, read a paper on Wednesday night before the Society of Arts in London on " Electri- cal Signalling Without Wires." After giving the results of his own experiments in this mode of signalling off the west coast for distances of three and five miles, he said there were remarkable possibilities of signalling througn space by means of eleatric waves, and that if any of the planets wero populated with beings like ourselves, hav- ing the gift of language and the knowledge to adapt the great forces of nature to their wants, it would be pos- sible for us to communicate by telephone with the people el Mars.

div.p: By the Author of " DAR KW001)."

CHAPTER 1. Had she lived Eefore the siege of Troy, Helen, whose beauty summoned Greece to arms, And drew a thousand ships to Tenedos, Had not been named in Homer's Iliad; Her name had been in every lino he wrote. MARLOWE. The Lady Beatrice Hampton, only child of the Earl of Hampton, had left behind her her youth and her early womanhood, and was still unmarried. She had beano lack of ardent suitors, for she had inherited from her mother an immense fortune, and was dowered by Nature with a rare and extreme beauty. She was witty and accomplished, a reign- ing belle, and a leader in society. Her fashionable friends were puzzled at her steady adherence to eetibacy, and no one was more puzzled than her father, whose greatest desire was to see her happily married. It was an unsolvable problem to the ear'., that his daughter should persist in refusing the most eligible oilers, and he had at last come to regard her a:3 a living mystery, impossible of com- prehension. Society at large shared this feeling in lesser degree, and the Lady Beatrice Hampton was looked upon, even by her admirers, as a beautiful mystery, a delightful puzzle, a marble-hearted and incomprehensible Sphynx. One March evening, in the drawing-room of his bOWII house, Lord Hampton sat think ng of his daughter. The night without was wild and stormy. The whale swept, through the streets of London, strong and fierce and chilling. The rain fell drear- ily and ceaselessly upon the pavements. The pleaeant room presented a strong contrast to the gloom without. A sea coal fire flamed in the pol- ished grate, emitting great tongues of 'dame, and. a soft, delicious heat, akin to that of summer. The great chandelier, resplendent with glowing globes, flooded the room with light. Flowers, fresh from the greenhouse, with the moisture yet upon their bright petals, wore crowded with reckless profusion into vases, whose delicate sculpture would have fired an artist's heart with envy. The carpet was like a green summer field studded with wild blos- soms. The chairs and celiac& would have tempted the most luxurious Sybarite to their embrace. The pictures and statuettes were like parts of a splendid

:imam. The heavy, warm-hued curtains -fell in sweeping folds to the floor, shutting out the gloom, the darkness, and the tempest, and shutting in the light, and warmth, and fragrance. The earl was tall and stately, with becoming portliness of figure, and possessed eyes as keen as they had been in their early life, a complexion of unusual ruddiness and fairness, hair and whiskers of an iron-grey hue and noble, manly sternness. He had almost reached the boundary line of three score years and ten, but he exhibited as yet none of the feebleness of age. His mind still retained its full vigour, and his manners were those of the courtly old-school gentleman. His thoughts were evidently anxious and troubled. Heroused himself impatiently at last, andstretched out his hand toward the bell-pull. At that moment the curtains. dividing the apartment from a second drawing-room were lifted, and the lady Beatrice entered his presence. " You sent for me, father ? " she inquired, ap- proaching him with a graceful movement, as if she floated rather than walked. "You desired to see use?" "I did, Beatrice," responded his lordship, with a seriousness that was almost stern. "Be seated. I have something of importance to say to you." The Lady Beatrice, a faint shadow crossing her brow, declined the proffered seat by a gesture, and stood leaning against the marble mantel-piece in an expectant attitude. She was a superbly beautiful woman. At least four and thirty years of age, she looked scarcely five and twenty. Large and grand in her propor- tions, her statuesque figure seemed the incarnation of the dream of a sculptor. Her face was the ideal face of a Cleopatra, splendid, glowing, perfect. Her hair was gloomy as a starless night, and luxuriantly plentiful, falling back from her pale, cold brows like an encompassing cloud. Mag- niiieent in persom, commanding in mind, her man- , ners were as fascinating and alluring as those of fabled sirens and enchantresses; and yet it was said that her heart was of ice. She was attiresl in a crimson velvet robe, which trailed after her in a ruddy tide. Her corsage was high on the shoulders, and cut square across the bust, revealing a neck and throat as white as milk. Jewels gleamed in the heavy necklace, on the bared arms, and Ui the gloomy puffs of hair. Lord Hampton looked at her with a father's pride, yet with a strangely yearning expression. This being, so cold to others, was equally cold to him. He wondered if she experienced any gentle, tender, womanly emotions ; and while he wondered the Lady Beatrice broke the silence. " You have news from your friend, Lord Adlowe, have you not?" she asked, carelessly. " Yes ; his lordship has returned to England," replied the earl. " I received a line from him this morning, informing me that he arrived in town last evening. I called upon him at once at his hotel, and invited him to dine with us to-day. He is all impatience to see you. It is of Lord Adlowe that I am about to speak to you, Beatrice." The Lady Beatrice bowed her head gravely with- out speaking. Encouraged by her attentiveness, the earl resumed: "Lord Adlowe comes back to us, after his five years' journeying in the East, more than ever your slave, Beatrice. He is tired of wandering, and desires to settle down into his proper place in society. He hopes that you will look favourably upon his suit. For my sake, receive him kindly, Beatrice." "I trust that my manner never lacks courtesy towards my father's guests," said the Lady Beatrice quietly. "But, Beatrice, I demand something more than courtesy towards Lord Adlowe. He has been for eight years your constant suitors—your faithful lover. He has never once flegged in his devotion to you. It was you who made him an exile and a wanderer. He has kept himself single, waiting patiently, hopefully, never reproaching you for your coldness, never forcing his attentions upon you." "Because he never dared to ! " interposed the Lady Beatrice, with an icy smile, "I do not like Ormond Adlowe, father. He is false and had at heart, his years of devotion notwithstanding. He has returned to England to renew his periodical Pcreeeut'ons of ire He is tired of roving, I sup- pe6e, and his coffers need replenishing. 4ef all my suitors I like him least. 1 must repast what I have said so many times to you and to him—l shall never marry." " and why not? demanded the earl, impatient- ly. " Have you realized that the time is slipping away, and that you are advancing in :'cars? How long will it be before you find grey threads in your hair, and be pushed aside in society by younger, fresher rivals? I shall soon die, and you will be left alone, the last of Your race, unloved and un- cared for, to drag out a miserable and solitary existence. I long to see you mistress of your own household, a happy wife, the mother of litale cling- ing children. Can it be, Beatrice, that you are still mourning for that misguided Geoffrey Trevel- yan—the unworthy scion of e noble house, the niidnight robber of his uncle—" " Stop ! " said the Lady Beatrice, huskily, a swift flush overspreadi»g her features. "I do not care about kearieg Geoffrey Trevelyan's name. They say he is dead. Let us bury his faults with him." " Yes, he is dead," said the earl, thoughtfully. " Ic died many years ago in a foreign land-- pool-n:4)ll°w ! After all, be was but a boy, Beatrice, and his untimely fate often saddens me. He had in him the stuff.' for a noble and honourable man, but was warped by harshness and evil associates. Had Lord Trevelyan, his uncle, whose heir he was, hated him less, or pursued him less vindictively for his crime, Geoffrey might have been living, happy and honoured, to-day. I don't blame you for grieving for him, for you were his betrothed wife. But as he was unworthy and is dead, your grief should be toned down to a regret for Ins weakness and folly. All men are not like him. You were but a mere child when he disappeared. Surely you do not cherish a love for his memory still." "I am not romantic, father," said the Lady Bea- trice, dryly. "You say that all men are not like him, meaning that Lord Adlowe is without Geof- frey's weaknesses and faults. Lord Adlowe Is no weak, but his is not the strength I like. The truth is, I cling to my freedom, father. lam not capable of love. I like to rule in society. I like to be admired and worshipped from afar, but I have no heart for my admirers to win. You have there the truth in a nutshell. I have no heart." She spoke wearily, and a strange sadness brooded in her midnight eyes. "Why must you disappoint the hopes I have so long cherished of claiming Lord Adlowe as my son, Beatrice? " asked her father, bitterly. "He is the most constant of your suitors, and I esteem him above all other mess.. Have votano love for rat, nco

div.p: greeting him with a smile. Drawiriq on easy-chair as near to her as he dared, Lord Adrowe bent upon her a gaze of respectful admiration—of adoring love.

The Lady Beatrice moved uneasily under his gaze, it seeming to her to be scrutinizing as well as admiring. She fancied he was trying to read her soul, and she took up the small hand-screen she had before held, saying), with an appearance of polite interest :

"I understood my father to say, Lord Adlowe, that you are stopping at an hotel. Is not your uncle Lord Trevelyan, in town ?" "No, he is at Trevelyan Park," was the response. "I shall run down to see him to-morrow. I bear, Lady Beatrice, that my uncle is more miserly than ever. The townhouse is let, and he confines him- self closely to the Park, leading there a savage and morose existence."
"I have heard the same," replied the Lady Bea- trice. "Lord Trevelyan has changed greatly during the past ten or fifteen years. You will visit him to-morrow ? "

"Yes. My uncle is very exacting, and would hardly forgive me if heknew that I had visited even here before coming to him. People would talk, too, if I were not attentive to him,"—and Lord Adlowe smiled—" for at 113 death he will leave me one of the rithest men in the kingdom. You know that my claims upon him are second only to those of Geoffrey Trevelyan, my cousin. Had Geoffrey lived, I should have little to look forward to, my father having left me only debts to support my title."

"Lord Trevelyan is fonder of you than he was of your cousin, is he not ? " asked the Lady Beatrice, staring into the fire. "He professes to be," was the reply. "I hope he is, for he hated poor Geoffrey as if he had been a deadly enemy. Geoffrey had no tack to manage him. Poor fellow! Geoffrey was not fitted to cope with the world! If he had lived, he would have covered his name with disgrace—" "Not so ! " interrupted the Lady Beatrice, a hot flush glowing in her cheeks, and an angry light shining in her eyes. "Geoffrey was a wild, pas- sionate, generous boy, with great faults, perhaps, but also with great virtues—"

"Do you number his assault upon and robbery of his uncle among the former or the latter?" ques- tioned Lord Adlowe, with ironical emphasis. "If Geoffrey were alive," he added, impressively, "my uncle would leave no effoit untried to bring him to punishment. Lord Trevelyan is very vindictive in his disposition." "He might forgive and forget, since he believes Geoffrey dead," said the Lady Beatrice in a low tone and with averted face. "It is seventeen years since we heard that Geof- frey was dead, is it not ? " asked Lord Aidlowe, as if musingly, but with the keenest and most furtive of glances directed toward his hostess. "We re- ceived a Brazilian paper—l think it was Brazilian; at any rate it was South American—with a notice of his death in its columns. We also received a letter from some Spaniard or Portuguese, stating that Geoffrey had died at his house, and had begged him with his last breath to write tidings of his fate. If I remember rightly, there was included in the letter a certificate of burial. Upon these data we believed Geoffrey to be dead." •‘ The evidence was conclusive enough, I should think," said Lady Beatrice, in a cold, hard, metallic voice.

"Of course it was conclusive," replied Lord Ad- 'owe. "But I have doubts sometimes of its truth. lam sceptical by nature, I believe. What if the whole story of the death were an imposture? Geof- frey knew that our uncle hated him enough to pur- sue him over the whole earth. He would not have dared return to England, for fear of imprisonment and disgrace. England is not large enough to hold him and my uncle at the same time.. Is it not prob- able that Gepffrey should have forged the proofs of his death, changed his name, and settled down in a distant country to await news of my uncle's death! Lord Trevelyan dead, Geoffrey can walk the earth again without fear, a rich and titled man." "A rather fanciful explanation, I think," said the Lady Beatrice, in a voice firmer than usual. "It lacks only one element, in my opinion—that of plausibility. If it were true and Geoffrey were to return, you would not be pleased, I suppose." Lord Adlowe's face darkened at the bare possi- bility of such an event. "Geoffrey's return would impoverish me," he said. "He is Lord Trevelyan's brother's son, and of course the nearest heir. Lord Trevelyau's only sister married Lord Adlowe, and I am the fruit of their union. If Geoffrey were to come back at my uncle's death he would inherit the Trevelyan title and fortune. But eighteen years of silence, and the proofs too,—surely he is dead I "

He uttered the last words in a tone of relief. His apprehension had been quieted by the manner of Lady Beatrice. For years he had been tormented by occasional doubts of his cousin's death, and he had finally persuaded himself that, if living, Geof- frey Trevelyan would have communicated the fact to his former betrothed. He had watched her keenly and closely, and had become convinced that she believed Geoffrey dead. The next words of the Lady Beatrice confirmed his opinion. "The Spaniard wrote that Geoffrey died of a fever," she said, quietly. He was worn out by his long sea voyage and his anxieties. He ventur- ed out imprudently the very day after landing, exposing himself to the noon day sun. We know that Geoffrey went to South America, for he wrote me a long letter within an hour of his going ashore. He wrote to his uncle by the same post, but Lord Trevelyan declared to to me that he had never re- ceived the letter. Some one Must have intercepted it."

Lord Adlowe flushed guiltily. I have always thought that Geoflrey had some enemy who incited his uncle against him," pursued the Lady Beatrice. "When Geoffrey was a lad his uncle loved him. He grew to hate him as he grew older, but it must have been because some envious person spoke falsely against poor Geoffrey, making his faults into crimes, and inducing Lord Trevelyan to believe that the boy desired his death."
Lord Adlowe moved uneasily in his chair.

"We have chosen an unpleasant subject to con- verse upon, Lady Beatrice," he said. "Let us dis- miss it from our thoughts. Geoffrey is dead. Your love for him has worn away into quiet regret. I have comeback to England to take my place among your admirers, to be your suitor. I cannot live without you, Beatrice," and his voice became full and passionate. " I have loved you for years. Have pity upon me, and become my wife. No, do not answer me yet, Beatrice. lon would refnse me now as you have done before. Give me a chance to prove my love. I will wait weeks, months—" " My answer then would be the same as now, Lord Adlowe, and is now what it was five years since. I cannot marry you." "1 refuse to accept that answer !" declared Lord Adlowe, with fierce emphasis. " Your father approves my suit. You shall yet look kindly upon me—yet promise to become my wife 1" The Lady Beatrice looked at him haughtily, her eyes flashing with anger at his persistence in offer- ing his unwelcome love. She met a gaze, strong, fierce, and passionate. She saw that her suitor's face was dark with unpleasant meaning—that he was thoroughly in earnest—that he would not take a negative answer. She comprehended that to reject him now, as she was tempted to do, would be to make him her inveterate implacable enemy. She felt vaguely that he had it in his power to work her woe. An involuntary shudder convulsed her frame, and she moved from him almost uncon- sciously, as if he had been an embodied pestilence. "You will take time for your decision ? " he asked, in soft, persuasive accents, and suddenly changing his manner—with a smile which seemed like a ray of light through intense darkness. The instinct of self-preservation was strong in the breast of Lady Beatrice. It was awakened now, she knew not Why. With a feeling of danger strong within her, she resolved to temporise with him. • "I will take time, Lord Adlowe, to consider. your oiler," she slid, her cheeks rivalling the hue of her,dress, her face pale as snow. " Since you prefer to wait, you shall have my answer some months houce—when you demand it." Lord Hampton entering at this juncture, the Lady Beatrice embraced the opportunity of escape. With emotion which both the gentlemen mistook, and which bath interpreted favourably to her suibor, she glided quietly from the room. (To be continued),

div.head: HUMOURING THE HORSE.
div.p: HUMOURING THE HORSE.

Mr. H. C. Merwin, in his" Road, Track, and Stable," says that the peculiar success of American horsp-trainters is due chiefly to the fact that they have consulted the- equine nature, and instead of subduing the horse's spirit have endeavoured to win his confidence. "Instead of breaking colts," he adds, "we 'gentle' them." He has seen a high-spirited stallion, on the fourth occasion of its being in harness, going so kindly, that the owner did not hesitate to take his child of three years with him. The case of Johnston, the famous pacer, illustrates what can be accomplished by humouring the sensitive equine disposition. "He was the most nervous horse that I ever saw," writes John Splan, his trainer and driver, " and I found that in shipping him about from one Week to another he became more nervous and irritable. If you left him alone in the stable he would tramp around. like a wild animal, and get himself in a sweat. If any- body went into the stall next to him and began to ham- mer or make anything like a loud noise he would try to climb out of the window. Whenever a stranger stepped into his stall he would give a snort and back into the farthest corner." With some difficulty Spiel' obtained the services of a quiet faithful "rubber," or groom, called Dave. Dave procured a dog as additional com- pany for Johnston, and these three remained inseparable through the period of Johnston's training. It was a. matter of course that the groom should sleep in the stall, but he never left it, day or night, having all his meals brought there. Under this treatment Johnston rapidly improved. He became less nervous, ate better, and in the event lowered the pacing record to 2.06±, a mark which has not yet been surpassed upon a regulation track. All the great trotters have had their grooms. Croldsniith Maid, like Johnston, had not only a groom— " Old Charlie,"—but a dog. For five years, Old Charlie was never absent frem her stall except for two nights. "They were a great family," says Mr. Doble, "that ord mare, Old Charlie, and the dog—apparently interested in nothing else in the world but themselves, and getting , along together as well as you could wish. When it was bedtime Charlie would lie down on his cot in one corner of the stall, his pillow being a bag containing the mare's morning feed of oats ; the Maid would enseonce herself in another corner, and somewhere else in the stall the dog would stretch liimself out. "About five o'clock in the morning the Maid would get a little restless and hungry. She knew well enough where the oats were, and would come over to where Charlie was sleeping and stick her nose under his head, and in this manner wake him and give notice that she wanted to be fed."

div.head: HOW MR. HENTY WRITES HIS BOOKS.
div.p: HOW MR. HENTY WRITES HIS BOOKS.

On a cool autumn afternoon (writes a " Chums "re- presentative) I paid a visit to Mr. Hon ty, that favourite of all book-loving boys, and found him enjoying an after- lunch pipe in his study. He was not at work, but some closely-written sheets of foolscap lay on his table. I presumed that my host had lately been performingin the penmanship line, but I was mistaken. "I don't write any of my books myself," he explained,." as I get a man to do it for me—an amanuensis. Of course," he added, with a smile. "it all comes out of my head, but he does the actual writing. I never see any of my work until it comes to me from the printer's in the shape of proof sheets. Yes, my amanuensis sits at the table, and I sit near him or lie on the sofa, and dictate the stories which 1 publish. What do I call a good day's work ? Well, say my man comes at half-past niue in the morn- ing and stays for four hours—till half past one. Wecan get through a good deal in that space of time. Then we knock off work, and perhaps my penman comes round in the evening for a couple of hours. Working morning and eveeing, I can get through a chapter—that is, about 6,500 words. I call that a good hard day's work." I agreed with Mr. Henty ; 0,500 words in one day is no joke. "Of course I don't keen that up every day," said the author " and, moreover, I do most of my work in the winter. In the summer I go in for yachting a great deal. I'm very fond of yachting, but the worst of it is, that I can rarely get away from town for any consider- able period, as lam en the staff of the" Standard." I write chiefly on military subjects, as, years ago, you know, I used to be a wer correspondent. But I don't keep strictly to army topics. I always write about the leading Dog Shows, and do one or two other things." " Then you are great on dogs ?" "Not particultzly. One needn't know much about dogs to write up a Dog Show. The judging is all done by the judges, and my work is to write articles about what the judges say. I'm very fond of animals. I have live cats and several dogs."

"So you want to know a bit about my life ?" said a grizzled old driver to one of" Chums" representatives. " Well, I've been at it now for over thirty years—that is as cleaner, fireman, and driver—and an you may say I've had a fairish spell. Do I like the life? Well, yott see, a man gets used to his own trade, and likely enough he wouldn't care for any other that he might turn his hand to, especially at ray time of life, But if a fellow wants a nice easy job, without responsibility, a job that he can go to sleep and dream over, I wouldn't advise him to have anything to do with this trade. A good many people imagine that an engine-driver has a nice easy time of it—just rushing along, every now and theh pulling a handle here and there, and having a a look at the signals ; but that's a great mistake. It isn' so much hard work that a driver has to do. His nerves are always on the strain. A mistake or a bit of carelessness over his signals may cause a big smash, and you can easily imagine what it is like in fog or a snowstorm, when you can't see a dozen yards in front of you. And in bad weather it's a comfortless job, I can tell you. Why, it was years and years before the companies would. let us have any shelter on the engines—`cabs' as they call- them—and do you know the reason? Simply because they got it into their heads that if drivers had a comfort- able shelter to get behind they would not pay attention to the signals. Of course that was all nonsense,because even if we hadn't our sense of duty to keep us up to the mark, we have enough sense to know that the driver and fireman are always the first to suffer in a smash." " Have you ever been in a accident ?" "Well, not what you'd call a big one, but, of course, I've had several little affairs. Once I had an arm broken. It happened like this : I was driving a slow passenger train,one foggy night, about as thick as ever I remember. W 6 were travelling some fifteen miles an hour. and I was leaning out on the right-hand side watching for the signals. • Well, by some carelessness or other, a goods waggon had been left with its end sticking out from the siding on to the main line. Of course we hit it, and I was thrown off the engine by the shock right on to the line, and I broke my arm and a couple of ribs too."—

The Guild of St. Matthew, which has just sent a strongly worded protest to the archbishops and bishops in connection with their votes in the House of Lords on matters affecting the welfare of the people, is a Church organisation of daily growing importance. Its council includes the Rev. Profes- sor Shuttleworth, of King's College; the Rev. Thos. Hancock, lecturer at St. Nicholas Colt Abhey,Queen Tictoria-st. ; the Rev. W. A. Morris, vicar of St. Anne's, South Lambeth ; the Rev. T. Hill, the Rev. F. L. Donaldson., the Rev. Percy Dearmer, and other London clergy. The warden is the Rev. Stewart D. Headlam. The Guild has a literature of its own and has done much to educate the clergy upon t he problems of labour and capital.

The French Government have arrested Sebastien Faure, one of the most dangerous of the" notice" group of Anarchists, whose influence for evil has been very noticeable. lie was Vaillant's friend,and. the guardian of that criminal's little daughter. Faure is an extraordinary fanatic, and has had a remarkable career. Re was born about thirty-six years ago, and is a member of a well-to-do, respect- able, and pious Catholic family. In his youth Sebastien was an ardent Jesuit—quite as fanatical in his religious opinions as he is now in his Anarc- hical doctrines. As a man possessing a brilliant, if erratic intellect and considerable education, Faure was one of the most dangerous of incendiaries. His lectures, especially in the South of France, were responsible for the delusion of hundreds of people.

It cannot be said that the " Times " of Saturday snowed particularly good taste in transferring to its leader page from the columns of an American paper the absurd story that Mr. Gladstone recently insisted on the immediate performance of an opera- tion alleged to be necessary for the preservation of his eyesight. The tale found currency through the ; agency of Mr. G. VT. Smalley, of the " New York Tribune," a gentleman whose anti-Liberal contribu- tions to the American Press have earned for him ,an unenviable notoriety across the Atlantic. I de not say that Mr,Smalley invented the tale. But when , a reputable journalist makes such serious statements he should be prepared to give his authority. The Pall Mall Gazette" precedent was not a good ,one.

That Mr. Gladstone's sight is failing is not denied. The Premier himself is painfully aware of the fact, and if, unhappily, an operation should at any time become necessary, he will, of course, be prepared to submit to it. But I learn that no such thing is thought of for the present ; and Mr. Gladstone's family are naturally indignant at the prominence given by the "leading journal to the baseless statements made in the American paper.

div.head: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
"THE POLLUTION OF THE MERSEY."

Mr. Joseph Dakin read a paper at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Debating Society heln at the Masonic-rooms,Bold-st., on Tuesday evening, on "how to prevent the pollution of the Mersey." Mr. T. J. Hulse occupied the chair. Mr.DAKIN, in opening the subject of the evening said that the state of the river was a disgrace and a menace to the health of the district. During the summer the smell arising from it was intolerable, and could be scented for more than half a mile away. It was only during the summer months that attention was forcibly drawn to this state of things. When they considered the population re- siding on the banks of the Mersey and its tributa- ries, and the number of large towns, and the innumer- able manufactories, all of which emitted their sewage, &c., into the river, they could form some idea as to the condition of the water. It was not at Warrington that pollUtion took place (although they did their share), but ; in the higher reaches of the stream. The water of a 1 tributary of the river as it passed through Macclesfield was extremely dirty. Manchester, Stockport, and the surrounding towns and villages polluted either the river or its tributaries. He was not aware that any of the townships along the banks of the Bailin had anvmeans of disposing of their sewage except by pouring it into the watercourse. But the Mersey`was not so badly poi- lilted as the Irwell which flowed into it, because the Irwell drained a more populous district then the Mer- sey. It commenced near liazslingden, and during its course it received the sewage and refuse of such towns as Bury, Bolton, Rochdale, Oldham, Manchester, and Salford, so that it was almost like an open sewer. The Mersey, after passing through Warrington was joined by Sankey Brook, and this did not contribute towards its purity. (Hear. hear.) A scheme for preventing pol- lution must be so comprehensive and so thorough in its operation as not to allow of the smallest village or manufactory carrying on the work of pollution with impunity. It was necessary that all the townships with- in the watershed of the Mersey and Irwell should com- bine to carry out a suitable scheme. But first a public opinion must becreated that such a thing was necessary. No doubt a considerable time would elapse before the public could be sufficiently aroused to take up the work with earnestness and energy, and he should consider himself amply rewarded if by spending the leisure hours of his life he could succeed in arousing the public to their duty in regard to this important question. (Applause.) He would suggest that every town and village interested should form a committee of men who had the matter at heart, to deal exclusively with the question, and out of these a number should be selected to form a central committee. It would be a powerful organisation, because it would rest on the opinion of a united people whose sons and daughters had always stood in the foremost rank of the world's great industrial army, and who on the fact of almost insuperable obsta- cles had completed one of the most colossal engineering feats of ancient or modern times. (Hear, hear.) He thought the problem of the disposal of sewage would be solved by the construction of a large sewer from Man- chester with an outfall dep3t en Cuerdley Marsh, and other sewers branching from it for the drainage of Stockport, 'Macclesfield and St. Helens, so as to. take in Sankey Brook. This scheme would be costly, but the expense would be spread ever a large area,and the benefit derived from it would fully recoup any outlay. It might be objected that there would not be sufficient fall, but this, he contsnded, could be brought about by artificial means. As to the ventilation of the sewers he would not y advise that they should be ventilated in the same man- ner as the sewers in Warrington, by means of perforated covers through which a stench was sometimes emitted, but eutzeested that a kind of chimney stack should be erected in various places, high enough to carry away the stench without its being noticeable. In conclusion, he trusted that some means would be found of making the river which passed through the town a pleasure instead of a nuisance. (Applause.) He then moved the following resolution :—"That this meeting calls .upon the local authorities to take decided action in order to protect the river and to assist as far as possible in its purification, and urges upon them the necessity of secur- ing from the Ship Canal Company immediate facilities for loading vessels, and the prompt construction of the Warrington docks." (" Oh, oh.") Councillor ARTHUR BENNETT seconded the resolution, and said that the subject was a very important one, for discussion. Warrington was itself largely responsible for the evil, and, until the pecple of the town showed some public spirit, and endeavoured to devise some remedy for it, they weuld have to suffer in that respect. They were now apparently not only suffering from the Pollution of the river but the extraction of the water from it. Under the Ship Canal Act they had power to. secure a certain minimum amount, and he thought the should take prompt steps to have what they were en- titled to. Whatever became of the Ship Canal, he thought the river should be left unimpeired. They had all been thinking during the last few years that the Ship Canal was going to make their fortunes, and that War- rington was going to be, the town of the future. At present it seemed as if they would derive very little benefit from it, unless they .took active steps in the matter. Tho first thing they ought to do was to ask for accommodation for the unloading of ships at Warring- ton. There was no such thing at the present time. It would be a small thing to ask, for Warrington had up to the present time treated the Ship Canal Company in a aecerous manner, and had done its best in a small way to help the undertaking forward at a time . when the company was undergoing considerable trouble. He thought they certainly might have facilities for the un- loading of ships in the vicinity of the town. Of course that would only be temporary, and he, at all events, would not be satisfied until they had 'docks, which he understood the Ship Canal Company were legally bound to complete within three years. If the company made the want of money the excuse for not constructing them, he thought as a last resource the Warrington people themselves should undertake the work, and he believed that instead of being a burden on the rates they would be a source of income. (Applause.) The debate was continued by Messrs. Diggle, Hulse, Horton, Robinson, Hall, and Bay. Mr. Dakin replied and the motion was passed unanimously..
