div.head: IHE EXAMINER, SATURDAI, FEBRUARY 24, 1894. TEMPERANCE MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: IHE EXAMINER, SATURDAI, FEBRUARY 24, 1894. TEMPERANCE MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.

The first of a series of four public meetings held in connection with the Warrington Temperance Federation, was held on Tuesday evening' at the Co:operative Hall, Sankey-street. There was not a very large attendatice present. The chair was ocupied by Mr. Robert Garnett, J.P., who was sup- ported by the Revs. R. A. Armstrong, (Liverpool) ; J. Yonge, W. 11. Drummond, and Messrs. D. Shilton Collin, (Liverpool); David Garnett, Wm. Roberts, (hon. sec.) ; S. B. Stringer, C. Pigot, and R. Storey. The CHAIRMAN briefly opened the proceedings by ia- tenducing the two principal Speakers. He remarked that they as temperance men were fighting a very hard battle, and they must remember how to fight it, with fair weapons. They were not fighting the brewers, the distillers and the publicans, but they did object to the drink, and it was that which they would fight. (Ap- plause.) It was to the quantity of the manufactured article which they ohjected,and it was for its diminution that they should agitate. They wanted, if possible to see it diminished in its influence over the people, not only in Warrington, but in the country in which they lived. (Applause.) Mr. SHILTON COLLEN, who was received with applause ' said he wondered that the people of Warrington were not afraid to let Liverpool people come amengst them became the town was associated with everything that was bad. Warrington had mixed itself up with all the devilry they had been fighting in Liverpool ever since he had been there; and it remained associated with all the evils of the city ; and they (the deputation) had come to Warrington that night to talk about the matter and see if they could bring them to repentance. They had not come to Warrington as sinless people themselves. There was a kind of rightecua retribution about what went on in Liverpool n relation to their town. Liverpool itself was engaged in the most wicked enterprise. They had a number of men there who shipped every week thousands arta thousands of cases of gin, rum; and beer to all parts of the world, particularly to the west coast of Africa, and these Liver- pool merchants were destroying the natives by the hun- dred and the thousand. A few weeks ago a Baptist missionary wrote him a letter in which he said that unless the Churches in England roused themselves and put a stop to the African trade in liquor in the district in which he was missionary there would be no negroes to convert in 20 sears. He (the speaker) did no see how they were to redeem Liverpool from the liquor curse whilst they allowed rich men to ravage Africa and des- troy the poor wretched people whom Lord Salisbury said ought to be treated as children, as they need not expect to be much better until theyhad put a stop to the great brewing industry. Drink was in every way a curse. The other week he was accosted by a Baptist minister who asked him if he thought he and the temperance party were justified in going about the country describ- ing drink .as poison. And his reply was : " Yes, it is God's truth." (Applause.) "Upon what authority do you make the remark" ? said the minister and he (the speaker) replied that he made it upon the authority of science and common sense. His scientific authority was no lees a person than Dr. Benjamin Richardson. (Applause.) He had commenced—as a moderate drinker —to study the question of alcohol. His researches were long and important, but they were followed by a conviction which induced him to give up tak- ing drink even moderately, and which led him to become one of their meet zealous reformers. (Applause.) Dr. Richardson's idea of drink was that it was useless as a food, injurious .as a tonic, and very very seldom useful as a medicine. There were some very few cases where alcohol was good as a medi- cine, but they were growing less every year as medical science grew. So dangerous, however, did Dr.. Richard- son consider alcohol, even as a medicine that he sug- gested it should only be obtainable at a chemist's and dileted with something to" nastify " it so as to prevent the cultivation of a taste for the poison. (Applause.) Alluding to the duties of religious bodies in respect to the question the speaker roundly condemned the churehes apathy, and lie contended that if they would only rouse themselves and face the questien as was their duty, it would be quickly settled. (Applause.) He looked upon the compromises of the Church in this matter as dis- loyalty to Jesus Christ. (Applause.) It had been said that drink killed ten persons to every one which the Church saved. (Applause.) If the Church could stand by and watch the progress of such a gruesome, such a horrible tragedy, then the Church could stand anything (Applause.) They must look outside the Church for their salvation in this direction. &Renewed applause.) Alluding to the action of the government he said the temperanee party were to blame for placing themselves in the position they occupied now. The Temperance party of England was large enough to crush any Parlia- ment, and had they fought with the zeal which was expected of them they would not now have been 'necked by a useless two thirds majority. He hoped temper- ance men were not expected by their party to agree with the government's action. He did not.; he was totally dissatisfied with it. (Applause.) A great deal lof leniency was being shown to what were termed "respectable houses," whilst it was proposed to allow the railway refreshment rooms to retain their licenses. It was a well known fact that one half the accidents on the railway was due to persons obtaining drink at the refreshment rooms. Then as " regards " respectable houses " why he did not believe in them. (Hear hear.) The Rev. R. A. ARMSTRONG, of Liverpool, who was received with applause, said to speak after Mr. Collin was not an easy task. He could not help thinking of the comments that might perhaps be made by some of those who heard him. He did not see many who looked like confirmed drunkards present. He thought those stairs approaching the room had been too steep for them. (Laughter). There might be one or two persons present who disliked excitement about social questions and he coutd imagine their .going away wondering that men would talk so extravagantly as Mr. Collin. The prevail- ing arguments, or what they called arguments, against total abstinence was that there was not very much drunkenness, and what there was, was not very bad, and it was foolish for people to excite themselves about the matter.; that the country was getting along very nicely, and that if they would only let it alone things would go on very well. That he found to be the pre- vailing opinion of some people, and of very intelligent people. People who prided themselves upon the way they studied public questions, and not being led away by fanatics. He thought they knew pretty well that as a matter of fact,the prevailing drinking habits of Society in this country were awful to contemplate. (Applause.) Who could be higher authorities on this questio n than the judges of the land. rhey told us that drink caused the major part of the crime of the country. (Ap- plause.) If this drunkenness were a ,new disease and we had an epidemic coming on us, it would alarm the whole nation. Every other matter would be put aside, to put an end to it. (Applause.) It was said that the j drink did no great harm. They laid in different coantries different vices becoming prevalent. In some countries, I opium smoking, and in others excessive tobacco smok- ing. But he had never heard of an opium smoker, or tobacco smoker who was roused to commit violence, to beat ls;s wife or to use violence to a little child, as was the case evith persons under the influence of drink. (Ap- plause.) In regard to the argument that it was better for men to rely on self control, than to bind themselves to total abstinence, the speaker said for his own part lie was a teetotaler primarily for his own safety, and neither he nor any of them- had any right to trust him- self in 'this matter. He couldn't think of any family of his acquaintance where someone or other had not suf- fered from alcoholic drink. Some people fancied that it was amongst the working classes where drinking was so much prevalent. But any mistister or doctor knew that it was pretty nearly as prevalent amongst the middle classes as amongst the lower classes. (Applause.) It was never hopeless to rescue a drunken man. They wanted to get at his sympathies, and to let him feel the humen brotherhood. (Applause.) For his own part lie be- lieved they had to fight this drink interest.. They must go at the whole system if they were to rescue their coun- try from the terrible and awful evil which threatened it. He called upon tilos° vvlio were there that night to set to work, and work for the uplifting of the people. Let them go to the rescue of the individual who needed help, and thus help in this cause of God. (Loud applause.) Mr. War. ROBERTS moved a vote of thanks to the speakers, and in doing so regretted that the room was not crowded. It was rather a reflection on .the temper- ance people of Warrington that they had not attended in large numbers to listen to the eloquent addresses which had been delivered. They had done everything they could to make the present meeting known. If this had been a comic entertainment,and the performers had blackened their faces, even if the proceedings had been in support of the temperance cause, there would pro- bably have been a large attendance. That was not creditable to the Christian people of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND seconded the metion. A good deal had been said about the small attendance, but in Warrington it appeared that good causes were not as ! heartily supported as they should be. Those who were present, however, could not have failed to thoroughly appreciate the capital speeches which had been deli- vered,and he hoped they would be taken to heart. (Ap- plause.) The CHAIRMAN put the resolution to the meeting, and it was unanimously carried. A vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, on the motion of the Rev. R. A. Armstrong, and alter it had be acknowledged the proceedings were brought to a corThlusion by Miss Roberts singing " Glory to Thee,my God, this night." THURSDAY EVENING'S MEETING. - -

There was -a —large attendance on Thursday night when the chair was occupied by Mr. J. C. Dalton (vice President of the League of the Cross), who was supported by the Rev. Father Harris (St. Ber- nard's,(Liverpool), the Rev. John Yonge, Messrs. Edward Boreland (U. K. Alliance), W. Roberts, S. 13. Stringer, and R. Storey. At the commencement of the meeting, the League of the Cross band played a selection, after which Mrs. Dalton sang" S?,enes that are brightest," in excellent btylt, and for which he was warmly applauded. The CITAIUMAN, in his opening speech, said that he

could assure them that it was with sincere regret that that he had to announce the absence of Father Sumner that night. Uncertunately he bed broken down in his work, and he had been obliged to leave the town. Nothing would have given him greater pleasure than to be among them that evening, for if the League of the Cross had a friend in Werripgton,that friend was Father Sumner. (Applause.) To their friends of the Temper- ance Federation in Warrington who held out to them the hand of friendship and the desire for further co-operation in the work of stemining the tide of intemperance that seemed to be making such terrible havoc among the people, the Leagee of the Cross extended their head heartily in return,—(applause)—and they told, them that they were fully alive to the interests at stake, and that they would do their level best to assist them to their ut- most in this work of humanity. (Applause.) It was with singular appropriateness that the League atilt) Cross--tie Catholic Total Abstinence League of tie Cress—should be invited to take part in the temperance sacniernent—(hear, • hear),—for to whom,if not to Father Theobesid Matthews was the title to be given of the apostle of temperance ? (applause)—and the spirit of Father Matthew livid in Warrington in the hearts of the faithful Irish people, and in the hearts of those who were in any way taking part in tke cause. In later times, who rendered such gigantic services to temperance as Henry Edwaideirchbishop and Cardinal Manning ? (Hear, hear.) To leave the past And come to the present, where was there a limn who had done moro for fallen humanity, than Monseignieur Father Nugent. (Applause.) They had on the plattorrn that night, a member of the Catholic priesthood, Father Elarrieewne was an able lieutenant to Father Nugeat,and when Father Nugent was away, he took his place. He (the -speaker) need not say anything to them about total abstinence, or the evils of intemperance. A man who was sober had his eyes open. He did not look through the bung hole of a beer barretThe evils of intemperance were everywhere to be seen by everyone except those who were wilfully blind. (Hear, hear.) Who was it that left his money at the public-house that shotild go to procure the necessaries of life for his wife and little ones ? The drunkard. Who was it that neglected his parents in their old age., but the drunkard? Who was it that neglected all the obligations of holy religion? The drunkard. Who was it that filled workhouses, and coals and asylums 2 The drunkard. The temperance party brought to bear upon the drink question well balanced minds. They were not enthusiasts. They did not speak in riddles. A great deal was said about moderation. He would be the first man to stand up in defence of the Irish people, for he would be false to his , own principles, but he must say that a number of that poor unfortunate people was led away by the curse of intemperance. No Irishman could be moderate in any- thing. (Laughter.) He was an enthusiast in every- thing. If he was a Home Baler, he was a Home Ruler, —a red hut one. (Laughter.) If he was a Unionist— well, they had Colonel Saunderson (laughter) who was as hot as he could be. There was no such thing as mod- eration in the Irish people, therefore moderation in that people was not practicable. Why did not the rich men come forward with their money to help on the work of temperance .? (Hear, hear.) Why had they not tem- perance places in Warrington for young men and women to go to .2 where periodicals aud ether induce- ments were provided so as to counteract the public- houses ? In conclusian, he would again say that the Catholics were always ready •to co-operate in the temperance work with other bodies. They differed in religion, and the Catholics were ever reedy to defend themselves against anyone who said anything against it, but with the question of total abstinence, the members of the League of the Cross were at one with the others, in the same spirit as Father Mattliew,when he co-operat- ed with clergymen and ministers of all denominations in temperance work. (Applause.) At the close of his speech the chairman sang " When other lips;" in an excellent manner. The Rev. Father Harris then moved the following resolution : " That this meeting rejoices to learn from the declaration of the Prime Minister and I the Chancellor of the Exchequer that the Government have determined to reintroduce the Liquor Traffic Local Control Bill early in the next Ses- sion of Parliament, and believes is to be a measure cal- culated to advance the social material and moral welfare of the nation, and it pledges itself earnestly to stipport the Government in their effort to pass the measure into law. -(Applause.) He said that it was a pleasure for him to come upon the platform to appear before people who were of no particular denomination or rather a mixed gathering. There was one time when, as a bigoted Catholic, he thought he weuld have nothinge whatever to do with parties of opposite colour to himself, but since he had became acquainted with certain friends in the temperance movement, he found that the society of non-catholic friends was doing important work. (Loud applause.) He found Catholic ideas were not the enly ideas in the world, and Catholics were accustomed some- times to have warped notions about things. New a days temperance men were respected,but in the early days of Cardinal Manning and Monseigner Nugent,told abstainers were looked upon as fanatics who, had lost their heads. This was now all changed. If it were not for the drink trafficothe churches would be filled on Sundays. It was therefore the duties of the churches to fight the drink traffic. He lived in Toxteth,a place where the veto was exercised,and publichouses were prohibited by the land- lord. What the landlord had done by his own power they wanted the people to do, audio any district where the majority wished to close the pUblie houses, those public houses should be closed. There was a bill to be brought before the House of Commons for this purpose, and there was a majority of members who would vote for it. What they wanted, was, that before the bill was passed into law, the people should become vetoists. It was no use trying to carry out anything, unless they saw the people were in earnest about it. People were beginning to see what the veto meant, and were beginning to adopt its principles. (Applause.) They talked about the number of public-houses in War- ringtop and were perhaps disgusted with them, but they had the same thing at Liverpool, where at every hand and turn they had those blessed public-houses standing. There was one thing, immorality, which was caused by drink. In Liverpool, it was simply scandalous. They had in their city gross immorality simply through this drink. The very atmosphere that they breathed in Liverpool was filled with impurity, and they could scarcely walk through the streets without being tempted. If they had net this drink they might do an immense amount of good with their people. (Applause.) 141 millions of money was spent in one year in drink. Three out of every four of the paupers were caused by it and six or seven out of every ten of the criminal class. It was time they aroused themselves to do something. Let them fight to the end, caring not what people would say of them. He (the speaker) cared not if the whole of England were against him if he had the facts that the country was going to ruin through drink. (Applause.) Let them fight, mark out the lines for themselves, and ride straight on. The day was coming—the times were brighter now—when they would shake off the chains of the drink traffic which had been put upon the necks of the people. (Loud applause.) Mr. E. BORELAND said he had had the pleasure of ad- dressing members of the League of the Cross,and he had never addressed them without having gone away from the meeting very deeply impressed that they had amongst tilt members of the League of the Cress a solid 4' band of workers for God and humanity. (Applause.) Referring to Mr. Chamberlain's remarks to a deputation the previous day, he said Mr. Chamberlain addressed an audience of eight, eight workingmen representing what they called the Radical anti-Sunday Closing Association. He (the speaker) did not know where that association was. He flattered himself on knowing something of the organisations for and against the temperance cause, but with one exception he had never heard of that organisa- tion before. It was certain that that organisation did exist, and there were eight members in it. (Laughter.) Mr. Chamberlain got the members in the rooms of the Liberal Unionist Association and he delivered to them a speech. He supposed they had read the papers that day. There was not in any of the papers a single name of any of the deputation, they might be Melchizedecks for all they knew. (Laughter, and a Voice : "They were from Birmingham.") %Veil, l:e hoped they would go back again to Birnineham. (Laughter. ) Some of Mr. Chamberlain's remarks were mane against Sunday Closing, and some Conservatives and Union- ists of this country were as earnest Sunday closers as any men. It would not serve Mr. Ghambe-rlain nor his party to be against Sunday closing in any part of this country in face of the demand made by both Conserva- tives and Unionist. (Applause.) Mr. Chamberlain said that the Veto Bill was a bill introduced by the Govern- ment for show, and never intended to pass. Well, per- haps Mr. Charnberiain knew better than Mr. Giadstone, or Sir Wm. Harcourt or perhaps better than the com- bined members of the Cabinet. He believed in the sin- cerity of the Government to pass the bill, not only be- cause it was right, but because it would help the party that had taken it up, and would not pay the party that dsopped it. He would like to ask Mr. Chamberlain what the Government would gain by dropping this bill. Would they gain anything? They would not gain the support of Sir Gilbert Greened], or any brewer throughout the length and breadth of the land. Lcrd Burton was a member of the Liberal party until a few days ago and he was prepared to swallow everyone of those political measures if they did not touch this temperance measure. He was now prepared to op- pose these meaeures simply to save his pocket and his trade. (Applause.) Lord Burton was a member of the, House of Lords, but he (the speaker) did not think he would be any more dangerous there than he would be in the House of Commons. He was one of the 172 peers who owned public houses. These 172 members of the House of Lords owned 1,539 licensed drink shops. (Shame.) There were 19 dukes holding 321 licensed houses ; twelve marquises with 106 ; 74 earls holding 645 ; arch-deacons owning 145, one bishop with twc licensed houses, and 61 barons holding 420 licenses. They had not only to face one House of Praliament ; they had to face the Upper house, one third of its members being interested in the continuation of the drink traffic in this land. They had their work before them, and it hadto be faced. Every man must put on the armour of a pure vote at the next election. (Applause.) The speaker urged the necessity of having men pledged to the temperance cause in Parlia- ment, and referred to the present anomalies existing in , the licensing laws of the country, and gave numerous instances showing the advantages derived by places in , Great Britain where no public houses existed.

Mr. Wet. ROBERTS, the secretary of the Federation was next called upon to address the meeting. He said he was extremely pleased to meet the cl,,rzyman they had listeued to that uli2lil. He had hoard of Father Harris before but that was the first occasion upon which he had had the great honour of being in his company, and he was one who had the greatest admiration for the work being done by the League of the Cross. (Applause.) It was once his great delight to be introduced to the late Cardinal Manning and to receive his blessing and he ,could assure them that he considered it one of die great- est honours of his life. (Applause.) And the interview served to infuse into him a new inspiration for his work —(applause)—and as they all knew inspiration was what was needed so very much among those who took up the arduous work in which they were engaged,especi- ally in Warrington. (Applause.) He did not think there was a town in Lancashire, no, nor in the whole country where the temperance people had been so disco uraged as they had been in Warrington. (Applause.) He would tell them why. The temperance people here were , unfortunately very poor. They had no wealthy men among them—if they had they were men who did not care to part with their money, and those who would like to spend their money had none Ito spend. (Applause.) Therefore they ceuldnot beild the grand palace which their Chairman had been speaking about, but he quite agreed with him that there was a great necessity in Warrington for a place fit for people to spend their even- ings in, away from the enticements of the intoxicating cup. (Hear, hear.) He thought that one of the great- est helps to temperance work would be the Providing of counter attractions to the public-houses—applause)— and that they should be provided in a manner fit for any respectable person to enter. He had said they had encountered a great deal of discouragement in Warring- ton. There was not a man or woman in the town who did not know that was true,perfectly well. (Hear, hear.) That night,befbre ke came there he had been in one of the most degraded slums ot Wa,rrington. He saw the men sinking away down the alloy; one earning a lamp. His curiosity was aroused, and he wanted to know who the men were, and 'oho did they think they were ? One was a brewer's candidate for the Town Council, and he was canvassing the poor creatures who lived there ; the ether fellow who was carrying the lamp was one of the tub washers at the brewery. (Laughter and" Shame.") Yes it was a shame. The sight made his blood boil within him. Those were the men who wanted to govern —and who were governing the old town of Warrington. It was a shame—a crying shame that in thi2 town of Warrington they had 80 many men representing this trade, stuck in their Town Council. It was a disgrace to the men and women who bad votes in Warrington to allow such a state of things. (Applause.) They were not doing their duty. (Applause.) He hoped they would receive all the assistance possibl e from their friends of the League of the Cross, for in Warrington the temperance party was as yet in a hopeless minority. As a speaker on Tuesday night had said there were too many people who were unable to speak out on this ques- tion ; there were so many people interested in such a • variety of ways in the drink trade, who were afraid to offend some rich gentleman that they dared not speak out. ("Shame"). He adjured them all to fight with new vigour —he implored them to consecrate themselves anew to the work. Then there were some of their ministers—he did not wish to speak too harshly—but it was en undeniable fact that they were unable to carry on the work of temperance because their places of worship were maintained by the wealth of those who were connected with the brewing trade. (Hear, hear.) How long was this state of things to go on. He begged of those men and women present, in Heaven's name,from that night to go into the work with new strength and help to sweep away this sinful wretchedness of the people. (Applause.) If they loved the children in the streets—the newsboys and the street arabs—they would continue this fight for their sake. (Hear, hear.) Most of their misery and wretchedness was due so the drunkenness of their parents. He knew this to be a fact, for though he had never made it known before he could tell them that most of his spare time and loose money was devoted to helping those poor children. (Applause.) He concluded by earnestly ap- pealing to them to help in the work of temperance. Mr. MufeeNs next proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers, which was carried by acclamation. The Rev. J. YONGE briefly proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairmanet rid in doing so said how pleased he was to see a Roman Catholic clergyman from another town present, and he expressed his regret that more clergy- men in Warrington were not taking part in the work. (Applause.) The vroposition was submitted and carried, and the meeting soon afterwards terminated.

div.head: SOMETHING ABOUT TWO BOYS.
div.p: SOMETHING ABOUT TWO BOYS.

" The mdst pathetic incident of my childhood is this : My mother had bees very ill for several weeks, and the doctor solemnly announced that she could not live more than two or three days longer at most. That night my father roused me from sleep and took me out of my little bed to bid her a last good-bye. I shall never forget the scene, which was new and awful to me. People were weeping all round the room, the air of which was heavy with the odour of candles and lamps, and reeking with the fumes of drugs. My mother knew and kissed me, and then they took rse-back to my bed. But ere I was led away someone opened the window a few inches from the top, and I noticed the grey dawn resting on the glass, and heard the cheep, cheep,' of a newly wakened bird. Since then I have associated that hour and sound with that unhappy episode. • " But (and to say what now follows I have written the foregoing paragraph)—we were all rasped and tor- tured for nothing. My mother proceeded to get well band over hand, and died quietly thirt y years afterwards She survived every person who stood et her iedsiole that night except Speaking of the illness of her son, a boy of nine,a lady says : " We had to sit with him night and day, giving him brandy, wine, beef tea Arc., to keep him alive, and expected every day would be his last. The physician plainly told us that nothing more could be done to save m. "

Yet in spite of the disease, and—we almost said—in spite of the doctors, the lad is well to-day. And this is how it all came about. There is amoral in it, too, but suppose we serve that up at the end of the story. All right, you say. Very well, then. It seems that this boy,George Westmoreland, had pre- viously been a strong, healthy little chap, as all boys ought to be. But about the middle of last November- -1891, that is—he was taken down. The family couldn't make out what ailed him. He complained of a bad pain in the stomach, and vomited a quantity of yellowish ,green stuff. Presently the pain was so sharp he couldn't lie in bed, and they had, so his mother says, to apply fresh hot poultices one after another. The whites of his eyes turned ) ellow, and his skin too. He was hot and feverish, and had to fight for his breath. Of course his mother sent for a doctor,and the doctor said his young patient was suffering from inflammation of the bowels. He gave mediciiies,which, however, did no good so far as the boy's friends could see. On the contrary,he grew worse,and a second doctor was fetched. This medical man differed from his predesessor, and gave out that George had an attack of rheumatic fever —in other words acute rheumatism—a disease Which no boy has any business with whatever. The treatment of this theory availed nothing : George was worse. He had now a hacking cough, and his ex- pectoration was so offensive that the people had to use disinfectants. He broke out into sweats, so heavy as to saturate the pillows. , He could take no nourishment save a little milk and lime water. He wore away to a skeleton, did the poor boy. He was nothing but skin and bone, and they had to lift him in and out of bed. Then he fell so ill that he would not notice any one in the room, and lay for hours never opening his eyes. Then came the time when a third doctor said he couldn't possibly live. What happened after that the boy's mother, tells. We give you her exact words: "In February last," she says, "my husband, as a last resource, determined to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. After a few doses the boy's breathing was easier and ,he took food. In three days he was able to sit up, and in a week's time he was up and dressed. He gained flesh and strength every day, and is now able to go about. Sometimes I look at him and can hardly believe he is the same boy who was so recently at death's door. Seigel's Syrup saved his life. Yours truly, (Signed) Mrs. Mary Westmoreland, 5, High Street, Plumstead, London, April 27,1892." Now, a half a dozen words, Little George had no bowel inflammation, nor a single touch of rheumatism. !That was the doctors' professional guesswork. He had a sharp attack of biliousness and indigestion, of which Mother Seigel would have cured him long before had her medicine been appealed to. Here is the moral to Con- clude with: Learn what the true remedy for illness is, and use it first instead of last.
Cardinal Vaughan's uncle, who has just -Celebrated his eightieth birthday, is the oldest Catholic bishop in Eng- land. Lie is bishop of Plymouth.
The Medical AnnuaVadvises Practitioners to remember that when recommending Coccus as food and beverage for invalid's, the name CADBURY on anyeacket of Cocae is a guarantee of purity.—Advt.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held on Wednesday morning at the Workhouse. There were present :—Messrs. G. Ratcliffe (in the chair), R. Heaton, J. Muir, J. Hill, R. Owen (junior), G. Pilling, A. J. Jolley, and A. Jolley, W. Houghton, W. Clarke, Turton, Fairclough, Longton, E. Auklaud, and Dr. Paterson; also Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (master), and H. Mines (super- intendent of the schools.)
" PALMING " A LUNATIC.-A GRAVE COMPLAINT.

Mr. S. DAVIES said he wished to draw the attention of the Board to a matter of a serious character, which had been discussed by the House Committee on Friday, and which ought to be settled without any further loss of time. A lunatic was at present in the }louse who had bee n discharged from the Prestwich Asylum as harmless. Unfortunately - from the first day he returned to the House he proved to be anything but harmless, and their medical officer had warned the in that the man was no longer responsible for his actions. He wished to point out that the matter was a very serious one and he wished to know whether some inquiry shouid not be instituted as to the action of the Asylum authorities in discharg- ing a man as harmless when he was a dangerous luna- tic. (Hear, hear.) The subject was too oserious to be passed over, and he wanted to know if it would not be prudent for them to take some steps in the matter.— The CLERK said lie thought the question would simply amount to the difference of medical men's opiaions. The man when discharged from the asylum had evidently been in the judgment of the authorities harmless,and it was simply a matter of the control which they had to exercise. There was no &LIU the doctor of Prest- wich would place his opini on against that of their own medical officer. The best thing to be done he thought was to write a complaint to the chairman of the Asylum Committee and point out that they were frequently being subjected to similar annoyances.—Mr. DAVIES moved that the Clerk be instructed to write a letter to the Chairman of the Asylum Committee.—Mr. RATCLIFFE seconded the mo- tion, and in doing so expressed his indignation, and characterised the action of the Asylum authorities as " palming a lunatic" upon the Board.—Mr. Mumn wanted to know if it was not a fact that when a depu- tation from the Board visited the Asylum they men- tioned that in their opinion the lunatic in question had been too long at the Asylurn,and that Ire ought to be sent back to the house.—The Cracux : If that is so, then the Asylum Committee are not to blame, but I am n informed that no such thing was mentioned by the deputation. Perhaps Mr. Muir is thinking of a deputation to Rain- Mule : Perhaps so. I will not be certain.— Mr. HEATON : Well, it does not matter much how the man came to be discharged, now. It is our duty to act as though he had never been in the Asylum. We are re- sponsible for his safety and for that of the house,and we. therefore,ought to lave the man removed to an asylum as quickly as possible. • (Hear, hear.)—A Member mentioned that the man had been for some time under the care of two attendants, and that he could not be removed to the Asylum because there was no room.— The matter then dropped, upon the understanding that the Clerk write about the matter Lo the Chairman of the Asylum Committee.

div.head: TYE COUNTY RATE.-AN ENORMOUS INCREASE.
div.p: TYE COUNTY RATE.-AN ENORMOUS INCREASE.

The CLERK mentioned that ho was preparing the esti- mates for the next half year, but could not submit them in detail at present. Alluding to the county rate he said he was sorry to inform them that another increase would have to be made. The fact was that anything con- nected with County Council meant further expense to them. For the corresponding period of last year the rate amounted to £2,276 17s. 9d., the next half year it had increased to £3,643, and to the present half year it had jumped up to £4,477. He could not help saying that it seemed hard for them as a Board that they were troubled with that account. Why the County Council, who spent the money did not collect it he did not know. They had to keep struggling and resorting to every pos- sible methodto keep the rates down, and then the County Council stepped in and spent their money with- out permitting them any control in the matter. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. WILLIAM IlocuieTos proposed that the pre- cept should be printed with the estimates and circulated among the members and the overseers to whom it would be useful, especially at the time of vestry meetings. He also moved that a comparative statement be drawn up by the Clerk of the rate since the County Council was formed. —Mr. HEATON seconded the proposition. Res- pecting the Clerk's observations about the Farisli Councils Bill he wished to say that the Bill was not yet passed. From the commencement he had seen that the County Council meant extra expense to them.—The CLERK said there was no doubt a con- sideratle amount of money was being spent by the County Council. But at the same time it was being ex- pended in the carrying out of some excellent public work. Most of the expense was incurred by the main- taining of roads in a proper:condition, whilst much more was expended in efforts to prevent

THE POLLUTION OF STREAMS AND RIVERS. This latter work, especially regarding the Mersey and Irwell, was being pushed with commendable vigour and it would be a happy day for the people in the country when this pollution and destruction of beautiful rivers should be ended. (Applause.) There was only one un- satisfactory part of the matter and that was the spend- ing of money by the County Council, and yet having to be collected by the Guardians. Of course, in Warring- ton and neighbourhood they had been used to an excep- tionally low poor rate,and were feeling it now that:an in- crease was being made to carry out necessary reforms. (Hear, hear.) One excellent feature about their finann2 was that they could not berrow—they had to pay as they spen,-, and—(facetiously)—were thus unlike certain individuals. (Latigiiter.) The CHAIRMAN : What about the pollution of Sankey Brook, Mr.Suttou ? —The CLERK said that according to scientific inves- tigations the brook would not be cleared of pollution for 100 years. The St. Helens Corporation had been in- structed by the Government to Use every means known to science to prevent the further pollution of the brook. (Hear, hear.) But the unavoidable cause of the con- tinuance of the pollution was that on the banks there were heaps of chemical deposit, through which the rain ran into the stream. It was calculated that it would be 100 years before this could he reinoved.—Mr HEATON : Well, let us not discuss it, for we shall probably not have to deal with the matter then. (Laughter.)

div.head: LATCHFORD AND THE PARISH COUNCILS TiILL.
div.p: LATCHFORD AND THE PARISH COUNCILS TiILL.

The CLERK submitted a communication from the Clerk to the County Council enclosing the notice of an enquiry to be held at the magistrates court, Newton, on March Bth, regarding the petition for the division of the district into wards. • Speaking upon the probable effect of the Parish Councils Bill upon the Union districts the Clerk said it would be necessary to consider whether the Ches- hire part of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authc,rity, including Latchford, should continue to be attached to the Warrington Union or should go to the Runcorn Union, or form a separate sanitary district.

WILL OF THE LATE -3,11 t. T. C. EDWARDS. MOSS.

Probate of the will has been granted in London, and the value has been sworn at .C 169,845 12; 9d, of the personal estate of Mr, Tom Cottingbam Edwards-Moss, late of Ennismore-gardens, and of Roby Hall, Lancashire, who rowed for Oxford in 1875, 1876, 1877, and 1373. and was M.P. for the Widnes Division of Lancashire from 1885 to 1892. Mr. Edwards- Moss, who died on December 16 last, aged thirty-eight years, appointed as executors of his will, which bears , date July, 1891, with a coelicil made December 7 last, his ' brother, Sir John Edwards-Moss, of 17, Rowland-gardens, I and Mr. Philip Henry Coxe, of 4, Great Winchester- street, solicitor. The testator bequeaths to his sister, Ethel, the lease of his house in Ennisniore-gardens, the furniture, and household effects, and implements of recreation, his carriages and horses and live stock, excepting his dogs. These he gives to his sister, Minna Mackenzie, with such of his effects at Pool House, Peolewe, N. 8., as may have been there a year. He be- queaths also to his said sister, Minna Mackenzie, his , yacht Medina, and power of appointment of a sumsof £20,000, to which, under their mother's will, he would be entitled after the death of his said .sister. The tes- tator bequeaths to his sister, Ethel, a sum of £lO,OOO, with the request (not to be taken as an obligation) that she will dispose of it and of some of the effects at Ennismore-gardens in accordance with memoranda left by him. These memoranda. aa.i affidavit attached to the will states, have not been found. Mr. Edwards-Moss bequeaths £5,000 in trust for Mary Geraldine Davidson, I of Pool House, Poolewe, and to her appointment, and he bequeaths in trust for his sisters, Ethel and Minna £50,000 each, to pay the income to each during her life, with power to her to appoint the trust fund in favour of any issue of the testator's father, excepting Mary I hyra Mackenzie. He leaves the Roby Hall estate and the residue of his property to his brother, Sir John Edwards, Moss.
THE CASE OF ABEZ BALFOUR. A. DOUBTFUL EXTRADITION.

SALTA, TUESDAY.—The ex-National Foreign Minister, Senor Ortiz, is now formulating Jabez Balfour's claims for immediate release. He bases his contention on Article 10 of the treaty, which stipulates for liberation thirty days after arrest. The period has:now expired, and he urges that the prisoner must be set at liberty. He also bases his claim on Art:cle 18 of the National Con- stitution. His lawyer is preparing the foraml claim for instant freedom, which trill be presented to the court at once. It is thought by ipanv here that the judge will probably accede to the request later; and meanwhile Jabez Balfour, though still in custckly, has not been returned to prison.

div.head: INTERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: INTERIAL PARLIAMENT.

FRIDAY. In the House of Commons on Friday eveninc, Sir E. GSM' answering Mr. Curzon, said explicit assurances had been received from the French Government that they were most desirous that their military force should leave Chantaboon at the earliest opportunity, and that " it would not remain a day after the Siamese had fulfilled their engagements under the treaty. Mr. MORLEY, replying to a complaint about the re- moval of paupers from this country to Ireland while Ireland enjoyed no right in regard to English paupers in that country, said he had directed a bill to be pre- pared to remedy the inequality _ _
- The Lords' - Amendments to the Local Gov.rn- ment Bill were further considered. Mr. Fow [Am

moved the rejection of the amendment requiring that any order of the Local Government Board fur the compulsory acquisition of land should require: confirmation by Parliament. Mr. BALFOUR opposed the motion, bat the amendment was negatived without a division. The Lords' amendment providing that the arbitrators should have power to determine as to compensation for any injury or inconvenience in respect to the management of the farm or the occupa- tion of the dwelling•house belonging to it was disagreed - with by 232 to 180. Other amendmenta made by the Lords were rejected by majoritics of 57 and 94. The amendment setting up a special rate for the expenses of parish meetings and Parish Councils was ruled by the SPEAKER to be out of order and to be an infringement of the privileges of the House of Commons. • 'rho limise adjourned at midnight.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on *Monday evening Mr— ASQUITE, replying to a question put lsy Mr. Viriceser, said Her Majesty's Government were not of an opinion that any necessity had arisen for a change in the law in-. regard to the immigration of foreigners into England. They were willing and very anxious to co-operate with other countries in any practical measures which might be devised for dealing more effectually with Anarchists and similar eaernies of society ; but in their opinion, the direction in which international efforts would be most fruitful was te be found not so much in the extension of the power of expulsion. on suspicion as in a more con- stant interchange of an opinion and combined action., both detective and punitive, between Her Maj•-sty's Gavernment and the police authorities of the different nations of Europe. Sir G. TREVILYAN informed Arr. Buchanan that the changes made by the House of Lords in the Scotch. Fisheries Bill had rendered the measure useless, and the Government therefore did not intend to proceed further with the bill.

Mr. MUNDELLA, in reply to Sir. C. Dalrymple, said het was in *communication with dae Pre,i,leut of the Local. Government Board as to the desirability of enlarging the powers of municipal bodies with regard to the estab- lishment of labour bureaus.

The House resumed consideration of the hord's amend- ments to the Local Government (Parish Councils) Bill. Mr. FowLErt's amendment to reinsert the provision struck out of clause 14 for the appointment by the pariFt councils of trustees in the place of churchwardens in the case of non-ecclesiastical charities was carried by 209 to 157. The House next considered the lords' amendment that the elected trustees of a non-ecclesias- tical charity should not exceed one-third of the whole body. Mr. GLADSTONE spoke warmly in favour of mak- • ing, the elective principle effective, and the amendment was disagreed with by 215 to 165. Many other amend- ments mode by the Lords were negatived without a division, including that which struck out of the bill the clause for the reform of the London vestries.

In the House of Lords the Commons' amendments to the Lords' amendment of the Employers' Liability Bill - were considered. Lord RIFos asked the House to agree to Mr. Cobb's amendment on contracting out, by which existing assurance societies were exempted from the operation of the Act for the period or three years. Lord DUDLEY opposed the compromise. Lord Salisbury was induced by an observation which fell from Lord Ripon to explain that in using the words cruel organisation," he did not mean trade unions, but Radical associations. He added, however, that there was not much difference, * because the unions formed a large part of the" cruel organisatioa "which was driving the Government on. The House rejtcted the proposed compromise by 137 votes against 23—majority, 114. Lord Ripen warned the House that in snaiataining the principle of con- tracting out it had " struck at the root f the hill." The other amendments were disposed of, and the House ad- journed.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday,Mr. G. Itussarl asked by Mr HOLLAND whether he had received any in- formation about the rumoured intention of the Indian Government to recommend the reimposition of import duties on cotton goods, said it was inivissib!e for him to anticipate the financial statement to be made in India.

' The ATTORNEY-GENERAL informed Mr. BARRAN that he was consulting the Lord CRANCELLOR on the subject of the compulsory registration of limited companies' deben- ture bones and of private assignments of book debts. Mr. fi A. Montur, answering ago stion, said that under the „ agreement now in course o negotiation, the Post Office) would take over the entire runk telephone wire system of the country, and the Post Office was gradually carry- ing out of the scheme of proViding trunk wires between' the important towns of the United Kingdom. • On tile order of the day for "the consideration of the Lords' reasons and Lords' amendments to Commons' amendments to Lords' amendments," on the Employers' Liability Bill, Mr. GLADSTONE moved that the order be discharged. He said he did so on behalf of the entire Government, in whose views the incorporation of the Lords' amendmert on the contracting-out question, would tend to poison the working of the hilt,and he was afraid, very seriously to compromise the position of the workine classes in the face •of their employers. Mr. Balfour called in question the correctness of the Premier's opinion about the feeling of the working classes, and cited in support of his argument a recent statement by Mr. Woods. That hon. member, however, interposed to say that ho was being misquoted; he thought that this was a vital partef the bill, and had always said so. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said it was only for a very small minority that the Government were deli- bereely going to sacrifice a very useful bill. M. W. M'Laneet said a small amount of conciliation on the part of the Government would have saved the biU. Mr. C. FENWICK and other Labour naemberaexpressed approval of the action of the Government. On a division being. called for, the Conservative and Liberal Unionist benches ' were almost minty. ' The fieures Were :—For Mr. Glad- stoners motion, 225; against, 6 ; majority for, 219. The House afterwards proceeued to further, consider the Lords' amendments to the Local Gorernment (Parish Councils) Bill, and rejFeted several more amendments. The bill having been got through, reasens for disagreeing with the House of Lords were agreed to,and the House. adjourned till Saturday, with the understanding that the Lords' further amendments Would be taken into con- sideration next Monday.,

WHAT a history of theft on a large- Land- scale is a book which has just been Grabbing. compiled by Mr. J. G. LEM, RB, M.P. The book is entitled: "English Commons and Forests: The Story of the Battle during the last Thirty Years for Public Rights over the Com- mons and Forests of England and Wales." The Parish Councils Bill is an aft empt to redress some of the wrongs of the rural population of England. Yet, assuming that it e'scapes the ten- der mercies of the House of L ords, how little will it do towards replacing the villagers in that posi- tion with regard to the land that their predecessors - held in the far-gone ages. There are still a few commons left in En gland, and the com- mon rights which the people enjoy are, • says Mr. LEFEVRE, but a survival of the collective , ownership of land which prevailed in the early stage of communities all over Europe. When the feudal system was introduced, and the villages w?.re parcelled out amongst the successful free- booters, the latter,though at first only regarded as having the rights of the people vested in them, soon began to look upon themselves as owners. There was no difficulty in giving these usurpations the sanction of law, seeing that the usurpers were themselves the law -makers. The Parliament of Barons in 1235 passed what is known as the Statute of Merton, allowing the Lords of Manors to enclose commons ; and, will it be believed, that it is to this musty piece of legality that some modern land-grabbers have appealed to justify their pilfering of common land. One of tho greatest service rendered by the Commons Preservation Society was the getting of legal and Parliamentary decisions which amounted to a repeal of this iniquitious law. We are told,f urther,tl) at under cover of 4,000 separ- ate Enclosure Acts upwards of 7,175,000 acres of common lands were enclosed, It is no wonder, therefore, that the people of England are—apart from a small class of land lords who in times past have selfishly legis lated for themselves—a land- less people. What a change there would now be in the social conditions of this country were those seven million alms of land in tho hands of the rightful possessors, that is to say, the communitY as a whole. Some parts of Mr. Lefevre's book is full of thrillimg interest. Take for example, the rescue of Berhhamstead Common, from a lorcilY "encloser " some thirty years ago. All the roads on the common had been blocked up, and iron fences five feet high were erected right across the centre enclosing nearly five hundred acres- ) The Commons Preservation Society, however, decided to contest this bold attempt at pillage, and after consultation it was decided to destrol the entire fence at a single blow. The story is then told in Mr. LEFEVRE'S book in the following words :

With this object, it was arranged with a contrite" tor in London to send down at night to Berkhanl" sted a force of 120 navvies for the purpose of Pl' Hug down the iron fences in as short a time a° possible. On March 6, 1866,a special train left Ens - ton, shortly after midnight,with the requisite nuin" ber of labourers, skilled workmen, and gangeill' armed with proper implements and crowbars. The train reached Thring at half-past one a.m. At 00' point the operation nearly miscarried. The contra tor, it ap peared,had sub-let his contract to anothe' person. The two met together at a public-hons! near EnstonStation the evening before the intend raid, arid drank so freely that neither of them "ora! in a condition to lead the force into action and tiia navvies arrived at Thring without a leader, aU with no instructions. Fortunately, Mr. Lawrel had sent a confidential clerk to watch the Pr:, ceedings frs,m a distance, and this gentler' perceiving the difficulty, took the lead of the f°l.crii A procession was formed at the station. A roar-to of three miles in the moonlight brought them,,e. Berkhamsted Common, and the object of the eIYO,I dition was then first made known to the rank file. The men were told off in detachments dozen strong. The substantial joints of the ral'in7cl were then loosened by hammers and chisels, utbe the crowbars did the rest. Before six m; ere whole of the fences. two miles in length, IvA'in levelled to the ground, and the railings were ltas a heap with as little damage as possible. It 1,-en seven o'clock before the alarm was given, and sg'he Lord Brownlow's agent appeared on the scene "r found that Berkharaeted Common was no longo7o enclosed. It was too late to do more than make energetic protest against the alleged trespa':r Meanwhile the news spread, and the inhabitants_?; the district flocked to the scene. Gentlemen in their carriages and dog-carts, shopkeepers Iru_': Berk hamsted and farmers in their gigs, labourers ; foot, tested the reality of what they saw by wandthe ing over the Common and cutting morsels o flowering gorse, to prove, as they said, that the i_afu' es fel ece was their own agsin. Thus were the 430 aei restored to the Common and two miles of l iron removed. It was said that the erection of tt iron fences had cost more than a thousand poun". it is satisfactory to note that the fouryears liti- gation which followed this bold assertion of pub* .s_

lie rights ended on every point in favour of the champions of the commoners. But some idea may be formed of how the law, or rather the expensive Processes of the law, favoured the rich and power- ful land-grabbers in their designs,when it is stated that the cost of the litigation in regard to Epping Forest amounted to no less a sum than 240,000.

Th THE Employers' Liability Bill is e Coming conflict. now dead, so far at all events as this Parliament is concerned. The 4evernment have in the opinion of all who were ?eel. y in favour of the Bill taken the wisest course in Withdrawing it, under the circumstances that .rhave arisen. Indeed, seeing that the House of 140rds has insisted upon the retention of the con- trading-out clause which they inserted when the /3111 Was first presented to them, the Government l'ave really had only one course open to them, and that is the course they have pursued. This eaaure was designed for the benefit of the work- 41groen of the country, and it was fram ed in re- sponse to the demands which they have made for taanY years past. There has been all alobg ample , eVidence that the Bill as it left the House of Com- l'afts bad the hearty support of the working el.asses, with few,and in some cases,doubtful excep- tifts• All the recognised labour leaders in and out of Parliament have pronounced in its favour, and so have the Trade Unions. Even the railway teen, so far as they have spoken through their trade Unions, are no exceptions to the rule, al- though their supposed hostility to the measure 484 been urged as an excuse by those who have wrecked the Bill. Seeing, therefore, that there is this unanimity of app royal on the part of those !lost directly coneerned,it may well be asked who it is that has had the audacity to withhold this great and much desired boon from the working elaases of the country. The answer is, of course, that it is that eminently representative ahember, the House of Lords, which has, to use the words of Mr. GLADSTO NE, infused into the 11 that poison which has destroyed it. Con- tracting out allowed, the Bill becomes a sham and tsnare, instead of a reality and a protection. tlt, in pursuance of their traditional policy of lnaking useless those re forms which they dare not ect altogether, the Peers insist that contract- ing out shall be allowed. This is a condition 'which the Government could not entertain for a inoment. To do so would, in fact, be a sheer act V Self-stultification. . Their object in promoting the Bill, and in pushing it through the House of Commons has not been to give the Peers another °l)Portunity of displaying the proficiency they have ,tattained in emasculating useful legislation, but to rnefit the working classes by a reform which has ueen long agitated for. The Bill at it has been tn. utilated by the Peers is not such a reform, and It is repudiated with contempt by those who are !a°re particularly entitled to speak on behalf of the industrial classes. Rather than accept an ;7'mPloyer's Liahility Bill, with the taint of con- 7acting out &fused into it, they will wait a ttle longer, Viten they will probably receive all That is in the present measure and something more 13eSides; for, as Mr. Fin•rwrcic said in the debate on Ziesday, the present Bill contains the minimum 01 working class deman,cls. In the meantime it is v. "3' clear that the trade unionists of the country • Intend to take up the challenge that has been thrown down to them by the House of Lords. ° Lord .SALISBErRY will probably, before many weeks ~4b3 over, hear a good deal more than he has bar- Pined for about the "cruel organisations" which L'Le scoffs at so glibly. The Parliamentary Com- nuttee of the Trades Union Congress met on , Wednesday and decided to convene a National Conference of Trade Unions and Friendly Societies t° be held in London on Saturday, March 17, at Which the action of the Lords will be considered land steps taken to secure the passing of a satis- actory Bill. We venture to predict that there is a great victory in store for the Trade Unions. It ould be a strange development of modern politics lf there were not. The. Trades Unions embrace !(33zething like a million of the best and most in- gent workmen of the country, and they repre- ajnt the opinions and sentiments of a vast propor- °ll of the workmen who are not yet upon their ailluster rolls. They fight for a cause which has the PProval of the representative Chamber and they a_r° ePposed by—the House of Lords, a ricketty :nachronism which holds its place in the Consti- co'ution of the country owing to the oversight or ,°ternptuous tolerance of political reformers. ;Lie result of a conflict between two such forces is, urelY, not for a moment in doubt.

Seeing that Lonnell's term of office, and, in consequence, ;"at of the Councillor who succeeds to his place, 'eilninatea in November of this year it might seem t4lhealeelY worth while troubling the burgesses of Ce ward with another contest at the present 41Ineture. But the Conservatives have thought clitrt'rently, and they have decided to make an dat,tenipt to secure this Liberal seat. The two can- that are in the field are both well 1-,e(Ywri to the voters of two of the asrds adjoining Orford. Mr. W. Furness, will champion the Liberal cause, made -Rgallent bid last November to oust Councillor from the representation of St. John's Ward, notwithstanding the exceptionally strenuous —°llB put forth by the Tories in defence of the sea, very nearly accomplished his object. Mr. ii-e,114 Damn, who is again coming forward on be- -01 the Conservatives, was defeated in Bewsey ritalll en November Ist by a substantid majo- -01 Apart from the unnecessary forcing of an vseetien)svith its attendant charges upon the rates, cern are one er two considerations which the thettra of Orford Ward might well bear in mind at die, present time. Against Mr. BAIRD as an in- ;l4'l4 we have nothing to say. So far as e, know he is an estimable gentleman. 121.4,, certainly, his friends speak well of him. thlit what in his public capacity as a candidate are we interests that he most directly represents 1' toe have iso hesitation in saying that if returned di the Town Council be will be regarded as another b_ rent representative of the liquor trade. He is a b 3, profession and he is closely connected 13.4 firm which owns a large proportion of the 4,, etuc-honses of the town. Now, may it not be shed in all moderation, is this particular trade not ready Sufficiently represented on Warrington ow enuncil It is, we contend, not merely r2,resented in its due proportion, as compared ,",te c uiother interests, but it actually dominates ouncil. We believe the electors of Orford ard F will take heed of this fact and will return r. , '"l'TEes in preference to Mr. BAIRD. There nbe little doubt that the real reason of the riesfor contesting this election is to add to the

div.p: preponderance of the publicans in municipal affairs. But, leaving that consideration out of account for a moment, the only other plea for forcing a contest is on the ground of political differences. In this connection, it may well be asked why a working class constituency like that of Orford should vote for a Conservative. In-so-far as he is a politicianMr.BArno will repre- sent Conservative ideas and Conservative methods What those ideas and methods are, so far as the working classes are concerned, has been abun- dantly demonstrated during the last few months. Lord Salisbury's sneers at the " cruel organisa- tions " of workingmen, and the desperate efforts that have been made to wreck the Employers Liability Bill and the Parish Councils Bill, which are above all things measures for the benefit and protection of workingmen in town and country, must have opened the eyes of even the densest "Tory democrat." In fact, upon both local and political considerations it is undeniable that Mr. FURNESS'S claims upon the electors are vastly superior to those of Mr. Baird.

LOCAL NEWS.

OiELAND-STREET WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY'. WIDNES. The usual weekly meeting in connection with this Society was held en Friday evening, there being a fair attendance. An admirable paper on "John Bright" was read by Mr. F. J. Poole, and was greatly appre- ciated by those present. An excellent discussion fol- lowed. If you want your WATCII RAPAIRED by skilled workmen take it to FRITCRARD.S. - Advt. A FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT RUNCORN. A rather serious accident took place at the residence of William Fletcher, 17, Briscoe-st., Runcorn, on Sun- day afternoon. His daughter had been upstairs, and in turning out of the room, she missed her footing, and fell from the top to the bottom of the stairs. She was picked up in an unconscious condition, and carried to the surgery of Dr. Mackenzie, who on examination ex- pressed a fear that the base of her skull was fractured. During Sunday she remained in a very critical condi- tion,but on Monday morning she regained full conscious- ness, and there is every promise that she will recover. Go to Parrcnlnn's, 51, High-at.. Runcorn. for the lest FIVE GUINEA WITCH a working man can have. —Advt. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. On Monday afternoon a youth named Alfred Hague, of Mersey-road,Widnes, met with an accident at Messrs. Gossage's soap works. He had taken a tool—a kind of scraper—to be sharpened after which he returned with it and stepped into a hoist to get to the room above. He put the sharp edge of the tool to rest on his shoe with the long handle of it standing in a sloping position. As the hoist ascended the tool handle caught against a plank and pressed the sharp blade through his shoe, severing two of his toes. He was immediately taken home and afterwards to the Accident Hospital where another toe had to be amputated. • COLLIER's OVKIS are going Wiest and day.— dvt. BOYS ON THE DOWNWARD PATH. At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, two lads named Michael Moores and Thomas Stanton, were brought before Messrs. Speakman and Norman, and charged with stealing 35Ibs. of coal, the property of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, on the previous even- ing. They were seen coming from the direction of trucks on the Old Quay section of the canal works, by P.S. Gill, who gave chase and captured them. He charged them with the theft, which they admitted. Having pleaded guilty in Court, Superintendent Ather- ton intimated that this was the fifth appearance of Moores, and that Stanton ran away from a Boy's Refuge in Manchester, on Saturday. There was no record against him.—Moores was committed to Knutsford for 14 days, and Stanton was bound over in 40s. to come up for judgment, if called upon, within six months. SPLENDID NEw CURRANTS 2d. per lb. at CoLusaa's.—ileiot. CAPTURE OF A SUPPOSED BURGLAR AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Police Court on Monday, before Alders man H. S. Timmis and Councillor Gossage, a man named John White was charged with having on Friday night the 9th inst. entered the house of Thomas Moran, of 24. Catherine-st., for an unlawful purpose. From the evidence of the prosecutor and his wife it appears that on Friday night the wife awoke and saw the prisoner in the bedroom, there being a light burning. She called her husband, and he, together with Mrs. Moran's bro- ther, who slept in an adjoining room, captured the pris- oner and took him to the police station. It seemed that he had gained admittance to the house by means of the back kitchen window as this was found to be open. P.S. McGregor stated that he charged the prisoner with being on the premises for an unlawful purpose, but the accused stated that he did not know what ke was doing as he was drunk. He however appeared to be quite sober. Prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.
