The usual weekly concert promoted by the United Alkali Co., was held in the Baths Assembly Room, on Saturday night when there was a crowded audience. The programme, which was given by the members of the Widnes Football Club Harmonic Society, was gone through in an excellent manner, and appeared to please the people very much. Almost all the artistes had to appear a second time: Programme. Songs ; selected Mr. F. Fox; "Round goes the wheel," Mr. Young; "Our Empire's Unity," Mr. T. Laws; " Royal Fusi- liers,"Mr. E. Gordon ; "Pa and Ma," Mr. J. H. Smith ; "An old love dream," Master G. Laws ; "Queen of my heart," Mr. J. Morris ; " I'm in the Chair," Mr. P. J. Kenyon ; " S'Ang that reached my heart," Mr. G. Wright ; and" The Races," Mr. H. Barber; violin and piano duet," Martha," Messrs. G.C. Full and J. Gillon ; and" Medley of Popular Choruses," Messrs. Gorden, Laws and Smith. The duties of accompanist were car- ried out by Mr. G. C. Full in an admirable manner. Over 6,000 delicious loaves sold every week at COLLIER'S. —Advt.

HYMNS AND HYMN TUNES.—INTERESTING PAPER. At the weekly meeting of the Ellesmere-street Mutual Improvement Society, Runcorn, held on Friday evening under the presidency of Mr. F. Clarke, Mr. John Flolford read a most interesting and 'capable paper on " A few ideas about hymns and hymn tunes." The essayist said that many a lovely hymn was utterly robbed of all its beauty and effectiveness by being read in a painfully mechanical manner; or v. ith little or no regard being paid to punctuation, or to the sentiments expressed. The same, he said, held good in the choice of tunes. Often enough a tune was selected which though good in itself was yet so little adopted to the construction of sense of the hymn that complications' sometimes arose. He gave some very amusing instances of this. A rather free and diverting discussion followed the reading'of doe paper, in which Messrs. Gandy, Palin. Casely, Jones, Cook. Parry, and Bentley took part. At the close a vete of thanks was accorded Mr. Holford. DELICIOUS CRISP CRUST round COLLIER'S bread.—Aiist. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.—RE-OPENING SERVICES. The ahive church was re-opened on Sunday aftea a thorough renovation and decoration. There were large congregations present at each service who expressed ' their satisfaction at the effective and tasteful manner in which the bftutification had been carriedout. During 1 the last two years upwards of £4OO have been spent in improving the sacred edifice. In the morning the preacher was the Rev. Dr. Preston, vicar' who based his discourse on a text beautifully illumined on the walls of the church. In the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. F. Nightingale, 8.A., of Widnes. The choir ren- dered special anthems morning and evening, under the leadership of Mr. W. E. Lancaster. Mr. A. Savage pre- sided at the organ. The collections were towards the liquidation of the debt incurred. A movement is on foot in connection with Holy Trinity to establish a sur- pliced choir, and it is anticipated that the arrangements will he completed so that the members thereof can take ' part in the service on Easter Sunday morning.

SUICIDE AT WIDNES: THE INQUEST. On Monday afternoon Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy county coronor, held an inviry at the Widnes Police court, touching the death of William 'Woolstencroft, whose body was found hanging from a beam,near the pavilion at the Widnes Football field, on Thursday the 15th inst. Mrs. Woolstencroft identified the deceased as her hus- hand, who resided at 9, Gerrard-st., Widnes. He left home on Thursday morning shortly before six o'clock to go to his work. About two o'clock the same day he was brourdit home dead. James Clarke stated that he and a man named Hughes went on the 15th inst to the Wid- nes football field to practice running, and found the deceased hanging from a beam by a rope placed round the neck. Witness at once informed the police of the discovery. I'. C. Farrish and P. C. Worsfold also gave evidence. The latter stated that deceased had evidently made an attempt to take his life before leaving home, as a piece of scarf was found at his abode attached to a beam, which corresponded with a piece found in deceased's pocket. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane." They also expressed their sympathy with decesed's family.
SHRTICE OF SONG AT W IDNgS.

A service of song entitled " Jessica's First Prayer " was rendered in the Waterloo:road schoolroom on Thurs- day night, by a choir of about 100 voices. Miss Gardner was the reader and Mr. W. G. Buchnall accompanied the singing in an able manner. Councillor Hoclgkinson occupied the chair. The proceeds will be devoted to the Sunday school fund.
_ PERE IRISH BUTTER. is. per lb., at COLLIER'S.—Advt. ASSESSMENT OF WIDNES.

At the weekly meeting of the Widnes Property Owners' Protection Association, Mr. J. Midwood presiding, mat- ters relating to property owners were discussed. The Chairman reported that the assessment of Widnes was as follows :—Railways, £22,992 ; works, £57.295 ' • other property, £71,780; making a total of £152,067. Up- wards of thirty new members joined the association.
JOSEJPII PRITCHARD, 51, High-street. Runcorn, keeps STIGMA/LES to suit all sights, from& shilling a pair.—Adat. MOCK PARLIAMENT AT WIDNES.

At the Parochial Rooms on Tuesday evening a mock parliament was held, in connection with the Widnes Churn Institute. The subject for discussion was the "Eight Hours Bill." Mr. Stuart Deacon (Premier) ably introduced the bill. The opposition was led by Mr. J. D. Brookes. On a vote being taken at the close of the debate it was found that the Bill was thnewn out by a large majority. COLLIRR'S use ever ten tons of Flou.every weak.—Advt. PAPER ON "CHARLES DICLENS."_

At the weekly meeting of the Brunswick Mutual Im- provement Society, held on Wednesday, a highly interest- ing paper was read by Miss A. Littler, on "Charles Dickens." The essayist briefly reviewed the life of Dickens until he rose to fame and fortune as a novelist, and then exhibited his various powers as a writer, by reading extracts from his works. A conversation fol- lowed in which Mr. W. Millington, Mr. Palin, and Cap- tain Le Couteur took part. There was a very good at- tendance. The president (Mr. T. Simister) occupied the chair.
IRISH 'NATIONAL LEAGUE AND EVICTED TENANTS FUND. •

The Widnes Branch of the Irish National League held an all night dance in the League rooms, Victoria-road, on Monday night, the proceeds of which will he devoted to the Evicted Tenants Fund. Owing to the exertion of the President and ,other officers of the branch, a large number of tickets were sold, and there is expected to be a very creditable amount transmitted to the Executive to the above named fund. The room was crowded. Danc- ing, including Irish jigs,and reels, interspersed with pa!-riotic songs,were kept up till an early hour in the fol- lowing morning, everyone going away well pleased with the night's enjoyment.
When in want of a CHASTE and ELEGANT WEDDING or BIRTfLDLY PRESENT go to PRITCHARD'S, 51, High-street.— Advt.

BAND OF HOPE MEETING AT RUNCORN. A public meeting was held in connection with the Sc. John's Band of Hope, on Wednesday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. M. Thomas, who gave an addresf on the temperance cause. Afterwards an inter- esting programme was proceedeta with. Recitations were given by Ruth Percival, AnnabPlla McLeod, Emily Richardson, Kate Whitlow. Polly Shaw, Lily Watson, John Harrop, and Joseph Bettley ; song and chorus Miss CdFPritchard ; solo, Miss Haynes. Choruses were ren- dered during the evening as well as a dialogue by the members—Katie Rheal. Hester Cooper, Ben Cooper, Willie Cooper, John:st., and Harry Baxter. Mr. Harrop spolo a few words on abstinence. The accompanist was Mr. J. Pritchard ; the conductor Mr. M. Thomas. The Doxology brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUAhY 24. 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUAhY 24. 1894.
THE CORONER AND Hie WORK.

On Wednesday afternoon, shortly after one o'clock,the body of John Hayes, aged 42 years;of 48, Lower Byrom- St., Manchester, was found in one of the locks of the Bridgewater Canal,Runcern. The deceased was engineer on board one of the Rochdale Canal Company's steam fiats, tilt. Humber. On Friday, January 28, he arrived in Runcorn, and on the following evening, about seven o'clock, he left the vessel to go into the town. He was subsequently seen returning to the boat, but despite diligent search, nothing further was seen of him until the body was found as stated above. An inquest was held on the body on Thursday afternoon, at tke Ceme- tery, before Mr., Worsley. Evidence of identification was given by Elizabeth Hayes, his wife; and James Thomas, foreman of the Rochdale Company's bats, as to when he loft the Humber. William Jackson, lock tenter, residing in Waterloo-road, gave information as to the finding of the body ; and P.C. Williams stated that he removed it to the mortuary, and gave particu- lars as to what he found in tho clothing. A verdict of "Found drowned" was reeorded. The Coroner inti- mated that he had held 14 inquests already during the present year, which was double the average number. He had also ascertained that there had been 24 drown- ing cases atthe place described as " a death trap" at Weston Point, which were directly attributable to the road. _

div.head: ritoPOSZD NEW eIiIIRCH FOR WESTOR.
div.p: ritoPOSZD NEW eIiIIRCH FOR WESTOR.

The first meeting of the Church people of Weston was held on Tuesday afternoon to consider the advisability of providing a new church. Among those present were Canon Maitland Wood (vicar) and the Rev. W. H. Stables (curate-in-charge). There was a good representa- tive assembly. It was show that the present building although in appearance much like a church, was also used fora school. The evening congregations. which had greatly increased of late, crowded the building. The services were very hearty. A new church was necessary After considerable discussion it was unanimously decided that a new church should be provided, and that an effort should be made at once to raise the funds. It was further agreed to hold a bazaar in the autumn, in aid of the building fund, and the decision as to whether it should be held in Weston or Runcorn was adjourned to another meeting. The following among those present were elected to further the object :—Canon Wood, the Rev. W. H. Stables. Mrs. Wood, Mrs. Sill, Mrs. Bankes, Miss Bankes, Miss D. Bankes, Mrs. Mather, Mrs. Ford, Mrs. Moores, Mrs. Tinsley, Mrs. Kenwright, Miss Ken- aright, Miss Rigby, Miss Gregory, Miss Goddard, Mrs. Robinson, Miss Peacock, Miss Wale, Mr. Sill (c4urch- warden), and Mr. Robinson (sidesman). The meeting discussed various schemes for the church. Many fav- oured an ornamental brick building. Irrespective of the site, which it is hoped Major Orred will give, £2,000 is required. Plans are shortly to be prepared. It is that the new sacred edifice shall be twice the size of the pre- sent structure.

div.head: GRUESOME DEN.
div.p: A GRUESOME DEN.

At Runcorn, on Thursday, before Messrs.e. Speakman and S. Taylor, Richard Pye, 31, Back Cooper-street, was charged on remand with cruelly illtreating his daughter, Mary Elizabeth, aged 10, in such a manner as to cause her unnecessary suffering. Inspector Uphill, of the Na- tional Society for the Prevention ot Cruelty to Children, stated that on Thursday, the 15th inst., he saw the girl, who was poorly nourished. Her body was dirty, and the only two garments she wore were ragged and dirty.. Her head was a mass of sores and vermin. Her hair was matted together, and her clothes were covered with ver- min. She had neither boots nor stockings on her feet. He took her home and found the prisoner in bed. Pri- soner, in answer to witness,said he was too fond of beer to look after the child. He admitted pawning her boots the previous day to obtain drink, and that night he got drunk. There was not a particle of food in the house, nor was there any fire or fuel, although the day was cold. The two mattresses were filthy,and altogether the place was in a wretched state. Prisoner had cursed and abused neighbours for giving the child food and cloth- ing. Prisoner and his brother, a single man, lived toge- ther. Dr. M'Dougall said he examined the child. She had been neglected for some considerable time, and had sufficient lice about her to propagate lice throughout the whole county. Police-sergeant Woolley stated thathe had known the prisoner five years as a man who seldom worked,but hung about tap locks and drank excessively. Prisoner pleaded guilty,and said he had been a widower eight years, and was willing to contribute towards his child's maintenance. The Chairman, characterising the case as a most revolting one, sent the prisoner to gaol for two months. BANKING NEWS.
We understand-il-;ii—ia.ir's Banking Company and the Alliance Bank, Limited,have taken over the old established banking business of Sir Samuel Scott, Bart., and Co., of 1, Cavendish-square, London.

div.head: COLLAPSE OF A VITRIOL CHAMBER.
div.p: COLLAPSE OF A VITRIOL CHAMBER.

. At St. Helens on Tuesday night the roof of a vit- riol chamber, 901 t. by 201 t. and 201 t.. high, at the Greenbank Works, St.. Helens, of the United Alkali Company, Limited, collapsed ,and, crashing through the bottom of the tank, released about 150 tons of vitriol. The liquid flowed down the bank on which the tank stood, into Garden-st., 100 ft. below. The crash and flow of vitriol created considerable alarm. As soon as possible chloride of lime was added to the variol in the street to counteract its effect. The chamber now looks a complete wreck, but the offi- cial estimate of the damage is only about £l5O for the vitriol, and perhaps £5O or £lOO for damage to the structure. Three adjoining chambers were burnt down in the big fire at these works in November last.

div.head: LITERA.RY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: THE LITERA.RY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.

The fourth meeting of the session in connection with this society was held in the Lecture Room of the Museum on Monday evening, under the presi- dency of Mr. Robert Davies. There was a fair attendance. Mr. J. D. Buckton read a paper on " Defence " and during the evening Mr. J. Dwerry- house (Moore), and Mr. J. Fairhurst (borough trea- surer), were unanimously elected members of the society. The secretary (Mr. J. Rymer Young) inti- mated that at their next meeting Mr. F. W. Monks would read his promised paper on " A voyage round the world." Early in April Mrs. Edlesten would give a paper on "Early Britain and its beliefs." This meeting in April would be regarded as the annual meeting of the society, and the elec- tion of president and other officers would take place on that occasion.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL COILRESPONDENT.

The efforts of the Runcorn Tonic-sol-fa choir on Wednesday evening, in the Public Hall, Runcorn, promises to be a great success. The members as well as the conductor, Mr. J. Holford, are to be con- gratulated upon their determination to produce the last oratorio, composed by Handel, namely " Jephtha." The work is acknowledged to be one of the most perfect composed by the great master. The choir have entered with earnestness into the repeated rehearsals, and there is every in- dication that they will successfully acquit them- selves in their onerous task. Eminent soloists have been engaged, and although Mr. Houghton has ex- pressed his inability to fulfill his engagement, through an affection of the throat, a worthy sub- stitute has been obtained in Mr. Tom Child of Leeds. The effort is worthy of the patronage of the inhab- itants of the town.

As indicated already in these notes, the Com- mittee having in hand the provision of lectures for the people, have arranged for the delivery of one on" Oxford," on Monday evening, by Mr. M. E. Saddler, M.A., the secretary of the Oxford Univers- ity extension lectures, in the Public Hall. In addi- tion to the address which will be beautifully illustrated, being of an interesting character, the object is a laudable one, it being to liquidate the debt on two former courses of lectures, which proved of great benefit to many residents in Run- corn.

The Co-operative movement in Runcorn and Widnes appears to be gaining considerable ground for at the annual tea party held on Wednesday evening, the secretary was in a position to state that the turnover during labt year, notwithstand- ing the dislocation of trade through the prolonged coal strike, had been in advance of any previous 12 months. The particulars concerning the doings of the Society will be found in the report of the gathering, which appears in another column.

If the reports concerning the proposed develop- ment of works in connect.on with the Manchester Ship Canal, at Runcorn, should become accomplished facts, there is no reason to believe that the construc- tion of the undertaking will ultimately prove so disadvantageous to the town as some people have been led to imagine. Certainly no definite infoz ma- tion is to hand with regard to the early provision of a graving dock, or the reduction of what has been termed unjust dues on vessels coming to the town, but there is reason to believe that the matters are receiving the attention of the directorate. The residents in the town will kail with satisfaction any definite statements respecting these Cnd other matters.

The question with reference to the closing of Norley school was advanced another stage on Tues- day, when the Rural Sanitary Authority were informed by the Education Depart ment, that they had intimated to the managers of the institution, that unless certain sanitary defects to which they had already drawn attention to were not speedily remedied, the annual grant would be in danger. There is apparently an eff )rt being made bv the Church party of the township to prevent the estab- lishment of a School Board, which is evidently a bugbear to the ecclesiastical section of this out-of- the-way Cheshire village, as it has been in other more populous distiicts. Why this is the case is difficult to conceive, seeing the innumerable advan- tages that accrue from a properly conducted insti- tution, under popular control. It is hard to understand why denominationalists should fight so tenaciously against the inevitable, for sooner or later the education of the children will have to be conducted with schools containing all modern requirements, and under the control of the rate- payers.

The proceedings at the monthly meeting of the Widnes School Board on Tuesday afternoon, were of a more animated character than usual. This arose through the management committee's pro- cedure being called into question by Mr. Lewis,who argued that there must be something wrong to account for the repeated changes in the teachers under their control. The Rev. Dean Finigan, who presides over the committee in question, declined to answer the queries put by the interrogator, on the ground of want of time,he having only received notice of the questions shortly before the gather- ing. He however, offered several reasons why the teachers might have resigned, and asked if the con- duct of the committee w as to be censured. Matters did not go so far as this. The outcome of the dis- cussion may be beneficial to all concerned, for the thorough ventilation of alleg ed grievances leads to the truth becoming known. If there is any foun- dation for the allegations made by Mr. Lewis, the sooner they are rigidly investigated the better for all parties.

div.head: F RODS TIAM.
div.p: F RODS TIAM.

THE LIBERATION SOCIETY.—On Tuesday eveniug an interesting meeting was held in the Town Hall, Frod- sham, under the auspices of this society, the subject dis- cussed being princip:illv Disestablishinent and Disendow- ment. Mr. Thomas Rigby, C. AldermAn, of Sutton %Yea- ver, prasided. Addresses were also delivered by Mr. John Fisher, London, arid Mr. R. Bate, C.C., whose remarks were based on the religious instruction given in our day schools.

PAROCHIAL COMMITTER.—A fortnightly meeting of the Frodsham Committee was held on Saturday evening, Mr. Alfred Thomas, J.P., presiding. The Clerk produced an agreement with the Public Works Loan Board for signature by the Chairman of the Sanitary Authority for the proposed loan, and the same was approved. Mr. Davies,the Clerk of the works,reported as to the progress of the water scheme. He stated that Messrs. Timmi ns had almost completed the excavations for the founda- tion of the Overton Reservoir, that the materials for the structure were being carted to the site, and that Messrs Timmins had got the required depth of the borehole-310 feet. Mr. Heywood referred 'to a report current in Frod- sham that there were no Frodsham men employed by Messrs. Timmins, and inquired whether such report was , correct. Mr. Davies replied that report was an incorrect one, as there were some seven or eight Frodsham men engaged on the work, and three Runcorn men. Mr. Davies did not think there would be many men employed on the contract. Messrs. Williams and Shore corro- borated the statement of the Clerk of the Works. Pans prepared by Messrs. H. Linaker and Son were approved by the Committee for proposed alterations to Stapleton House, Frodsham ;and for alterations to Mr. J. G. Rycld's property in Church-street, prepared by Mr. S. Davies.

div.head: PENKETR.
div.p: PENKETR.

VISITORS TO THE HOLY LAND.-Mr. and Mrs, Robert Garnett, of Hall Nook, Penketh, accompanied by the Misses Fanny and Hilda Garnett, will leave the village to-day en route for London and from there tc. the Holy Land. It will be remembered that Mrs. Garnett some time ago undertook the same trip and afterwards gave alma very graphic descriptions of her travels at meetings both at Warrington and Penketh. • BAND OF HOPE MEETING.—On Friday night last week.a Band of Hope meeting was held in the Wesleyan School- room. The programme for the evening was pro- vided by a party of Good Templars from Warrington. The meeting did not commence until late owing to some delay. Color Sergeant Mantle was in the chair. Tem- perance addfesses were delivered by him and also by Sergeant Roberts, Bro. George Clarke Etc. A song and recitation were also given by Bro. W. Gallop. A vote of thanks was passed at the conclusion to the Warrington friends.

CONCERT AT WIDNES.

On Monday a concert was held in the Lacey-street school in aid of the Widnes Victoria Entertainment Party. There was a crowded audience Mr. H. Wade Deacon J.P.,C.C.; had been announced to preside but he was unable, through ill-health, to attend,the chair being occupied by Mr. B. Brown. The Widnes Subscription Prize Band, attended, under the able conductship of Mr. J. B. Harper, and played the selections "Elixir of Love" and " William Tell " in a most praiseworthy manner. The following programme was also sustained in an ad- mirable.manner, the artistes each acquitting themselves excellently. Songs "The Storm Fiend," and "Anchored," Mr. A. Shingler ; "Come back to Erin," and "Kathleen Mavourneen," Miss E. Guise ; " For Ever and for Ever" (encored). and ".Killarney," Mrs. Ainsley ; " Pilgrim of Love," Mr. H. Pilgrim. Humorous songs. " The Ocean Trip " (enc‘ored) Mr. W. McCririe ; " The Birthday Party " (twice encored) ; and " The stammering Sweet- hearts," (encored), Mr. A. J. Paton. Violin solos, " The Heart bowed down" and" When other lips," Mr. F. Booth. The humorous sketch "The Barber's Shop," was given by seven members of the entertaining party and caused much laughter. The duties of accompanists were performed by Professor J. J. F. Ainsley,F.S.Sc.,and Master A. Barber in the most satisfactory manner. During the interval a vote of thanks to the chairman and artistes was passed on the motion of Councillor Hodgkinson and Mr. T. S. Swale.

A RUNCORN MAN DIES F 12.07,.:, INHALATION OF GAS. About five o'clock on Saturday evening, a Runcorn man named William Blease, of Warrington-road, North- wich, aged 20, who was engaged as a labourer at the Chemical Works of Messrs. Bowman, Thompson, and Co., Limited, Lostock, was found lying insensible im one of the towers connected with the ammonia-soda branch of the works. A telephonic communication was des- patched to Dr. Joynson, the works surgeon and local inspector under the Factory Acts, and Mr. Gerald Joyn- son at once proceeded to the laboratory, to which place the unfortunate man had been rem-wed. It was then evident that life was extinct, but a7rtifical respiration was applied for a considerable time without effect. It is believed that death was due to the inhalation of car- bonic acid or some other poisonous gas. It is stared that deceased had no business in the place where he was found, and that the cause for his presence there is un- known. Mr. H. C. Yates opened the inviry respecting the death of William Blease, on Monday afternon at the Bowling Green Inn' Witton, Mr. Henry Bates was fore- man of the jury. The only witness called was John Blease, brother to deceased; who stated that deceased lodged with him in Warringtoh-road. They both went on the two o'clock shift, and during the afternoon he frequently saw his brother. About five minutes before he was found lying insensible, deceased was working the liquorpump and appeared to be all right.—The in- quest was adjourned in order that the Factory Inspector might be present.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. There were present Mr. J. Mclntyre (chairman), Mr. S. H. Woodhouse (ex-officio), Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, Dr. Gastaldi, and J. Hanby, Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., J. Brandreth, E. Aaron, J. D. Jones, C. W. Whitley, A. R. Norman, J. M. Williams, H. E. Heywood, J. Parr, E. Bratherton, T. Baxter, C.C., T. Handley, T. Lea, T. Lewis, T. Ford, W. Pickering, C. W. Davenport; J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: EDUCATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE EDUCATION QUESTION.

A letter was read from the Local Govern ment Board with reference to the proposed deterthination of the ap- pointment of Mr. Thomas Bowyer as Inquiry Officer in the Runcorn Union'. and transmitting an extract from a communication which they had received from the Run- corn School Board on the subject. The Board requested to be furnished with the observations of the Guardians on the representations contained in the enclosed communica- tion. The School Board pointed out that as his appoint- ment by the Guardians in 1887, was made at the re- quest of the School Board for the benefit of the School Attendance Committee, the Board felt that it rested with them to give the reasons why his services should be returned. Prior to his appointment, much difficulty was experienced from the fact that parents could not be induced to apply to the reliev!ng officer for payment of school fees for their children, who were in consequence absent from school. To obviate this, the matter was represented to the Board of Guardians, who consented to appoint Mr. Bowyer, School Fees Inquiry Officer, thus avoiding the necessity for sending applicants to the relieving cfficer. His Board also granted the Local Committee of Guardians the use of a room in their offices so that their meetings for investigations might be held away from the Union office. This arrangement put an end to the evils, by them being attended to, and it had worked admirably ever since. The present Board of Guardians in proposing to dismiss Mr. Bowyer were pro- bably not aware of those facts. There would be no ob- jection to Mr. Bowyer attending at the Guardians' Board meetings, but for the fact that they were held at Dutton, a place six miles away, and difficult of ac- cess. All the day would be required, and he could not be spared from his regular duties. His Board could not ascertain why he was wanted at Dutton. He submitted the cases to the committee of investigation which met in Runcorn, the parents being present. His duty was then at an end, unless the investigatioa was to be re-opened at Dutton, which did not appear. The committee re- commended the payments to the Board, and could ans- wer any questions that might be asked. The amount at stake was only about £lO per annum, and it was a separate charge upon the township of Runcorn.—Mr. Brandreth said that the salary was not a separate charge upon Runcorn. They helped Runcorn to pay their in- quiry officer. (Laughter.)—Mr.Taylor : Nothing of the sort.—Mr. Brandretli (continuing) said he was sick of the whole business.—Mr. A. R. Norman was pleased to hear Mr. Ilrandreth was sick of the business, and he moved that the Runcorn Committee attend to the Run- corn cases, and that the thing remain as it was.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded. Why they wished to alter the ar- rangements he could not understand.—Mr.Flanby moved as an amendment that the Guardians reply to the Local Government Board that they had considered the reasons which influenced the Guardians in their original appoint- ment,and they were perfectly satisfied with the arrange- ment as it existed.—Mr. A. R. Norman said he would withdraw his motion in favour of Mr. Hanby's, and Dr. Gastaldi seconded the motion.—Mr. Brandreth said that there was no one in the rural district who had to pay fees, and the people of Runcorn ought to be ashamed of themselves in charging the Union with fees. They ought to have free education.—Mr. Taylor said that they were sick of hearing Mr. Brandreth say so much about the question. (Laughter.) He thought before the question arose that day that it was fully settled. It was all about a paltry £5. (Laughter.) He was really pleased to hear Mr. Brandreth say that be was sick of the question.— Mr. Brandreth moved that the reply to the Local 6overn- meet Board be that the Guardians do not retract from their position at all.—Mr. Parr seconded.—Mr. Handley said that they did not wish to put the taint of pauperism upon the peonle. People who applied to the relieving officer had felt that it was a stigma, and it was there- fore arranged that the attendance officer of the School Board should receive applications, and that committee to investigate cases. He opposed Mr. Brandreth's Deo- tion.—Mr.Hanby said that the present arrangement was a satisfactory one.—Mr. A. R. Norman endorsed every- thing that Mr. Brandreth said as to' the desirability of having free education,but Mr. Brandreth's remarks were against an Act of Parliament which they could not alter, and they would have to pay the fees until the Act was altered.—On a vote being taken, Mr. Brandreth's motion was carried by ten votes to seven.

div.head: HOMES FOR INEBRIATES.
div.p: HOMES FOR INEBRIATES.

A letter was received from the Manchester Board of Guardians with a copy of a memorial which they had addressed to the Horne Secretary urging him to introduce a measure into the House of Commons for the purpose et amending the provisions of the Inebriates Acts of 1879 and 1883. If the Board approved of the object, they asked them to adopt a similar memorial and sent it to the Home Secretary. In the memorial it is stated that in the opinion of the memorialists it was desirable that the Acts named should be amended, and supplemented by further legislation with the view of making persons coming within the definition of habitual drunkards in the Act of 1879 amenable to the jurisdiction of justices, should be empowered to send such persons for a limited turn without their own consent to institutions provided ; for their reception.—The Guardians of Toxteth Park. Liverpool,also wrote with reference to the Liquor Traffic and Chronic Inebriates Bills, enclosing a petition stating 1" that your petitioners in the discharge of their publi c ' function are called upon to relieve the destitute and to pay out of the funds in their hands, the cost of pauper lunatics. That your petitioners have abundant oppor- tunities of observing the causes which lead to destitution and lunacy, the most conspicuous of which is the exces- sive indulgence in alcoholic drink. That your petitioners believe that by better regulations for the sale of alcoholic liquor by placing it more under the control of the masses ot the people themselves, one of the great active forces producing social degradations, far-reaching misery, and mental degeneracy, resulting ultimately in pauperism, disease, crime, and death will be diminished. That in a portion of your petitioner's township where public- houses are prohibited, by the condition of the leases, occupied mostly by a working class population, the amount of pauperism is very small and a lew death rate. —Mr. Hanby moved that the Chairman sign the peti- tions on behalf of the Board.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded the motion. He said that the proposal was the only method for the conversion of drunkards. It was his experience that this could not be done in England except by Act of Parliament.—Mr. Brandreth said that he would be pleased to support the Manchester petition, but he thought the Liverpool petition was too political as it brought in the Loc.il Veto Bill.—Mr. Hanby and Dr. Gastaldi said that that was the petition they nseant.— The resolution to sign the Manchester petition was passed unanimously.

div.head: RUNCORN CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH
div.p: RUNCORN CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH
ANNUAL TEA MEETING.

The annual congregrtional tea meeting in connec- tion with the above church was held on Wednesday evening in the Bethesda schoolroom. A good num- ber of persons sat down to tea, after which a meet- ing was held, under the presidency of the Rev. J. Simpson. The chairman, in the course of his address, pleaded for personal holiness, and stated hat John McNeil once described a congregational gathering where the reports from different societies of the churches were heard with applause, all showin that much work had been done in certain directions. Then Christ was heard coming up the steps, who asked what about the personal holiness of the people attending the church. Where were the reports of many turned from darkness into light ? There was no reply, because there was no such report to present. The people outside the Church might believe in Christianity. but they did not believe in the man who attended the Christian church. Be stated that they had much to congratulate themselves upon in con- nection with Bethesda, and remarked that the evening services had been so largely attended and there was such a demand for seats that those kept apart Lea long time for children had now to be let. He urged them to be punctual and regular in their attendance at the services and tried to prevail upon them to be present more par- ticularly in the morning. Mr. Chadwick stated that Mr. Simpson had addressed them on a very important subject, and he hoped his remarks won', d well in the minds of the members of the congregation. eunctualitv was the soul of business, and it might be said to be th-c same regarding worship. To him the devotional part of the services was of more importance than the ser- mon.—A pro,:ramme was gone through, in which Miss Johnson and Mr. E. Worrall rave a duet with consider- able effect; Mr. and Mrs. Burn were loudly applauded for their interpretation of a duet with guitar accompani- ment. Mr. W. Outhwaite gave a recitation, and a dialogue entitled" April Fools," was given by Messrs. George Acton, J. Ainsworth, and E. Roberts.—A part of the proceedings was devoted to the sale of the articles • left over froin the recent baz tar. The ladies who pre- sided at the stalls were Mrs. T. Handley, Mrs. Cameron Miss Lydiate, Mrs. Turner, Mrs. Powell, Mrs. Littler, and Miss Littler. A considerable number of articl es met with purchasers.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

THE WATERMEN'S DISPUTE. Up to Saturday morning there was every likelihood ' that the members of the Upper Mersey Watermen and Porters' Association, would cease to navigate their craft in the afternoon, through no terms having been arranged with the Manchester Ship Canal Company (Bridgewater Undertaking), and other water carrying firms, in aceord- , ance with the circular issued by the association on the 7th inst. This contained their demands with reference to increased tonnage rates, -minimum weights, over- time, non-handling of cargo, Sunday labour, and hours of rest, full particulars of which have already been pub- lished. On the other hand the company considered the demands excessive, and stated that the average wages lof the flatmen for the week ending January 27th were as follows :—Manchester section: Captains, £1 12s. 7d. I hands, 1 73. ; Liverpool section : Captains, £1 113 s. ; hands, £1 83.; Runcorn section: Captains, LI. us. 3d.; hands, £163. In addition to this the men have lodgings on board the flats, and are also supplied I with fuel, light, bedding, and certain clothing. The men state that the wages received by them are 15s. and 103. per week for captains and hands respectively, but, on the other side, it is said that the amounts ought to be 163. and lls, respectively, which are the standing wages,. exclusive of "ton-money," which practically doubles the pay. The standing wages are intended for subsis- tence in case of failing trade, or when ths canal is frozen. The question of hours and the handling of cargo is also- involved in the dispute. On Saturday morning the president and secretary cf the Watermen's Association (Mr. Billam and Mr. Gat. ley) waited upon Mr. Henry Collier and other represen- tatives of the Canal Company, at Manchester, when the subject was thoroughly gone into. Matters were dis- cussed In a most agreeable manner, and ultimately it was understood that a basis for the arrangement on satis- factory agreement had been arrived at, for Mr. Gatley, during the afternoon, despatched to Runcorn and other important centres on ths Bridgewater Canal, a telegram instructing the fiatmen to remain at work, pending a $ ttlement of the dispute on Wednesday. It was de-- Sded at the conference not to publish the proposed C3rm3 until the negotiations had been completed on the date named. Tke information on becoming known gate I universal satisfaction, fer the dislocation of the water- carrying business, for even a short time, meant throw- ing out of employment a large number of persons be- side those actually engaged in navigation. At a meet- ing of watermen, on Saturday night, at Rnncorn, the fiatmen expressed their gratification at the prospect of an amicable settlement of the dispute.

div.head: PROPOSED GRAVING DOCK AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PROPOSED GRAVING DOCK AT RUNCORN.

; The provision of a graving dock at Runcorn is receiv- ing the earnest consideration of the directors of the Canal Company, and it is confidently expected that the conduct of the operations will not be delayed a moment longer than possible. The necessity of making con- • veniences for the repairing of vessels becomes daily more important, and the decision of those in authority is keenly awaited. There used to be four shipbuilding yards at the Old Quay, in close proximity to the Mersey, and if the graving dock was placed in this locality, it would be in a splendid position on the bank of the canal. The stonework of the old docks is also undisturbed, to that to a great extent matters are ready to the hands of the company. The recommencement of constructing vessels would be a boon to the town. It is understood that instructions have been received in Runcorn to build three new barges, about a hundred feet long, 20 feet beam, and clese upon ten feet deep, for the company. These are larger than the fleet of lighters constructed a year or two ago. Rumour has it that other important developments are about to be made in connection with the canal in this part of Cheshire, and that Runcorn will become a very important centre of the undertaking. Several matters are engaging the careful attention ef the directors.

div.head: COLLISION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: COLLISION AT RUNCORN.

A somewhat serious collision occurred on the Man- chester Ship Canal, near the Runcorn Docks on Sunday at noon. The Dagmar and the Bridgwater, two tugs belonging to the company, were moored to the side of' the waterway. The Royal Prince, of Newcastle, in tow ot the tug Agnes Seed, was proceeding t) Manchester when she became unmanageable, evidently through the strong current. She first struck the Dagmar, damaging her bulwarks, and then glided into the Bridgwater, which was moored abreast of the Gower, cutting her sponson beam in two and caused serious injuries to ber bulwarks. Fortunately she broke adrift, otherwise she would have been cut in two. The Royal Prince to all appearance escaped uninjured.

div.head: SETTLEMENT OF THE WATERMEN'S DISPUTE.
div.p: SETTLEMENT OF THE WATERMEN'S DISPUTE.

On Wednesday afternoon a conference took place in Manchester between Mr. Collier, the manager of the Bridgewater Canal. and the Manchester, Liverpool, Run- corn, and Warringfon agents (Messrs. bolt, McKay, Meadowcroft and Evans) on behalf of the Ship Canal Company; and Mr. Billan, Mr. Gatley, and several others representing the watermen. The proceedings were conducted in private, and extended over four hours. At the outset the representatives of the men in- timated that the demand with reference to flatmen mat to handle cargo was withdrawn. The discussion was conducted in a very amicable manner, and the length of the interview was in a great measure caused by techni- calities that demanded attention. With respect to the tonnage rates a sart of cempromise was, effected, so far as concerned the Manchester docks and local traffic. Tile watermen have thus obtained concessions. It is be- lieved on both sides that the arrangement arrived at will Fbe a lasting one. The announcement that the dispute had been settled withaut the necessity of a strike has given great satisfaction ia Runcorn, Preston Brook,. , Warrington, and other centres, which are so deeply in- terested in water carriage.
MESSRS. FAIRCLOUCiEI AND SONS AND THE CANAL.

The action brought by Messrs. Fairclough and Sons, Mersey Flour Mills. against the ship Canal Company,. for the alleged stoppage of the plaintiffs mill through:. the extraction of water from the river by the defeni- ants, will be heard next Thursday. It is alleged that not only has the volume of water entering into tile, Mersey .from the Bollin been diminished since the open- ing of the canal, but that the tide is longer coming up, to Warrington by the river than by Vie canal, nnd navi— gation.on-iir,.. river is impeded. The Mersey Conserv— ancy Board also intend to take action in the matter. The Ship Canal Company have been taking steps to come to some agreement in the liattcr. They have already raised the sluice gates at Latchford Locks 18 inches which wilrratise, mare water to go lute tlio river.

div.head: DR. GOILNALL AND THE WARRINGTOZT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: DR. GOILNALL AND THE WARRINGTOZT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
StIAW IS "TOO PREVIOUS."

At the conclusion of the ordinary business of the. Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday,. Mr. W. J. SHAIV said :—I wish to draw your atten- tion to the fact that the time of Ole adjournment of the question of Dr. Gorriall's contract as vaccination officer, is now n an end. I now rise to support the application that I made a year ago that the ap- pointment held by Dr. Gornall be taken from him and attacheil, as it was formerly, to the medical officership, of the Union. The appointment was held by Dr. SpinkS• but unfortunately it was taken from him in something like the 3.,•ear 1870, not through his own fault, but. through some fault of an assistant. Dr. Gornall held th& appointment of public officer of health and he obtained the post of vaccination officer when it was taken from Dr. Spinks. I only ask you out of reason to place the two appnintments together as they were beforu Dr. Gornall held the appointment. I find that after Dr. Gornall obtained the appointment he was appointed medical officer of health to the borough of Warrington. He then resigned as officer of health to the Union but retained the appointment of vaccination officer. Now. we have in our two medical officers, two young and energetic officers, and I propose that this appointment. snould be taken by them conjointly. One of the chief' reasons why I advocate this is because Dr. Gornall, as. medical officer of health to the borough, is always in the. thick of infectious diseases and I do not think it right. that he should be allowed to do the work of vaccination. officer under those circumstances. I maintained that a.. year ago—l maintain it now. What I propose is that the appointment should be divided. Dr. Braids as the, medical offic2r for No. 1 district to take the vaccination in that district,and Dr. Peacock to take the vazcinationB. in his district—No. 2." Mr. HEATON : I second the motion. The CLERK: There is no motion before the Board.

Mr. SHAW: It iS the adjourned motion. The CLERK : There is no motion—the matter is out of order. There are two difficulties in the way of Mr.. Shaw. In the first place it is not twelve months since- the question was adjourned, and in the second place the motion which Mr. ilaw endeavours to move now is not the one which was moved when the question was ad- journed. Mr. Shaw : Oh . 'l'he CLERIC : The motion then moved by Mr. Shaw was to the effect that 28 days notice be given to Dr. Grornail to terminate his contract with the Board as vac• cination officer but that he be permitted to apply for re- appointment. Mr. SHAW : Oh, but—

The CLERK : Allow me to finish please. Mr. Shaw • moved the moti,in I have mentioned and it was second- ed by Mr. A. Jolley, and after a long discussion It was decia?d, upon the proposition of Mr. Rylands, seconded by Mr. Helton that the matter be adjourned for twelve' months dating from 19th April. So that in the first . place ale prescribed time had not elapsed, and in the second place Mr. Shaw had not spoken upon the origi- nal motirm. The matter is out of ,order and cannot ho discussed.
Mr. RA/CLIFFE (in the chair) : I thought that would be in the way. The matter then dropped.

tohn Hedgeock, plumber, Mill;street; was charged at the Warrlngtan Borough Court, on lgonday, with fubously driving a horse aand trap in Horseinarket-street enTibruary 14. Sergeant Taylor' said that on the day in question he saw the defendant drive a horse and trap backwards and forwards -,twice, in Horsemarket-street, and then proceed towards Marlicet Gate at a high rate of speed. Although witness shouted and held up his hand, defendant never took any notice. He would be going about ten or twelve miles an hour.—Constable Delahay corroborated and said that he would be going about ten miles an hour.—William Mother and William Rowlands also gave similar evidence.—lnspector. Thomas Ireland, the old Cheshire Cheese, was charged at the Warrington Borough Court on Mdi3day, that on Jai]. 19, he sold to the prejudice of Eliza Hill, certain whisky adulterated with 44 per cent of of water. In- spector Norman 'aid that on the day in question he sent Eliza Hill into the Cheshire Cheese for a pint of whisky. He afterwards went in and took the whisky, and told the landlord he would divide it into three parts and he could have one. The landlord agreed and on the whisky being submitted te the public analyst, it was discovered 7.,0 contain 44 per cent of water, or 19 per cent more than was allowed by Act of Parliament.—Mr. Arthur Browne, who appeared for the defendant said that the day in question was the day when till' Venango went through the Latchford locks. 11r.Ireland had made ready what be thought sufficient whisky for the day, but about thirty gentlemen came into the houae,and strangs to say, they all wanted whisky. Mr. Irelaud was out at the time, and Mr. Ireland, who was net accustomed to mix the whisky was obliged t 4 do so, and unfortunately she put too much water in. The whole thing was quite a mistake, and there had never been a previous charge against the defendant.—The bench fined defendant 203. and costs. Thomas Nixon, of the Black Bear Inn, was fined 103, and costs for having whisky adulterdted with 29 per cent of water or 4 per cent more than allowed by Act of Parlianaent. The defendant said that his wife had mixed the wiiiiky that day., and had put too much water in by mistake.—Mr. White (magistrates' clear) "The poor wives.are at fault in both cases." (Laughter.)

Music LICENSE. Mr. Percy Davies applied at the Warringten Borough Court, on Monday, on behalf of John Davies, landlord of the Baths Hotel, formorly the Millstone Inn, for a muslc license for that public-house. The Chief Constable said that a few weeks ago, Mr. Davies applied for tempor- ary authority for John Davies as licensee of the Millstone publie-house. Up to that time, he (the Chief Constable) did not know the applicant. After the application was granted, Davies came to him and told him that he had been in business in Liverpool, and also somewhere, in the neighbourhood of Old Trafford, and he received a good;character from each of those places. Be also learned that Henry Gittens, who for ten years lived at the " Swan," Bridge-st., was brother-in-law of the appli- cant, who had recently lost his wife. He understood that Mr. Gittens and his wife were going to manage the "Millstone." He only hoped that Gittens would not give the same amount of trouble to:the police as he did at the" Swan." He, did not wish to be vindictive but there was a good number of parsons on the lookout, and if he (Mr. Hunt), failed in anything it would be brought to the magistrates' notice very quickly.—Mr. Davies said that his client was answerable for the conduct of the house, and there was nothing aeainst his,character. He was at present tryingto get rid of a business in Worsley, in order to look after the place properly. If he was going to employ his brother-in-law he was a nswerable for what was done. Ile (Mr. Davies) understood that it was nine years since Mr. Gittens was summoned last.—The Chief Constable said that was in the-year 1887.—Peter Lawles, also applied for a music license for the Corporation Inn. —The magistrates retired to consider their decisions and when they returned Alderman Holmes (preeiding magistrate), said that they had decided to gra'. t both applications, but there must be no misbehaviour in the " Millstone."

div.p: A MIDNIGHT _DESPER.kDO..

At the Warrington Borough Court on Tuesday morn- ing' Patrick Burke, a rough-looking man, and a stranger in the town was charged with being a rogue and vaga- bond found frequenting Battersby-lane, at twenty minutes to one that morning with intent to commit a felony, and he was also charged with assaulting Mr. Whitfield and his son.—Mr. Hunt stated that about 12.30 that morning P.C. Lewis met the prisoner near Battersby-lane, but after asking him a few questions and searching him he allowed him to go, and the prisoner proceeded towards Warrington. When the prisoner was passing Mr. Whitfield's provision shoo. he put his foot through a large square of window. Mr. Whitfield came out, and a man vvno saw the prisoner put his foot in the window told Mr. Whitfield who it was. The complain- ant went up to him and asked the prisoner what he had done it for, whereupon the prisoner struck him a vary heavy blow on the Lead. A scuffle ensued and Mr. Whit- field was struck repeatedly. Mr. Whitfield's son who came to his father's assistance was also assaulted. With the assistance of a man named Laurence Gleave the prisoner was brouszht to the police station. Evidence in corroboration of the Chief Constable's statement was

giveia-bi P.C. Lew, Laurqice Weave, and the cona- plainants.—The prisoner said he must have a mania for doing such things when ho was drunk, but he didn't remember anything about it. He had served four months in gaol for a similar offonce, and the magistrates committed him to gaol for three months' hard labour. CRUELTY TO Floask s. At the Warricgton Borough Court, ycsterday, Thomas

Clare, hawker, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state on February 10. Inspector Luff, B.S.P.C. A. , said that he saw the horse at Market Gate on the 10th inst. and noticed that it was in a poor con- dition. being completely worn out. Defendant had bought it for 253. There was a great deal of trouble with hawkers owing to the selling of horses which were complained about to some one else, and thus keeping, them at work and causing the animals pain, instead of killin4Wiern.—Defendant said that the horse was killed, but the magistrates adjourned the case until Monday, Iso that the inspector could find out if thisowas true. Thomas Drinkwater, Pinners Brow, was charged with working a horse in an unfit state on February 14. Inspec- tor Luff said that he saw the animal attached to a 'lons in Corporation-st., and as it appeared uneasy, he exam- ined it. He discovered that on the top of the withers 'where the collar touched the skin there was a very ten- der portion,where the hcrse could not bear to be touched even with the finger.—P.C. Barlow and Ipspector Spinks corroborated, and the magistrates fined defendant 2a.6d and costs. HAYING' IT 111 TOR LORB SALISBURY AND MR. Bersoon. at the Warriagtan Borough Court yesterday, James Hayes Sankey Bridges, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street at 11.15, the previous night, and also with assaulting Police Sergeant Taylor, while being conveyed inti the cells.—P.C. Itylstt said that he was in Sankey-street when he saw the prisoner very drunk, and he was obliged to bring him to the police-station.—Prisoner was asked if he wished to ask the officer any questions, t• which he replied, in a non- chalant manner, "Nothing, only they have broken rny neck and smashed my ribs." (Laughter.)—P.S. Taylor who appeared in the box with a black eye, said that he assisted the last witness to bring the prisoner to the police-station. He was very drunk, and using some violent language towards Lord Salisisury and Mr. Bat- four—(laughter)—saying that he would have it in for them. He acted almost like a madman. (Alderman Harrisou: "He must have been -mad.") The prisoner struck him several times on the way to the police- station, and on being taken to the cells. prissmer gave him a violent blow in the eye, while he was unlocking the door.—The prisoner again accused the police of breaking his head and smaAhieg his ribs.—The magis- trates sent him to gaol for 21 days without the option of a fine.—Mr. White (magistrates' clerk). "He. can get his ribs mended there." (Laughter.) BRBACIIES TRH FACTORY ACT.

George Wallington, builder, Froghall-lane, was charged at the Warrington Borough Court yesterday, that on January 30, he had emp:oy-ed a young person named James Edward Tickle, more than seven days without having obtained a medical certificate. He was further charged that he had net the prescribed form or register of the employment of such young person. Mr. Charles W. Shaw, H.M. Inspictor of Factories said that the law required that when a boy was engaged, a medical certi- ficate should be obtained within seven days. and also a register kept. This the defendant had not done, al- though the boy had been employed for five months. He was 15 years of age.—Mr. Wallington admitted the offence, but.said that it was quite an oversight, and was quite unintentional.—The magistrates fined defendant 2s. ed. and coats on each charge. Joseph Matthews, Mersey-at., was charged with not giving ncitice to the Inspector of Factories ot his having opened a new saw. mills, and also with not having an abstract of the Act exhibited in his works.—Mr. Shaw said that it was necessary to give notice to the Inspector upon opening a new business and as this was the first case in this neighbourhood he would not press for a heavy penalty.—Defendant who pleaded ignorance of the law, was fined in the costs. William Barri% Bank Quay, was also charged with not giving notice to the inepector of his opening a new ,saw mills in Bank Quay. This case was similar to the last one and defendant was also fined in the costs.

THEFT OF A DRESS.—Mars, Ann Davies .was ehere•ed with stealing from the dwelling house of Frederick Joseph Browning, 13 Lower Ship Yard, on January 24, a maroon dress piece; and a handkerchief, value 13s. The chief constable said that the complainant was a ship canal labourer, and on January 20, he lost his wife. The 'defendant thereupon come t, :the house and offered to look after the house and children. On January 23, she went away rather suddenly. A few days. afterwards, the complainant became very mech &Tressed in spirits, and cut Ws throat, which necessitated his removal to. the Infirmary. Be remained. there. until FebrUary 24, and was brought Ware. the inagietrates and discharged. On getting home, he miee4d the dress and other a rtieles and the matter wae reported to DeteciVe Monaghan who discovered that they had been pledged At Morton's 'pawnshop, Bridge Foot by the prisoryer on the very day she had left Brownings house. Monaghan arrested prisoner, and brought her to the police station. When charged with the nett,- sT:e sail that she had been sent by Browning,. to pawn the articles—Frederick Joseph Browning on being sworn denied that he had over given prisoner permission to take the articles away.—Chadatte Massey, and Edward Green, and Detective Monaghan having given- evidence, the Magistrates imposed a fine of, of 203. or fourteen days imprisonment -in default.- - FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Aid. Wright, M. W. Pierpoint. and-Councillor Roberts. SHOCKING ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.—Eliza Brady, 46, Watkin-st.,was charged with assaulting Mary Jane Owen with a flat iron,on Thursday afternoon. The complain- ant, whose face presented a pitiable spectacle, said that some time ago some one lodging with Mrs. Brady had taken a bass from her house. She went to Mrs.Bradv's house for it, when Mrs. Brady replied that she owed her 4s.,and struck her a violent blow in the face with a flat iron, and knocked her to the floor, and struck her seve- ral times. - A bricklayer named Richard Drury, Pulled Mrs. Brady off her.—Several -witneses were called in support of coniplainant's stery, and P.C. Wood said he was called to Watkin-st.because of the row,and when he got there- he thought Mrs. Owen's eye was knocked out it was bleeding a° much. He took Mrs. Brady to the Police Station, and when charged with the assault, she admitttel it.—Prisoner said that she was struck first by the complainant, and that there was a fight between them. She denied using the flat iron.—The Magistrates inflicted a fine of 103. and costs, or 14 days' hard la- bour.

ASSAULT ON A WIFE.—John Lee,Academy-st.,was charged with assaulting his wife, Annie Lee, on Wednesday. Mrs. Lee stated that her husband came home on Wednesday and found fault about the tea not being ready. She asked him fotiorne money to get some, and he gave her a shilling. He went out again,and she got the tea ready. When he came back without any warning, he came be- hind her and hit her on the head with his fist. She had been constantly turned out of the house by her husband, and all one night she had had to bleep in the Police Sta- tion. She would very much wish for a separation.— The Chief Constable said that he knew that Mrs. Lee had been brutrily Mused by her husband, and it had been going on for months. Lee was a very clever man at his trade as confectioner, but was such a violent man, ad- dicted to bouts of drunkenness. Mrs. Lee had a beauti- ful home, and it was very clean, and Mr. Taylor, the Police Court Missionary,had done all he could to reform the husband.—Mr. Taylor said that he had visited the house, and he believed that drink was the cause of all the unpleasantnesa.—The magistrates decided to adjourn the cas,, for a month on defendant promising to behave himself towards his wife in the future.

Houghton's wireworks,' I where he stopped her. Mr. Davies contended that it I was not an'ordinary drunk case. The day was very cold and the defendant's sister had asked her to have a glass of whisky. and It was that that made her drunk. She had never been brought up before. The magistrates Imposed a fine of ss. and costs, 15s. in all. Mr. Davies thought that was very hard in a case of that sort.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 24, 1894,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 24, 1894,
lIEETOG OF REOHAMTES AT, RUNCORN.

In connection with the local tents of the above order a crowded meeting was held in the Bethesda Lecture Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday,evenirg, udder the presidency of the Rev. J. Simpson, who was supported by the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, Coun- cillor Dimond (Southport), Bros. Warburt.on (sec.) Lea (trea.), Cartwright, Palin, and Richa.rdson.-7- The chairman at the outset said he considered that the temperance party in Runcorn required to be awakened, so that they would pursue their efforts with increased determination. The settlement of a number of the social problems of the age would be effected by the removal of the drinking customs that prevailed. He urged all present to do what they could to uproot the evil, and to destroy it. They ought not to make drink- ing attractive as the• Bishop of Chester was trying to do; but ratbereradicate it root and branch, which was the bnly salvation for tkeir country.—.-Mr. Warburton spake of the progress of the movement in Runcorn. He showed that there were now two adult and twojuvenile tents in the town, and that whereas in 1874 they had Drily a handful of =embers, they now numbered 280, and had behind them a sick fund of over 1470. The funeral expenses were contributed by the district lodge, which had in hand over £3OO for that purpose. He pointed out that the juveniles were taught to conduct their own business, by the initiation of members, and the election of officers.—Councillor Dimond gave some particulars as to the spread of the order during the past 25 years. Then they had 15,000 members all told. In 1883 they had increased to 35,000, and two years later to 55,000. Since then they had increased in vast numbers, adding to their ranks 10,000 men every year, so that now the order embraced 135,000 mem- bers. The juvenile lodges contained 70,000 boys, who knew not the taste of intoxicating drink. The average age of the members ten years ago stood at 39, but now it had been reduced to 29 years. He strongly pressed upon temperance workers the necessity of increased effort in promoting their noble cause, and thus bring abut an improved state of things.—The Rev. J. Pulford Williams alluded to the opposition that was being directed against teetotalers by the brewing trade, and remarked that this was in order to save their fast sink- ing craft. He hoped that the Grand Old Man would be spared to wipe away the stain on what was otherwise a bright and unsullied career, by doing away with grocers' licenses. (Applause.) They bad every reason to be encouraged in their operations, for all around them they saw signs of progress. What they should do was to press the Government to pass a measure giving rate- payers more direct control respecting the renewal of licenses. The Christian Church ought to rise up in earnest in the conflict with the brewers, who by their nefarious calling were trying to destroy the morality and spirituality of the people.—During the evening a well selected programme was gone through and the items greatly enjoyed. The mandoline and guitar baud gave a couple of selections ; songs were contributed by Mrs. Temperley, Miss Sirakin, Miss Hayes, Mr. Branch and Mr. E. Worrall. Miss Littler gave a reading; Mr. and Mrs. Burn interpreted a dnet, with guitar accompani- ment; and Miss Cartwright played a pianoforte solo. The ascompauirnexts were played by Mr. Price.

How many times had the " excellent" grant been obtained in each of , the senior girls' schools during the last 10 years? 4. He had not heard of any dissatisfaction among the teachers. Be was informed that the resignations would not have been ten- dered if the teachers considered they, had been fairly dealt with by the members of the School Management Committee.—The Chairman stated that the complaint should have been sent to the committee in the first in- stance, and he was sure it would have been considered. —The subject then dropped and the minutes were passed.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM.

Amon the 1,500 Warriugtonians who accompanied the home team on Saturday to Oldham; on the occasion of the most important match of the season, there were few who were not intensely interested. Oldham have been beaten once during the season, and that was by TyWesley, and oemsequently show a much mere credit- able sheet than Warrington. However, it was a general impression that Warriagton would come out of the fray adorned with the wreath of victory. John Bata was away, and his plass' was filled by Evans to whose positioa at three-quarters,Broady was relegated. A snow storm prevailed most of the time, and though the players deserve much credit for keeping the " ball a-rolling " •under these circumstances, more credit was due to the gate of 4,000 people who defied the' biting blasts of the bleak blizzard, and kept themselves warm by their en- thusiasm. The teams were of,the following composition: . Warrington: Full back, F. Heesom, •, three-quarters, F. Broady, P. Carey, C,. Potts, and H. Barber; half backs, J. W. Evans and James Bate; forwards, Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, J. Taylor, G. Dakin, J. Buckley, W. Berry; and J. T. Thorniley. Oldham : Full back, W. L. Farmington; three-quarters, W. McCurcheon, S. I,ees, D. Gwynn, and J. Hirst; half backs. H. Varley and A. Lees; forwards, J. Chadwick, J. Boardman, G. Furness, J. Murrell, E. Hughes, r. Boaster, T. Sellers, and J. Barnes.

1 • aeuurn, MULL V . Sellars started against both wind and snow, and although no reply was forthcoming, Oldham's stay at the Warrington quarter flag was of brief duration, for Carey backing up some excellent work of the forwards, dribbled inely into the home half. Fine kicking by Bate was seconded by the resolute tackling of Carey and Potts of Pennington, who was hard pressed near his charge. Sellars and Boardman gained a little relief, but Warring- to/1 asserted themselves, and successive essays by Jolley, Turner, and Potts almost proved. disastrous. Gwynn tried to clear in accepting a pass from Varlev, but Potts soon had his man, and again the Oldham geel escaped in a marvellous manner. Broady checked the onward career of Boardman and S. Lees, and as quick was the return to the home lines, Bate kicking judiciously, whilst Evans toe found touch. The players presented a . pitiable sight, and it was not with any degree of cer- tainty that they were distinguished. A mark to Bate saw that player again kicking high to Pennington, and Jolley was held on the line. From a pack here Evans, Babe and Broady paseed, but the venture did net prove profitable, for AeCutelieon spoiled the sequence, and OLdharn at last reached the quarter-flag. Here scrim. DiaeS ensued, and the monotony was relieved when the visiting forwards screwed well,and cross dribbling again saw Oldham save luckily. From a long throw-out Carey beok the oval eplendidly, and looked all over a scorer until Gwynn gra3.-Aid him when he was about to run between the posts. A grand bit of work by M'Cut- cheon and Purities again made the Oldham man breathe more freely, but Heesom for the first time In the match with • lofty kick made the locals beat a hasty retreat. Pcona some loose play Thorniley got ever, but for some reason (apparently only known by the referee) the point was over-ruled. Instead of the try Warrington were penalized, and Jolley met the kick, the county forward ltadin!"' the way again to the line in company with Bnckley and Turner. A knock-on spoiled the essay, and f'Ottd met a kiek by Hurst, raciag up and booting Pennington on his line. A sliee'oflucklavoured the home custodian, fur after losing possession he re- covered with a host of opponents round him. McCut- cheon cleared, but fine kicking by Bate behind the pack maintained .Warriagtores aggressive tactics. Oldhire ware again favoured with penalty kicks, whilst after another spell of scrimmages Berry led the way to Pen- ningtoe, and When ht the act of guiding the ball over the line the greasy state of the ball spoiled the well- meant intention. Jolley dribbled finely, but over-ran the oval, and again a chance was missed. whilst Broady kicked injudiciously, and a second minor was sent up. Heesom piloted back the drop-out, and passing by Evans and Bate saw the latter giving 'Barber his first oppor- tunity in.the match. ge failed to round Hurst, but punted neatly to the line, A vigorous tackle of Potts delayed the game a little, but on resuming Barber again showed his eterling worth by making another bold bid for a • try; Warrlngton again experienced hard lines, just before the interval, for a fine rush saw Penn- ington failing to field the oval, and only at the second time of asking save near his posts, the whistle then sounded with no substantial score. On resuming, play for a while was witnessed at midfield, but another pen- alty kick to Oldham gave them the desired advantage. A strong rush saw Heesom just kicking dead in time. Hurst responded to the drop-out, and though Oldham attacked well they met a defence equally true. Varley gave Hurst a chance, but Barber .and Carey upset the well meant intention, and Turner became conspicuous, with one rush which again forced play at midfield. Barber improved Warrington's position, and the visitors were again having,the best of it until Lees got well away from a wrong thrh*.out,but Broady upset McCut- cheon before lie got dangerous. The game was near the Warrington line, and it was left to Bate to put the finishing touch to smart. play by Thorniley, Turner, and Taylor, and the quarter flag was reached. Heetiom maintained his reputation as a safe custodian, and a kick by this player negatived one by Varley. Thelatter bad his revenge a minute later, for charging a kick by Bate he got possession, raced to Heesom, and passing to Purnies, this player was successful in notching the only tangible point of the game. Turner dropped eut, and the Warringtoniaas forced their way past the half-way flag, fine efforts by Bate, Turner, and Nevins, being applauded to the echo. Barber repeatedly baffled Herat and on one occasion got past Pennington with a dribble only to see Hurst race up and save. A mark to the ex- Leighlte gave relief, but though the Warrington line was reached the visitors did not relax their efforts, and another dribble reached half-way. Smart passing by the Oldham backs was stayed by Carey and Broady. During the last few minutes of the game fine rushes by the Oldham forwards saw Heesom effecting some fine saves, and the final result was a win for Oldham by a try.

WARILINGTON " A " v. OLDHAM "L"—The second meeting of these teams took place at Warrington on Saturday. and as the visitors arrived late two 25's were agreed upon. Warrington pressed early in the game and a rush by Holmes, Handles, and Coggins forced the op- ponents back in the first minute. Then the, home team started some passing, but little judgment was displayed, and Thomas and Underwood transferred the ,scene of contention to the Warrington 25. Although the ball was being mostly monopolized by the forwards, some in- tereeting play was witnessed, and then a fine bit Of work between Handles, Hampson, and Bailey forced the leather into the Oldham quarters. The game was not destined to remain here long, for. the active and dashing forwards, ' of the visitors, headed by Whittle, William, and Lees, came away to the opposite quarter flag. The warfare raged in the home territory, but Warrington tackled splendidly, and then, Boscow, who played grandly throughout, cleared the impending danger. Hampson, Hohnes, and Wilcox were prominent, but they were un- able to-resist' the effortii•Of their, , heavier and agile op- ponents, who, assisted by LaWton, Thomas, and Filling- ham, swooped down on the Warrington. fold. Boscow for a time kept his antagonists at bay, but at length from a pack near the line Lawton shot over, scoring in a good position, the place, however, failing. Oldham still continued to press, their superior play keeping the leather hovering in the Warrington half, until Cross in- tercepted some passing, and effected a good clearance. Some good work be Hampson, Holmes, and Fairhurst improved the position, until Oldham returned, Boscow clearing grandly, half-time arriving with Oldham a try to the good. Upon the resumption cf hostilities, Boscow was early called upon, to which he replied splendidly; a rush by Handles, Helmes, Goggins, and Hampson en- hancing the position. Then Edleston made a fine dribble, whilst shortly afterwards Cross kicked the ball to the line, Hetherington just beating him for possession, a minor only accruing. Oldham again settled down to their work, and screwing the scrimmages in splendid fashion were quickly attacking the home citadel. Bos- cow Was very fine behind, and then Mannion and Clarke effected a relief and the Warrington forwards, who were playing considerably better, dashed away down the ground. Notwithstanding the heavy ground the gun() was very fast, and the determined way in which the home team tried to get on level terms and the equally determined efforts of the visitors to keep out their lighter opponents, made the contest quite interesting and .exe citing, which was increased as Bailey tore away with the ball to half-way. This was nullified by Thomas, with a fast rush in the loose, but the time was fast expiring when Warrington retaliated by a counter rush to half- way. Here Clarke pounced on the leather and dribbl- ing splendidly to the line enabled Cross to equalize the score no goal resulting, a fast and exciting game result- ieg in a draw of one try each. RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.—Considerable interest was centred in the match at Park Avenue on Saturday. Both teams were fairly strong. There was a small attendance only 1,000 people being present. The ground was several inches deep in snow, a snowstorm prevailing throughout Yorkshire. Faulkner won the choictof ends and Dewhurst kicked off. Back play was not possible, , the ball being like a huge snow ball. Morris got the ball from Hughes, and ran well, Faulkner trying his utmost to get on further. Ward taking the ball, saved a certain score. Play continued chiefly forward, and all a rush and a dribble. Munro, Dewhurst, and Toothill on the home side, and Faulkner, Langley and Stubbs on the Runcorn side, playing witleconsiderable dash. At half- time, when the snowstorm was increasing, there was a clean score sheet. After the interval for several minute's Runcorn were an the Bradford. Passing was impossible . Crompton dropped at goal, a minor resulting. No tangible point was scored, and the game was left drawn.

RUNCORN " A" v. CLaucarrox.—The raturn engage- between these teams took place at the Irwell-lanis enclosure, Runcorn, on Saturday, in wretched weather, before a mere handful of spectators. Rain was falling heavily throughout the match, and the ground was a perfect quagmire. St. Anne's was the original fixture, but owing to some misunderstanding between the secre- tariee of the naughton and St. Anne's Clubs, the former put in an appearance at Runcorn, so that St. Anne's will now hove to come to Runcorn on Easter Monday. The match needs but little comment, as from start to fieish the visitors were simply not in it" with the League ceamisions, who, considering the state of the ground, played with an irresistible dash and energy, running up the formidable score of 1-9-s to nil. Tee scorers were Clarke, 2; Lightfoot, 2; W. Gayter, 2; Myers, Wood- ward, F. Gayter and Gregory, one each.

RTINCORN RIDCRBATION v. DITTON RINIRBATION.—These teems played their return match at Runcorn, on Satur- day. Ditton arrived short-handed, and the home toms wore without several of their regular players. On arriv- ing sift the ground it was found to 'Avery soft and cover- ed with water in several places,and a game of two quar- ters were played. Runourn won the toss, and Ditton kicked eft it was soon noticeable that good play was impossible,tho men not being able to keep on their feet. Nevertheless, the gaine was fairly open, the ball going about very rapidly, and at half time no score had been registered. On turning round play was of a scrambling character, chiefly amongst the forwards, and nothing of note occurred. The end was welcomed by both sides. and the game terminated during a heavy downpour of rain. The final result was a draw. Runcorn Recreation, two miners; Ditton Recreation, one minor. WIDNES T. ASPULL. —Widnes received a visit from As- pull on Saturday to play the return League match. The home team was intent on avenging the defeat, one dropped goal to nil, they received at Aspull. The match had aroused a great amount of interest,but unfortunate- ly the miserable weather spoiled the gate. Aspull. who played 14 men during the game,. were outplayed, and during the first half rare.y crossed the half-way line. Alford, receiving a pass from Drummond, was enabled score, but Barber failed at goal. Clarke also got over, but the point was disallowed. However the home players were not to be discouraged, and by some good forward play. Johnson scored, bnt the goal kick, taken by Barber again proved a failure. Widnes still con- tinued to press, and several touch downs were credited to them. Half-time arrived with the score Widnes 2 tries to nil. The second half was far more evenly con- tested than the first. Aspull tested the home defence a time or two, but found it toe strong. Time was called with the score unaltered. Final: Widnes 2 tries (6 points) to nil. IttriCPORN Ir.VICTORIA speciallyarrs.nged match between the above teams took place on the Irwell lane enolosura, Runcorn, on Wednesday afternoon.
