BIREBNIOLUD WANDIRIRS V. ST. aIILENS RECRBATION.— At Birkenheael, on Saturday, before very few spectators. The home team turned out in a variety of jerseys, as the St. Helens team arrived with uniforms similar to that of the Wanderers. The Wanderers kicked off, and ex- changes among the backs followed, scrimmames ensuing; at the.lialt-Way line, Ellison kicking too hard r and regis- tering a minor for the visitors. Atter the kick out, St. Helens passed well, but were speiled by Watson. A long aeries bf brilliant kicks was of interest, Snape play- ing beautifully for the Wanderers. Then Seddon got off, passed to Ellison, and the latter lost a capital chance by throwing forward. Another free kick to the home team brought needed relief, and the Wanderers' forwards rushed away to the 25 yards line, Hurst and Herbert being prominent with smart play at half, Herbert nar- rowly escaping a score, but a minor was the only result. Dobie, Elliott, and Morgan for the Wanderers, with Fildes, Dolan, and Reynolds On the other side, worked hard, and then Seddon punted well into touch., The Recs. rushed off, and Hur.,.t was compelled to kick dead. Seddon restarted, and;the Rocs. at once attacked, penn- ing their opponents in the bettom corner, and at last Snape had to kick dead. Seddon had a fair catch in front of goal, but Molyneux's resultant kick was charged down, and Hurst dashed away through the Recs., and repeated this immediately afterward. The Recs. now dashed off with a good dribble, and seemed. certain to score, till F: Hughes dropped on the ball and stayed the rush. Seddon got ['Ad inside the 25 territory, Harper pas3ing to him smartly, and Seddon dropped a beautiful goal, a fine performance under the circumstances of both ball and ground. In a rush which ensued from the re- start, S;. Holeng gained a lot of ground. A free kick was given the Wanderers, and Kelly took it, the hall going to Ellison, who mulled badly and Elliott. dropped on it, amid cheers, but Kelly just missed the posts with his kick at goal. Final result :—St. Helene Recreation 1 dropped goal (4 points), Birkenhead Wanderers 1 try (3 points). • A'SSOCItiTION.

IiVARRINOTON PARISI( CHIFRCH V. Sr. GEORGE'S MIS- SIM—This match was played at Manchester-road. Parish Church kicked off, and at once made tracks for the visitors' goal, only to be repulsed by the Wilcocks. The home team worked the ball back again, and from a free kick Nicholson scored the first goal. This was soon followed by another from a scramble in front of goal, Gill scoring. At half-time the score was two to one in favour of the Parish. After the interval the visitors start- ed and missed a splendid chance in front of goal. The l'arish forwards now worked the ball down the field, Mayes adding the third goal. The home team continued to press, and Hanapson receiving the ball made a good attempt to score, the ball being cleared by the visitors' full back. It was worked ba,ck,and Nicholson receiving a pass from Hampson, scored the fourth goal for the Parish. On time being called, the Parish Church ran out winners by four goals to none. WIDNES PAINII CHURCK V. TVIEDROOIC.—The Parish Church team journeyed to Tuebrook, on Saturday, to play their West Lancashire League fixture, but though they had as 11111 Ch of the game as their opponents, were compelled to return home, defeated by 3 goals to one.
WIDNES V. CROSSES (LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT LEAGUR.)—ThNe teams should have met at Liverpool on Saturday, but the Whines team did no make the jour- ney as they wore unable to raise a team.

div.head: TILE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A
div.p: TILE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A
WARRINGTON MAN.

At the Oldham Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. G. B. Taylor and other magistrates, a loom job- ber, named Albert Ward, thirty-three years of age, was placed in the dock on a charge of having at- tempted to Commit suicide by stabbing himself in thelichest, and neck on thQ morning of Ninaday, the ! sth inst. The Chief Constable (Mr. R. Peacock ),said the prisoner came to Oldham on the Ist February, and went to lodge with Michael Gleeson, at Ripponden-road.. Before that the man had been employ- ed at a Warrington mill, of which town he was a native. He started work at the Watershedding,s Mill, and on the night of the 2nd inst., after working but one day, he bad a heavy fall whilst in a fit. He was afterwards queer in his manner, and at one o'clock of the morning of the sth inst., he slipped out of bed and went downstairs, and began to smask a large quantity of ornaments. lie was taken upstairs, but lath on he got up and again went downstairs. Two other lodgers who slept with him followed !Ward and found that he had cut his throat with a pocket knife, and was stabbing himself in the chest. They stopped him, and be was taken to the In- firmary, where he remained until that morning. In answer to the magistrates' clerk, the prisoner, who ap- peared to be still very ill, said that he came from War- rington,where he had many friends.—The man's brother who stepped forward, told the bench that he had been working in Watrington for many years, but the prisoner liad been out of, work from New Year's Day up to the time he went to Oldham. He added :that his brother was not" right "in hi 3 head when he stabbed himself, and that his being in that state was in consequence of the fit and the fall.—The Chairman (to the prisoner) : Are yen all right now P—Ward : 1 feel all right. I know what lam doing; but I feel very weak. I want to go home with My brother.—The Chairman: Will you at- tempt such a thing again P—Prisoner No, Sir.—The magistrates allowed the man to go home with his brother the latter giving a promise that he would look after him.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this authority was held at Dutton workhouse on Tuesday. There were present Mr. J. Mclntyre (chairman), Mr. S. H. Woodhouse (ex-eicio), Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Hanby, Messrs. J. M. Williams, 11. E. Ileywooo, J. Brandreth, E. Aaron, T. Lewis, T. Ford, C. T. Whit- ley, J. Parr, C. W. Davenport, W. Pickering, E. Bratherton ; Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. div.head: PAROCHIAL COMMITTER.
div.p: PAROCHIAL COMMITTER.

At the meeting of the Appletdn Parochial Committee hold on the 16th inst. it was decided that it be pointed out to the Local Government Board that Stockton Heath and •Wilderspool in the contributing places of Hull and Appleton and adjacent to the town a Warrington, from which place omnibuses plying for hire and running through Wilderspool and Stockton Heath, every 15 min- utes, and frequently at the terminus of the route in Stockton Heath, the drivers cause a good deal of annoy- ance to foot passengers by blocking the crossings of the streets and taking no axed scanding while waiting, before commencing the return journey, which might be avoided if the authority had power to make by-laws to regulate their conduct, and that the Local Government Board be urgently requested to confer the powers of section 172 of the Public Health Act, 1375, in respect of the contributory places of Hull and Appleton.—The report was adopted.

SLAUGHTER HOUSES Oti HALTON AND WESTON. At a meeting of the Halton Parochial Committee on Saturday. the Rev. J. Flanby in the chair, the clerk (Mr. J. Ashton) read a letter from the Local Government Board when it was ordered that the clerk should inform the Local Government Beard that there is one slaughter house in Halton and one in Weston, but now that the Ship Canal which passed through both townships was completed it was anticipated that foreign cattle would be landed te the townships, and it was very desirable that the authority should have conferred upon them of the powers of eectien 159 (except the first paragraph), and section 170 of the Public Health Act 1875,in respect of the contribution places of Halton and Weston.—Tho minutes were confirmed.

div.head: HELSISY WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: HELSISY WATER SUPPLY.

At the meeting of the.lsby Parochial Comtnittee which was held on Saturday evening under the presi- dency of Mr. 3. Nandreth, the scheme for a water supply for the township submitted at the last meeting was further considered and the Clerk produced the plans and read the several reports and estimates of which the following is a summary—Belve and Priest,Liverpool, £2,7ls,exclusive of land, inquiring and legal expenses ; Moorson, Manchester,£2,Bo4, exclusive of land and way- leaves ; Bedford, Nottingham £3,429, exclusive of land and professional fees; Timinins Runcorn, £3,200, inclu- sive of land and engineers and law charges. After along discussion, it was moved iey Mr. Davies and seconded by Mr. Gueet that 'Mr. Radford'a scheme be accepted. An amendment was proposed by Mr. White as follows: —From the estimate of the four engineers, the work fir supplying fleleby with water, would cost upwards of £3,200 which meant thecost ofmaintenanco would be an annual charge of £3OO en the rates, and as the prospects from the consumption and select water would be so small on account of many having a good supply of water I beg to rnsve that the water question be deferred until there is more need of it, or un%,il a Parish Council can take it up.-:-Mr.Ellames seconded the amendment which was carried by five votes to three.—The report was passed on the motion of Mr. Brandreth.
TUB TIOANO NOBLY AGAIN.

The Local teovornment Baird forwarded a copy of a letter received from the Rev. C. R. Nunn, of Norloy Vicarage, in which that gentleman stated that on Nov. 30th,the school was closed im deference of a recommenda- tion of the Rural Sanitary Authority, after which ho pointed out the reasons far his action, and considered the closing of the schOol an extreme measure, and was calculated to defeat the purpose of the Authority by children running about the village. He showed that the esteemed Guardian for the parish, and a member of the Authority had stated that he should not close the Chapel Sunday school, whereas the Church Sunday school had been completely disorganised. On Dec. 26, the school was closed another fortnight on the medical officer's report " that fever was still prevalent in Norloy "—an utterly false report. The committee's, action was felt to be a gross injustice and misuse of powers. He had shown the greatest readiness and desire to carry out the Sani- tary Committee's suggestions, even where in several particular exceptions might fairly he taken to them. He appealed against the action- of the Rural Sanitary Authority, which Was felt to be harassing, unnecessary, and inconsiderate, too readily taken on the strength of incorrect reports, and without adequate investigation. —The Education. Department forwarded a letter which they had addressed to C. B. Nunn re Norley National School. In this they etated that they received a copy of the correspondence which had passed between him and the Authority on the subject of the sanitary condition of thd premises. They reminded the managers that several defects in khe premises,* including the sanitary arrangement.were mentioned in the last annual report as requiring immediate remedy, and that unless the neces-e sary improvements were effected without delay, the an- nual grant to the school which fell due on the 28 th.,would be liable to forfeiture. Plans of what was postponed in order to carry out these requirements should be submitted to the department as soon as possible, drawn in accord- ance With the, requirements of Schedule VII. Pending the necessary alterations the managers should be careful to comply at once with any order which the Sanitary Authority might think it necessary to make—Mr. Far- rington said that it had been stated that he had said something against the Norley schools. He denied that he had said anything to anyone in Norley, about the schools being a disgrace. The strongest term he had used was on Nov. 28, when he said that the school was much behind the requirements of the times,and he main- tained that.—The Chairman regretted that the medical officer was not present that day.—Mr. Woodhouse said that he was one of the managers of the Nerley schools, and would be happy to fall in with the wishes of the Board. The managers of the school had always been anxious to to avoid the formation of a school board, but he did not think they could entertain the idea of extensive improvement at their own cost. They were prepared with plans to be submitted to the education depattment. The schools were on a restricted area and any extension would en- tail the acquirement of more land. He thought the place was too small. He was afraid that water would have to be carried to the school, for if they sunk a well, the water would not be suitable. —The Chairman said that the Board had some very unpleasant work to perform and they were bound to do it. They never thought of harassing anyone, as the vicar of Norley appeared to think they did. If be would meet the requirements of the Education Department, they would not take any action against him.—Mr. Heywood-said that the vicar stated that the Guardian of' the parish had said that he would not close the chapel school. He had no recollec- tion of that.-L—Mr. Hanby thought ,that it would be a sufficient answer to the Local Government Board to say that their action was based •Jpon the report of the medi- cal officer of health, and they had every reason to be satisfied,with that report. He moved that an answer to that effect be sent.—The motion was carried unanim- ously.

div.head: TUE KINGSLEY SCHOOLS.
div.p: TUE KINGSLEY SCHOOLS.

The Rev. A. P. Reynolds, vicar of Kingsley, acknow- ledged the receipt of the Clerk's letter, dated the 7th Inst., authorising the reopening of the schools but recom- mending that the managers should not admit any dren from houses where the disease had been contracted. He asked for a list of the cases to enable the manakers to act upon the request. Writing later, he drew atten- tion to the list not having arrived and remarked that surely the want of thoughtfulness was not all on the side of the school managers.

div.head: RUNUORN PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNUORN PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The Clerk reported that on Monday afternoon a meet- ing was held in the Town Hall, Runcorn, of repreenta- tives of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority and Run- corn Urbax Authority, to disduqs the steps to be taken with reference to a letter received from the Local Government Board. There were present—Mr. Lightburn (in the chair), Mr. Imison, Mr. Lake (law clerk), repre- senting the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners; Mr. J: M. Williams, Mr. J. Brandteth, Mr. H. E. Heywood, and Mr. J. Ashton, representing the Rural Sanitary Authority. The Local Government Board in their com- munication stated that they had under consideration a proposal to investigate in connection with an applica- tion from the Town Councils of Manchester and Salford and the Stretford Local Board, to be constituted the Port Sanitary Authority for the protection of the public health in the customs port of Manehester. The letter, after explaining the limits of the said port, went on to state that at the present stage it was practically impcssible to Indicate, with any attempt at precision, the arrange- ments, which may be required as suitable, with a view of the local circunastances. It was, therefore, for the local authorities to consider the proposals which have been made to the Board by Manchester, Salford and Stret- ford. Doubtless,. too, the riparian authorities would be prepared to discuss, as an alternative scheme, the set- ting up of a joint board as Port Sanitary Authority, and other plans of port sanitary administration might be put forwatil as adapted to local requirements. They asked for an expression of the views of the representatives of the authorities, in order to arrange for an official in- quiry, and desired to know where it should he held. After careful discussion it was resolved that a letter be forwarded to the Local Government Board asking for a copy of the proposals, and suggesting that the inquiry should be held in Runcorn.—The report was adopted unanimously.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

Mr. Brandreth in presenting the minutes of the Finance Committee said that there was a bill from Dr. Selby for £5 for notifying 40 cases of infectious disease.—The minutes were was adopted and this closed the business of the meeting.

div.head: EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY BILL.
div.p: THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY BILL.

TRADES UNIONS TAKING ACTION. A conferenee.'consisting of the Parliamentary 00m. mitten of the Trades Union Congress and the London Trades Council,was held on Wednesday,to consider what • s steps should be taken in view of the failure of the Ern-- - ployers' Liability Bill. The Conference strongly pro-- • • tested against the action of the House of Lords which has led to the abandonment of the measure by the Gov- . ernment, and determined to hold a monster ctemonstra- A tion in London on Sunday, March 18. The denim:tetra- ' tion will be preceded by a couference on the 17th, and representatives from all the organised trades in the h. country will be requested to take part. Speakers at the demonstration in Hyde Park will all be selected from the' • leaders of the trade unions, and the Government will be ee asked to reintroduce the bid 'next session. The London demonstration will be followed by similar meetings in. •1, the large towns and cities of the provinces. Hr. C. !. Fenwick. M.P., Mr. J. Burns, M.P., Mr. J. 11. Wilson, M.P., Mr. B. Tillett, and Mr. James Maavdsley, hare been appointed a sub-committee to act with a similar- number of gentlemen appointed by the London Trades , Council for the purpose of carrying out the neodsary' ..; arrangements for the demonstration. " THE WRECKING OF THE EMPLOYERS' LuBILITN- BILL." A Parliamentary correspondeq Of the" Manahester Guardian," writing under the above heading on Wed- • nesday night says :—Among • Tories in town Caere is SI Much show of delight at the success of the shabby stratagem of yesterday; which it is believed was in- spired by the author of all the mischief and moet of the ill-feeling- of the past year—Mr. Chamberlain. Tbe com— ments of most Liberal members run thus. It might have been better if the, Liberal Whips had found out in time that the form of motion Mr. Gladstone wised to adopt—" to lay aside the Lords' amendments "—wee not in order. It certainly would have given satisfac-- tion if Mr. Gladstone could have adopted either a line which directly challenged the Attitude of the Peers or a line which knocked down in distiect terms once MOM- the poor little card-castle, Lords Dudley and Camper-- down had eecons:aucted. But, given the facts, obvious - to all yesterday, that the contretemias was from the rules of the House and net from the issues involved,. the trick of running away from a division was too • transparently insincere, and the shouting of the Tory press to-day, is so overdone as to make it plainer than • ever who are the real destroyers of the bill. , Those who listened closely,noted that both Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain let the cat out of the bag by declaring their absolute indifference to the fate of the , bill. A few independent meu like Sir Albert Roiiitt, Mr. • , lßouslield, the author of the " unhealthy industries "., dense, and several other Tories, and also Wham! Union- ists wished to get the bill through. But. it trielield by all who have ratched the debates and weighed the senten- , •ces of Lord Salisbury and his friends that this whole movement in Parliament against the bill has been syste- matic from the first. The agitation among the North Western men has been a mere instrtimeet, ills aimed, of a definite policy of the . capiWlists to prevent-Mr. Asquith's Success. The capitalist section who oppose it by direct and indirect methods, are the same men whoo are against all democratic reform, and their p am n object throughout has been Co paralyse trades unionism almost more than to save their pockets from the doubtleis heavier liabilities to be imposed by the new Act. Some indignation is expressed by Liberal members at the almost hysterical comments on the debate and the severe criticism on Mr. Gladstone's attitude which have appeared in one Lendon journal, today and have promptly been made the topic tar Tory jubilation. From conversation with a number of the most advanced Radicals and friends of labour in the House, I am able to state that these comments in no way represent the feeling in the House. The universal thought was put forcibly by one well-known member thus :—" The right tiling has been done, but in the wrong way. What the House wanted was exactly what the forms of the House precludeda-a third and a decisive battle on the main issue, of whether the charter of labour was to be complete and inalienable or only a Temple Bar elastic enough to let through a coach and-six. But the state- meet that the Radicals in the House, were exasperated with Mr. Gladstone aed wish his departure from the scene is absolutely untrue and ridiculous. , The exact reverse is the case. What the House did feel when baulked of its straight fight was that we had had enough of this stage fencing with their lordships under forms and rules which prevent any solid result or even any adequate statement of facts and arguments. And the situation quickened and stimulated the wish to get these issues before the country and to light them out in the open, and to fight them out while we have the old and beloved leader with us.

• Some rumours are about to the effect that pressure will be put on the Government to re-introduce the Em- ployers' Liability Bill next session. This is most impro- bable. The bill would run the same course,however mucti debates and. stages might be shortened in the Commons, • • and after the same struggle with the Lords we should be in much the same position regarding it at the end. The real effect of yesterday's proceedings is to bring the general election nearer. It is now plain that repetition of bills, restating of arguments, conciliatory granting of "breathing time," opportunities' for repentance and withdrawal from false positions,the whole paraphernalia of dealingamicably with their lordships,is a mere waste of the,time of Parliament, and of the country. It is urged that as the Constitution now stands we ;ire badly off enough in haying to submit once to the vagaries of the Peers. To repeat the operation unnecessarily is mere , pandering to the despotic arrogance of Lord Salisbury. If we want to provoke the Lords to further indiscretion the cool-headed men say, let it be on fresh issues, and the more the better. Thus the result of yesterday will not be a fresh attempt te get the bill through Parlia- ment, but a thoroughgoing campaign for the bill in the country ; and if it is a more sweeping bill, such as was boldly foreshadowed by Mr. Fenwick yesterday, there are many friends of labour. .who will rejoice: A COMPARISON. The" Pall Mall Gazette "has drawn up the following comparison of the provisions of the existing law on em- ployers' liability, with the provisions of the Bill which the Government have now withdrawn. It shows clearly that rather than grant power to " contract out "to those who wish for it, the Government have to withdraw a bill nine-tenths of Which would have been of great bene- fit to the Working classes generally : THE LAW AS IT IS. ANOTHER ABSCONDING BANK MANAGER.

--- A warrant has been issued for the arrest of John Rob- inson. of Blyth, in Northumberland. He was clerk to 00 local Burial Board, agent for the Shipwrecked Mariners Society, secretary to the Gas Company, and the seer tary and manager of the Blyth Deposit and Advance Bank. A few days ago he failed to pay the scavengerf their wages. Soon afterwards it was found that he bac' left the town, and that the books of the bank had beet* removed. The man's disappearance has:caused much citement in the district. Most of the depositors in tte. bank were miners, and on Tuesday they flocked into tbe place eagerly seeking their money.

div.head: "THE PRERS V. TRE PEOPLE."
div.p: "THE PRERS V. TRE PEOPLE."

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee of 1 1 e Lancashire Liberal Federal Council, held on Tues- -1147 at the Reform Club, Manchester, the following reso- lntion moved oy the Chairman Mr. J. div.head: DOG SHOW AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: DOG SHOW AT ST. HELENS.

The second annual show of dogs, pigeons, rabbits, and cavies in connection with the St. Helens Fanciers' Association was opened on Wednesday in the Volunteer Hall, St. Helens. There had been £375 offered in prizes, and this had brought together 857 entries from fanciers throughout the country. The judges were :—Collies, Mr. Hugh Ainscough ; other dogs Messrs. J. div.head: TEMPERANCE MAGISTRATES AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MAGISTRATES AT ST. HELENS.
PLEDGE SIGNING IN COURT.

At St. Helens, on Saturday, before Councillors John Forster and J. B. Leach (magistrates on the platform at the meeting of the United Kingdom Alliance on Friday night), a young collier named George Minns or Owen, of Barber-st., was charged with refusing to quit the Crooked Billet public. house. Higher Parr-st., and with assaulting Con- stable Say.—The Officer stated that about half-past nine he was called to the house. Prisoner was using threa- tening language, and refused to leave. Witness took hold of him, upon which he struck the officer a violent blow on the head. A struggle followed ,arid witness was kicked several times.—Prisoner said he was drunk and did not know what he was doing.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner had been convicted several times.—The Chairman : If I were you I should take the pledge straight away. It will do you all sorts of good, and it will save you coming up here. You are quite ready to admit that it does you no good,and it oets youiinto such scrapes as these.—Prisoner: I shall take the pledge.— The Chairman : We will fine you ss. and costs for re- fusing to quit-95. altogether—or seven days, and will dismiss the charge of assault. I hope that treating you leniently like this will be the means of making you re- form. Will you turn over a new leat.—Prisoner : Yes, sir.—The Chairman: You are a decent sort of a man, and should know better. In another charge of drunkenness preferred against a respectably-dressed yourr, woman, named Eliza May, of Bruce-st., prisoner stated that she toek in washing. She left home at eight o'clock on Friday night, and took drink at public-houses with ,another woman. She was found drunk at half-past eleven by Police-constable Hurst.—The Chairman asked the prisoner whether she had any friends, and on receiving a negative reply asked if she would have to Coto prison if a fine was inflicted.— Prisoner: I suppose I shall.—The Chairman : We pro- pose to dismiss the case altogether if you will promise not to do this again. You promise to turn over a new leaf .—Prisoner Yes.—The Chairman : Well, we will dismiss it altogether.—Mr.Mundin' the police court mis- sionary,took the cases in hand,and both prisoners signed the pledge.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED OF ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED OF ST. HELENS.
DEPUTATION TO THE MAYOR.

On Tuesday afternoon, the Mayor of St. Helens (Alderman Sinclair) received a deputation of un- employed in the new committee-room of the St. Helens Town Hall. About 150 men, chiefly chemi- cal workers, headed by Mr. Peter Wliinley, pre- sented themselves, and the Mayor seemed sur- prised to see such a large number. He had under- stood that only a small deputation would be there. Mr. M'llinley said that a number of the unemployed called on him, and asked him if something could not be done. He was himself surprised to see so much distress. The men wished the Corporation to start public works— vie., the extension of the main sewer, the new water works, and the laying of water pipes. The" task" at Whiston Workhouse had been stopped, and there was a probability of 200 more men being thrown out of em- ployment by the copper smelting plant at tke Globe Alkali Works being stopped.—The Mayor said he was sorry to see so many men present who were out of work. He had no power to start public works. He was, as they knew, only one of the large Corporation, but the statements he had heard would be conveyed to his col- leagues. He was quite sure that it was the wish of the Corporation to find work for as many townsmen as they could, but he could not personally give any pledge to any particular work. He would, however, take care to represent to his colleagues both in the Committees and in the Council what they had said, and he hoped they would soon see something done (seveial of the deputation : " Hear, hear.") In answer to Mr. M'Kinley, the Mayor said he had thought about the labour bureau, but did not then think one was desirable in St. Helens.— The deputation then thanked the Mayor, and with- drew.

div.head: RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR
div.p: RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR
EARLESTO W N.

DELAY TO TRAFFIC. A little before eight o'clock on Thursday morn- ing, when the 6.20 goods train Liverpool to Leigh was running between Collins Green and Earlestown an iron brake block fell from a coal wagon belong- ing to Scrowcroft and uompl\ny of Wigan, and getting fast in a crossing, caused the trailing wheels of the wagon to be swept from under. The train ran a short distance in this way, when it broke loose, and another wagon belonging to the same firm, left the metals, and was thrown across the up and down lines, completely blocking them. The driver,owing to the fog was unaware of what had happened, and he ran on with the portion of the train which was attiched; to Earles- , town, where he was stopped opposite the Viaduct Works the failing wagon having been dragged three quarters of: a mile off the rails. The permanent way was damaged, one wagon now lies at the bottom of the enbankment. The traffic between Liverpool, and Manchester was com- pletely blocked, and several passenger trains were con- siderably delayed, the through trains having to be worked via Warrington or Wigan. A gang of men from the Viaduct Works were early on the scene, and they succeeded in getting the line cleared by shortly after ten o'clock when the ordinary working was again resumed.

div.p: A
C WILKINSON'S SPECr ELIXIR
HAYDOCK MINERS AND THE LATE
STRIKE.
PRESENTATION TO THE REV. J. H. RIDDETTE.

On Saturday night, at a largely-attended soda gathering of miners and their wives at Ilaydock, near St. Helens, interesting presentations were made to the Rev. J. 11. Riddette and Mrs. Riddette, who during the strike were assiduous in collecting money and distributing the necessaries of life to starv- ing families. Mr. John Norcross, secretary to the Haydock Miners' Lodge, presided.—Mr. James Blacktop proposed : "That we, the niiners, their wives, and friends assembled at this meeting tender our heartfelt thanks and gr.ititutb to Mr. and Mrs. Riddette for the love and sympathy they extended to as during the lock- out. We believe no other system or organisation could have been better conducted; therefore, we heartily thank the rev, gentleman and his wife, who so nobly assisted us to win for labour each a glorious and far- shining vietory ' • and also in endeavouring to further the best interests of workingmen in the neighbourhood. May we ever remember that when we were in need they were friends indeed."—Mr. William Addison seconded, and said the meney for the presents had been subscribed for by members of all denominations. (Applause.)—The Chairman said Mr. S. Woods, M.P., and the Rev. Henry Wilson had promised, but were unable to attend.—The Rev. C. F. Aked, of Liverpool, who had been invited, wrote :—" I cannot come on a Saturday. Dent you know that that is the only day when some parsons work? Anyhow, it is the day which is sacred to my ' study, and 1 am going to have a Featherstone hero with a fixed bayonet outside my study door for eight hours on a Saturday so that no mortal can enter. I am hoping that an Eight flours' Bill for parsons and literary men men will be introduced in an early Parliament, but until that becomes the law of the land I am afraid I shall have to go on working fourteen. But, Saturdays! No, thank you! May you have a real good time. May there never be such another c,eal war as the last. But should the master and the gambler force upon the country such another conflict, may you find friends as true, leaders as wise, and men and women of the seam heroic mould as won for labour its glorious and far-shining viotery."— The resolution was supported by Dr. Dowling and Mr. Jacob Billinge.—Mr. Edward Walkden secretary of the Ashton and Haydock district ef the Miners' Federa- tion, on behalf of the Haydock misers, offered con- gratulations, and dealt with the causes of the recent dispute, and the progress of the struggle. He did not know whether it was fortunate sr unfortun- ate hinsselfebut at the present they had a board of con- ciliation. They had on board a class that he had always spoken against, and until he was convinced otherwise be would continue to speak against. They had get one of the legal section to say what was right or wrong on that board. For twelve mouths they (the miners) were entirely bound in honour to obey that board whether it was against them or not, and for the present the em- ployers had contented themselves with letting the miners have what was their due rights—namely, no reduction in wages. The miners were not content with that, and they had told the empleyere that there were three im- portant questions they wanted to lay before his lordship at the earliest possible day. They had expected on the 13th inst. that decision weuld have been given, but, un- fortunately, Lord Shand was abroad. They had now to wait until the first week ie March. They (the miners) wanted, first, the fixing of a minimum rate of wages— (applause),—and that that rate should be a living wage. (Continued applause.) If there was to be an inquiry in- to the wages of the men, they wanted also at the same time a strict inquiry into the profits of the employers— (applause),--and did it net sound to sense that the workmen who had to produce the capital for those who lived at their ease and could go to the South of France te enjoy themselves for three months should know what their profits were. The miners also wanted a voice in the fixing of the big contracts. What was it that caused the great lockout more than the railway corn- , parries and gas companies ? (Hear, hear.) In conclusion he heattiry joined with them in , making the presentation to Mr. altd Mrs. Riidette. There was not a minister in the wirsle of Lancashire who had done more for the miners than Mr. Riddette. (Applause.) The Chairman then presented Mr. Riddette with a gold keyless watch and guard being the inscrip- tion "Presented to the Rev..). H. Riddette by the miners of flaydock, February, 17, NH," and Mrs. Edith Agnes Riddette with a gold bar brooch studded with pearls, He also presented to them an electro-plated cruet. The presents had been subscribed for by 400 persons. Mr. Riddette, in replyiag, said he looked upon that gathe: - ing as a historic one in the annals of their village to com- rnmemorate a historic struggle,and,ashe really believed, abistoric victory. (Applause.) fie thought it a matter of congratulation that that victory should be on the side of labour rather than on the side of capital. The victory was, in his opinion, due to three primary causes—first, the sacacity and leadership of men who officered the Miners' Federation; second, by the heroism splendid discipline, and, above all, the self-restraint showed by the men ; and third, by the righteousness of the cause for which they were fighting. (Applause.) fire resolution was carried with acclamation, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: ANARCHISTS.
div.p: THE ANARCHISTS.

The inquest concerning tee death ef Martial llourdin, the Anarchist who was killed by the bomb explosion in Greenwich Park, was opened on Monday. Evidence of identification was taken. Several schoolboys in the park at the time of the explosion were examined. They said they heard a loud report, saw a cloud of yellow smoke, and ran up the hill till they came to a crouching object. It was Martial Bourdin maimed and blood- stained, kneeling on the path and crying, " Take me home, take me home !" Other witnesses described the nature of his injuries and his death in Vie hospital. So fierce was the explosion that a piece of bone was found 60 yards away from the body. The inquest was ad- journed for a week. Colonel Majendie made further progress on Monday with his investigation with regard to the explosive. The documents :ieized at the Auto- nomie Club have thrown light on the secret work of the Anarchist organisations, and within the past few days communications have been made to several foreign Governments. A strict watch is kept in the London railway stations and at the Channel ports to prevent the escape of Bourdin's accomplice.
