Sir,-1 was much interested in the note of F.W.R. on the above subject. As one wishing to learn further on this matter, would he kindly say how he gets the Bir- kenhead gun-time here? how he detects the error of a deck without seconds-hand to a second ? and whether a clock such as that at Trinity should not keep time within lsec. pe 3k ? lam glad somcnne in the town takes sufficient interest in the matter to keep a record. 'lce want of a good public cl:•ck has long been a striking fact. Possibly this one. has never had meted to it its due.—l am, &c., yours truly, HICKORY HICKORY.

MR. HOWELL ON VEGETABLE PHYSIOLOGY. Sir,—Would you not have thought that it was enough for one pair of shoulders to bear the weight of having to prove the historic accuracy of the" fall" without the additional burthen of defending the dogma cf seminal reourrection ? But not so, thinks Mr. J. S H. He, like the cunning juggler, can keep, not one, but many, balls going in the air at once ! Or is it rather that he has found his " call" too hot or too heavy for him and so has dropped it? Has he elected to give up Father Adam in despair and to talk nonsense about the revivification of dead seeds? He actually quotes St. Augustine on a question of vegetable physiology! Let Mr. Howell be careful. His status as a logician is settled, but his standing as a man of science still trembles in the balance! Beware in time. The question of " fall "or no " fall" might be regarded as very much a matter of opinion, but here we have a matter of fact which cannot be decided by reference to any traditional authority. Let us come down to these facts. A grain of wheat consists 1, of its integument; 2, its white body—chiefly starch and gluten; and, 3, the germ or embryo. Now, of the three, this last is the only one having life or the potenti- ality of life. And yet, according to the reconcilers, this ices not die but only that which never lived. Q.E.D. One lives and learns. Mr. H. says I am a materialist. That is one piece of information which has come all the way from No. 9, Montgomery-road, Chiswick, London, W. From this enlightened locality I also get tke fact that a seed has a soul—and " a conscious life." This has enhanced my respect for cabbages and potatoes immensely ! The " Christian meaning" of a seed's dying is "the dissolution of soul and body." This is the Christian way of looking at it but not "the scientific meaning also, may I add " ! Will Mr. Howell leave i,relevant quotation and tcll us which of the three does ' tiie,—and blow they manage it ?—Yours, &c., JOHN PEERS.

div.head: RATIONALISM VERSUS REASON.
div.p: RATIONALISM VERSUS REASON.

Sir,—l am asked by Mr. Peers, " What position as a reasoner can a man hold, who accepts the Fall' as a fact and rejects special creation,' both of these state- ments having equal authority as coming from the book, upon which, and upon which alone, the pretensions of this creed are founded." Well, sir, that would depend on several factors. If (like your correspondent) he simply looked at things in a superficial or shallow man- ner, I should think but little el him. As to creation, Cardinal Manning shall answer for me (Religio Viatoris 3 ed., p. 5), " They who believe in the creation of man from the slime or the dust of the eart h can have no difficulty in believing the simplicity of protoplasm, and they who believe in the descent of man from a single pair can have no difficulty in believing the largest development of differences of man and races, ipter eandem speciem. It is the exclusive and primeval identity of the species for which we contend." I must ask Mr. Peers to point out where this contradicts either the text of the Bible or Science; I must, however, pro- test against your correspondent's misuse of my words "special creation," since I hold in common with all Catholics " special creation" in Cardinal Mansing's sense. Nor am I alone with Cardinal Newmau's argu- ment for the" primeval fall." His brother prelate thus speaks of it, "Given then the freedom of the human will and the dominion that God has permitted to man over the course of this world, the preponderar.ce of evil and of suffering—if it were so—which is not granted— is at once removed from the Divine will,and traceable to the human. The whole course of human history is the record of the freedom of the human will. The evil and suffering which deface the world are the tares of man's sowing, the supersemination of the free will turned from good to evil. The face of the world has a look of anguish because man has marred what God has made," (Ibid p. 35). The logic of the discussion, seems to be this :—The historical accuracy of the " fall" was questioned or denied by Mr. Peers, the onusprobandi, then rested with him, but he brought no shred of evidence to support his denial, and waves aside in an infallible (sic) manner, all proofs and authorities whatever ; and notwithstand- ing anything I or anyone else may say, he in his supreme egotism, will continue to do so to the end of the chapter. Thanking you, sir, for your courtesy not only to myself, but to all who have the interests of truth at heart, whether popular or not.—l remain, yours faithfully, JOHN S. HOWELL. 9, Moatgomery:road, Chiswick, London, W.

div.head: Feb. 18; 1894.
div.p: CRUEL SPORTS. Sir,—The current number of the organ for that invalu- able association the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals contains the following paragraph: 46 We are glad to announce that the Sport Regulation Bill, drafted by Mr. Salt, secretary to the Humanitarian League and submitted to the R.S.P.C.A. for approval has 'been examined by counsel and introduced into Parlia- ment. It provides that :—(1) Any person who either (a) takes part or assists in the hunting, coursing or shooting of any animal, which has been kept in confinement, and is released for the purpose of such coursing or shoot- ing, or (b) keeps or uses or assists In the management of any place kept for the purpose of such hunting, coursing or shouting, or permits any place to be so used shall be liable on conviction in manner provided 1... y the Summary Jurisdiction' Acts to a penalty not exceeding twenty pounds for each day on which he commits such offence.'" The Society has approved the above Bill, with a few suggestions, and it is easy to understand that its members must feel considerable satisfaction in being released from the false position in which they were placed before by the urgent need of such a measure. It appears absurd to punish a man for csing his temper with a horse, donkey or dog and striking it impatiently while the law, permits him the same day deliberately to torment and mangle to death other animals almost equally domestic; paddock led deer, tame rabbits from the hutch, and pigeons from the trap. Hitherto a lad has been fined, birched or sent to prison for setting his terrier to worry a cat, but he could net be legally restrained frcm performing the same or greater cruelties on creatures of a different species, though quite as much under human control and in the same need of protection. It is nigh time to purge the laws from discrepancies which render them contemptible in the ayes of the public, and weaken the hands of those pledged to administer them. All friends of justice and all lovers of mercy will do their best to promote the suc- cess of the new Bill which has this object in view.-1 am, Sir, yours truly,'

div.head: E. CARRINGTON.
div.p: E. CARRINGTON.
THE "PERPLEXING" PROBLEM.

Sir,—ln my former letter I presumed too much if I ex- pected that" Harry Esmond" ever wished to be relieved from what he ca': a" perplexing problem." He started under the burden of a self-imposed stumbling-block, namely, that Ciirist is the orig,iaal author of the popular doctrine of the death of seAs ; whereas the idea is as old as the days of Aristotle and probably much older,as it may be traced in Egypt, Judea,Cireece and Rome long gener- ations before Christ. -

The mind of philosophers, and the common-sense of all .observers were naturally enough struck with the change and dissolution of parts which were evidently noticeable in the bulk of the buried grain, and the verisimilitude to the laws of decay and death of the investiture, the ex- ternal wrappings,n,nd integuments of the corn-seed. The detection of a minute portion of the seed in which lay the life germ was to be the heritage of future days. But whatever may be the ignorance of this fact, the judg- ment of those early ages stands to this hour with respect to the dissolution and decay of a great bulk of the seed, as the most natural and fitting that could be conceived; since even now when the exact physiology of the process is known,or at least nearly so,eminent writers on Botany do not hesitate to use the language which Dr. Balfour ,employs to describe the change and disintegration which takes place as a "dying or dissolution of its ex- ternal wrappings and integuments. There is no question as to anything that can be called" dying "of the ger- minating element of the seed that is, the embryo, nor is -there aught of the kind that implied in the words of Christ to that effect, ttie presumption of cavillers and pedants notwithstanding. But when I am accused by your "perplexed " correspondent of "the merest quib- Wings " in limiting the dying of the seed to its external wrappings and integuments, and find myself upheld by an eminent botanist in +Key recent editions of his most aleborate works, I can well afford to dismiss" Harry Esmond" from any further notiee, except to remark that his pretentious preference of the statements of a mere sciolist when compared with Dr. Balfour is a suffi- cient index to the nature of his perplexity and to the sincerity of his efforts to get rid of it. That he should pose 39 a member of a Christian Church, and grasp at such a worthless figment to discredit its Divine Head, is something more serious than a" perplexing problem." And now a few remarks on the effusion of the übiqui- tous John Peers. His reference to Dr. Balfour betrays a mixture of ignorance with his usual insolence. Because the Edinburgh Professoszses language which belies and discredits the utterances of our local illuminatus, he

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: must needs be throwing" sops" merely " to the Sunday School"! The fittinc, reply to such a remark is, that it is an impudeat slaner, with infinitely more truth, it might be said that in his "affliction of Cacoethes Scribendi "—as one of your correspondents justly puts it —he himself is never at ease, unless he is flinging his "sops "to catch the attention of the sceptical tag-rag and bob-tail with which the modern public is infested. Nor does his acquaintance with Dr. Balfour's works exhibit itself in his remarks. The book quored from " is a mere primer"; all the more necessary, Mr. Peers, that it should be accurate and not misleading. It is dated he says 1874, my edition is 1878; but a much larger work of his on botany dates 1882 in which the same principles with increased emphasis are laid down. Further in a considerably bulkier work still, intended for University students, Dr. Balfour published a very expensive "class book," of which a review appeared at the time in " Hooker's Journal of B kany," with the following eulogium :—" In Dr. Balfour's Class Book the author seems to have exhausted every attainable source of information. Few if any, works on the subject con- tain such a mass of carefully collected and condensed matter, and certainly none are more copiously or better illustrated." Now, this is the eminent author whom a comparatively unknown amateur in botany has the audacity " to dare to publish in any scientific journal," what the raid amateur presumes to call a popular blun- der, that blunder, forsooth, being that the wheat-grain to the extent of the vast proportion of its bulk, "must all be changed and dissolved—in other words, die—in order that the living germ may be nourished and bear fruit."

I will not waste my time over his idle jargon about this great bulk of the corn-grain " never having been alive and therefore could not die "—yet,accordinito his own word-mongering, it must once have lived or how could it have become dead matter as he lays it down in a former postulate (see his letter of the 10th inst.) But, having given some time to the study of cell-structure in the different parts of the plant from the germ to the fruit, I have extreme doubts as to the truth of his point stated, arising chiefly out of the contradictory state- ments upon the subject in one and the same writer. Whether I am right or not in this opinion is of no impor- tance just now. It interferes in no respect with the pro- priety of those who chose to regard the changes which take place in the grain beforc the living germ can start on its growth, as a form of death. That in every age • it has been seen as clearly as it is seen in this, that one. fractional part of the grain did not die in any sense, but lay embedded in its integuments and extornal wrappings ready to unfold its life may be admitted. But one thing I will not admit,that that man is aught but a presump- tuous fool who assumes from the words of Christ that He conceived that the living germ or embryo partici- pated in the decomposition or dissolution of its integu- ments. On the other hand, that He spoke the language of His day and regarded with approval the common sense of observers who could only liken the signs of dis- solution and decay in the great body of the grain to a kind of death is not only certain, but commands even the sanction of eminent scientists at the present hour.— Yours truly, 21st February, 1894.
BEN CHAYIL.

div.head: SOCIALISM.
div.p: SOCIALISM.

Sir,—With regard to your correspondent " Common Justice," I would say common justice would demand that the individual who pens his name to his letters should receive the same observance from those who deign to reply to him. When I feel ashamed of my opinions, it will be a signal of a change. Common Jus- tice desires to know how I reconcile my remarks. That the active principle of all Socialism is selfishness, and that I have never seen a real Socialist? And then he fellows by asking do I mean that those who profess Socialism are not as selfish as their Socialistic princi- ples ? If I wish for an illustration of the selfishness of Socialists it is to be found in the concluding remarks of Common Justice. Here is his answer to the following declaration by me :—" I shall believe in the Socialism ; of the individual who says one man's labour can only ; equal so much, but as the world appraises my labour at so much above its value, take it (the surplus) let it be divided amongst those whom the world appraises at less than their value." To this he replies :—" Mr. flowcroft , fails to see that the Socialist by a foolish self-sacrifice in business, would benefit those who stood least in need of it,and cripple his own capacity for usefulness." Let us judge these rema:ks by a previous declaration by Common Justice :—" What the Socialist objects to is that wealth which is made by the worker should be ap- propriated by those who do not produce it.!' ro this we must of necessity add, in common justice, neither has the individual a right to a large participation in the labours of others, than he himself develops, and, if this be so, he who receives more than the true value of his labour, robs the man, who by the appraisement of the world receives less,and it is toe duty of Common Justice or any other man who believe.; these principles he advo- cates to return that surplus ? lam not talking about a "spontaneous exercise of personal benevolence." lam speaking of returning that which from the tenets of your faith does not belong to you. ; To return to my first declaratioa that the active prin- ciple of all Socialism is selfishness. If this were not so , there would be few Socialists. It is by appealing to the cupidity of those who have not, with descriptions of what might be under a state of Socialism that Socialism gains her converts. Appeal to those who have and show them how much worse off they will be, and see if they accept Socialism. It is not by the enunciation of the virtues of the principle, but by the idea of some in- crease of wealth of the individual that converts are made. Again, selfishness is at the bottom of the prin- ciple which would tax those who have,for the benefit of those who have not, or rather, for the imagined benefit that would be derived from becoming shareholders in national industries. I have seen no national industries which can compete successfully with private ventures, even after allowing that national industries as ship building,tec.,pay less to their hanis,and havesno interest to pay on borrowed capital. Why is this? Because the incentive to economical manufacture is greater in • the case of private enterprise, and in peivate enterprise the right or wrong of a thing is decided on the spot and has not to be referred to someone who knows nothing of , the subject. Again,Socialism is selfish because it would seek to make the ability of the individual the property of the nation. Let your national works run in open competition with private enterprise,and the thing would not last long. How is it I have never met a real Socialist ? Why, because all the Socialism I have seen is bounded on the North by John O'Groats and en the South by Lands End. Who are louder in their declamations against the influx of foreian labour than our London Socialists. The land which consumes the labour of nearly every nation on earth on all true principles of Socialism must draw no ; line within the two hemispheres and must not seek to ; retain the whole of the benefits of the accumulated capital of others to itself. This is not so. however ; the Socialist would seek to uphold the superiority of raee,as , we do that of the individual and argue that he hal. a right to get as much of their labour for as• little as his cwn as he could ; and, as I have said before, I am not sure that with an universal state of Socialism, the British workingman would be better off: And if this be so Common Justice would find few English werkingmen Socialists, if it were I,lrsly to iinprove the condition of the foreigner only. And now for Hallam and the reign of' Henry VI. This, period was a remarkably Is voura lale one for the labourer as owing to the declinations of the black plague, it gave the labourer a similar advantage ,to that which would ensue from following out to- remarks of Mr. John Peers, regarding the curtailment of f,rnilios. We are told that in this exceptionally favourable period, that a labourer coula buy with his week's wages of Is ed., 24lbs of meat and a busfH of wheat, when wheat was at 6s. per quarter. To commence, a labourer, did not need 24lbs• of meat in a week and other things which he did require are not taken into consideration. The average price of wheat in Newcastle last week, as given in the " New- - castle Daily Chronicle," was 255. 33. A, man earning 15s. per week then would be able to buy in wheat. , roughly speaking 42 bushels—a man earning 14. 6J. pat . week, with wheat at 6s. per quarter,could buy a.bushels.. His labour now evidently purchases the product of lab- our with a smaller expenditure ; but the flesh meat which is not the result of any great expenditure of labour, was less then. The same result occurs all round. Labour produces more now for a less expQnditure than it did, then. The workman of Henry VI. had himself to clothe and his wife and family, and if he attempted to clothe them as even a labourer earning 15s. per week in agri- cultural districts may clothe his family to-day he would be the same with his cheap beef as the Yankee was with Chicago. " Stranger," says he, " I could once hay,. bought the site of this city for a pair of old boots." " Ave," says the stranger, " then why didn't ye." " Well, stranger," says he, " guess I hadn't got the boots."

But 15s. per week does not so fairly represenl the average wage of to-day as is. 6d. represented the aver- age wage of Henry Vl.time. It is not as much as the Iw- eat wages paid in this district to agricultural labourers by 3s. per week, and the wage of a labourer in this town may be anything between 18s. anal E 3 or £4. I certainly believe that the average wage of the working class in the whole country is above rather than below 255. per week.

My question in my last. ran as follow, " Ar,-- not thd people of to-day as a whole better off, &e." In conclu- sion, Mr. Editor, I must apologise for the length of my letter, but had it been twice as long it could have only skimmed the subject.—Yours truly, Middlesbro', Feb. 18, 18.94.
I. V. HOWCROFT.

div.head: HORRIBLE DISCOVERY AT BELFAST.
div.p: THE HORRIBLE DISCOVERY AT BELFAST.
SUPPOSED MURDER OF EMIGRANTS.

The discovery of human remains in Belfast has created a great sensation. On Thursday, another skeleton as found in the same place. The commonly-accepted theory now is that the remains are, those at etnigrnt9, who,. prior to sailing for America, had stopped for the night in one of the many common lodging-houses situated some years ago in this part of the city, and that they were murdered for whatever money they I•al upon them, the bodies being secreted in this way.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 24, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 24, 1894.
NOTES ON GAMES AND 1-VISITING THE ANTIQUITIES. ATHLETICS. AN HOUR AT THE MUSEUM.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

"Bleak blew the blizzard's biting breath," is a quota- tion that erred not on the side of exaggeration on Saturday. The appropriateness of the application was very amply felt by the Warrington team arid their large number of admirers, at the match at Oldham. It was not the prospect of experiencing a blizzard, however, allured that large army of Warringtonians to the "gloomy glades and milly glees" of Oldham. On the contrary it was the hope of seeing the Warrington team appropriate the laurels of victory in this, one of the most important matches which they have been engaged in during the cup competition. The presence of the blizzard, and the sloppy state of the ground only 'enhanced this hope the more, and there were few of the wirepullers' admirers who did not contemplate, with unctious satisfaction, a prospect of the players of their home returning covered with lionour—and mud.

Alas ! Dame Fortune stretched forth her capricious hand again, and dashed to the ground those cherished hopes. Though in many cases the game appeared to be quite equally contested, yet there w- , 3 other times when Warrington's form dimmed and paler ki it the contrast with the form of their adversaries. Still r 3 far as the chances of scoring were concerned there were no reasons of a practical character why Warrington should not have issued from the contest riith the majority of points. The team had exccar,lly poor luck, and there were periods when the Oldh. spectators showed that they recognised this by the manner in which they shouted " hard lines Warrington."

During the first half, the play was rarely away from the Oldham lines, and although the home men showed capital defensive tactics, Warriugton made chances of getting through, which no one seemed smart enough to take advantage of. In the second half, however, when Oldham had the assistance of the wind, they adopted tactics, and displayed many a piece of nice skillful play which was generally initiated by Varley, who was chiefly instrumental in the obtaining of the only try which was-scored. Throughout the game, however,the forward play was the main feature, and there were few opportunities for the backs to work.

The competition up to Saturday stands thus : For. Agst. Pld . Won. Lost. Drn. G.T. G.T. P; Oldham l4 -.11 ... 1 ... 2 ... 17 21... 3 5 —2l Swinton l3 8 0 5 10 17 .. 1 4 ...21 Warrington Wigan l3 ... 6 ... 3 ... 4 ... 5 7 ... 2 4...18 Salford Tyldesley Broughton Rangers l2 ... 4 ... 5 ... 3 ... 7 3 ... 611 -.11 Rochdale Hornets Barrow Broughton l3 ... 0 ...13 ... 0 ... 3 5 ...25 28 ... 0

While the first teams were antagonising each other at Oldham, the" A" teams were equally busy at Warring- ton, but unlike the first teams neither could beat the other, although Oldham very nearly " did the trick," Warrington only Equalizing almost at the close of the game. The game from start to finish vs as a very fast , and exciting one, which was the more surpriLing con- sidering the state of the ground. The match was chiefly noticeable for the grand play of Boscow at full back. He displayed a great amount of the skill which once made him famous in football circles all over Lanca- shire. But for his play,Oldham might many times have got over the Warrington lines. The Warrington team were nearer defeat on Saturday than they have been for a great many weeks past, and they will have some foe- men worthy of their steel to-day when they meet Sal- ford. They have not appeared before the Warrington public very frequently of late, as they have been doing battle on "foreign soil," but they have now the greater number of their fixtures on their own "soil," so that a good list of victories may be looked forward to.
BY LUKE BLUNT.

Perhaps it will not come as a sudden shock to the generality of the town's people if I state that there is a museum in Warrington. Yet I have good rea- son to believe that to many the statement contains a startling revelation. It is a fact that in this borough there are persona who are totally ignorant of the existence of the institution: A few years ago—now this is true—there was a man who went in for the study of geology. He was a man very careful of his means, and t e did not care to spend money in the purchase of specimens. So once a week for two years he travelled to Liverpool to in- spect the specimens at the Museum-there. At the end of that time it occurred to a mutual friend to inquire why the g, agist shunned the Warrington , institution and vi,iited the one at Liverpool. Act- ing upon the pfomptingsof this feeling of curiosity he asked :
"Why don't you use the Warrington MuSeura and save the travelling expenses ?" " Aweel," said the geologist., who was a Scotch- man "ye knaw I dinna fret aboot ems expenses—if it canna be saved."
"Bat the Warrington Museum would suit ." "Friend Thomas, noo, dinna mak' sport on a studious won. Ye knaw there's no museum here shoots."

In a while he was persuaded to go and see for himself. The discovery almost broke his heart. He thought it was a retribution on his squander- ing of the money, so he gave up the study, and when anyone tried to persuade him into it again he said sadly:
" Nae, Isiae ! Alice bitten r,wie shy. I'll kep' on the safe side Iwo."
I have it on the authority of on who is con- nected with the institution that there are many, who have resided here for years,who are not aware of the existence of the museum.

I was induced to write about the subject, how- ever, through paying a visit to the institution in company with a well-known local gentleman, who was very enthusiaetically advocating the opening of the museum and art gallery on Sundays. He considered it would be a great boon to the majority of the public of Warrington. On the Continent he had noticed that the Sabbath was the day upon which such institutions were chiefly visited, and the closing of them would mean wresting frOm the people one of their chief sources of instruction and delectation. At the present time the institutions are opened in Birmingham, London, Liverpool, Manchester, and other large towns. " But "he re- sumed " I would not advocate the opening of the Warrington Museum at the compulsory loss of any man's Sabbath. We could not oxect the museum 'officials to be on duty. What I shoul4 propose is that a committee of reliable ratepayers should take 1 the matter up, and offer to the coin- mittee to take turns in acting as stewards. The question is discussed very much among certain sections of the public, and why it does not come up for discussion at the Council I cannot very well imagine." Another point, however, occurred to me as beiug, worthy of some attention. That is the necessity of eome sort of guide book for the benefit of he visitors. It occurred to me that if a man is to get much information or instruction from a visit to the Museum he will have to be very well read on a variety of peculiar matters--his chief novel so to speak, will have to be the "Eniclopedia of Natural History," and his other book of entertain- ment the still uncompiled volume on " Local antiquities." These are studies, if they were possible, which the ordinary labouring man or mechanic could not pretend to take up—not because of the fear of becoming too flippant and frivolous, but simply because the game would not be worth the candle. And the consequence is, that one may go into the museum without the slightest knowledge of the hiatory of the simplest exhibit, and after an hour or two of persevering inspection,it is possible to come out a veritable receptacle of erroneous impressions. Yet many of the things one may have inspected are invested with a charm of legend, and crowned with a halo of antiquity,which would awe, and create a fe6ling of reverence in the soul of the meanest, did he but know it. For instance we were in one of the rooms, standing over an old oak chest which some centuries ago served as a safe for the plate at Grappenhail Church. It is a mast antique piece of furniture, being about three feet long and consisting of the scooped out trunk of an oak tree. As I stood over the relic thinking of the legend that is attachea to it, I was disturbed by a wrangle be- tween a male and a female. They were talking in a subdued tone about the safe. The man contended that it was a relic, and an old coffin. His wife said :. She reckoned it wasn't a relic. She knewit waergt, because relics were only small things, like "crucifixes." He said, in an impassioned whisper "how tha does talk! IV hy,anything' s a relic so it's more than a hundred years ewd ? " " Is thee granny a hundred year ewel," she ex- claimed in a loud tone of contempt. "Oi alus thowt ' tha wen.* foo' Ned, but this yere settles it. Cawing a piece of owd beam a relic! It dosna say much for thi scripture laming, that it does'nt ! " Then be started in and raged, and in a while the. attendant had to come and interfere.

Very diem misleading ideas of a similar charac- ter, get abroad, owing to there being no guide book for the instruction ot those who are not sufficiently well " read-sip" upon the antiquities. In the Art Gallery there are many subjects besides the pic- tures, which might well be catalogued. But perhaps the most important section which requires to be catalogued in some way is that embracing the natural historyexhibits.Th ,re are dozens of ordinary looking animals here, with histories of a more pre- possessing character. Take for instance that little insigniticent wren-like bird with a name as long as itsbody—Dendrocca Blackburnia. Few, who look iat t, are aware that the name means " Miss Black- burn's Warbler," and that it is a rare specimen pre- served by a Miss Blackburn, who lived in Warring- ton a century ago, and who was a great and noted naturalist. Then across the room in a case are some duck like birds, with legs which have their centre joints under the tail. They are named Pylopades— which means Rump Foot, a name given them be- cause their fees can ha brought right past their tails, for this gives to them great 'living powers. At the end of the room there is a skeleton of a parrot. You will notice- how fiat and broad its head w— and how it reminds you of that bald-headed gentle- man friend. A catalogue would tell you that the head is very much like that of a human being ; that the features denote brain, of which latter the par- rot is said to have a larger supply than any other bird—but which dose'nt prove that the human par- rot has more brain than any others of kis race.

Hard by there is to be seen the raven. This bird is a very' remarkable one,though you may not know it. Unlike most other birds it has a voice, not a twitter nor warble. It can be taught to talk and perform tricks,. and is able to live on almost any- thing. A short distance away you will see a bird laselled "Crow" and another "Rook." One in twenty will perhaps recognize the distinguishing characs teriatic. If you had a catalogue it would say: "Observe the whiteness on the gills of the rook. That is its bars face. Rooks are very barefaced, and crows are w" .The envy has no whiteness about its jaws." There is another little insignificant bird called the "spotted flycatcher." It looks very or- dinary; but your catolgue would tell you that, the bird was the onlyone of a raretyever seen in England ' and that it was shot at Fiddler's Ferry in. 1865. A short distance awaythere is a rat-like animal labelled "Norwegian Lemming." You will probably ignore its presence to look at the large tiger, with its mouth opened abnormally wide. Yet that little Lemming, is of more interest. You have perhaps heard the theory that animals. commit suicide. That rat like creature is one of tie best known exempe- ficadoras of the argument. It lives in the Norwegian mountains and is very prolific. About every two years its numbers become so great that they cannot all find subsistence. At such a dilemma—so scien- tists say—about one third of the number sally forth in a large army. and scamper over hill and dale dawn to the sea. Here they unheedingly leap into the water and are drowned. Some naturlists ,eontend that, the act. is one premeditated, audit is to remove the miseries of a glutted population— other naturalists say that it is the animals lack of sense in trying to imitate the Vikings and get an unassisted passage •to England. If the former theory be true, what a simple and easy method, unattended by any expense, is at the disposal of tha hundreds in this country who seek to find a way to prevent aver population I But to proceed. There are—dozens—aye hundreds—of exhibits in the museum which could be rendered highly inter- esting to the general public were they only briefly described in a guide book. The objection raised to this, I believe, is that the expense of printing a catalogue would be too great. Perhaps so, but why I not supply a type written guide to each case. This wou,d not cast much, and additions could be added. easily, a; they axe received!

SOME NOTES FROM MY READING. BY Mn. Joizisf PEERS. 'Then brother," said my uncle Toby, "it would be of vast advantage for us were we to exchange spectacles occasionally with our neighbours:" "And see oursel'a as ithers see us," put in Eusebius. "Not a very flattering style of portraiture, betimes," said Mr. Shandy, " nor one calculated to encourage our vanity or self-esteem. .'The lesson might be bitter but salutary—but the practice will never be popu- lar. People, one and all, very much prefer to look at things through their own spectacles and from their own point of view. Such an exchange would be the death blow, to the popular fallacy as to the belief in one's own eyes. It would require a very powerful pair of truth-rendering glasses to con- vince the average Briton that he never saw the sun set or rise, from the 'vantage ground of his native isle! Nevertheless he would be quite will- ing to endorse the proud boast that the same lum- inary never does set upon the British Empire. We love and cherish our own conceptions. These it is that we see through our own spectacles and the image so formed, we straightway adopt and baptize in the sacred name of truth. Thence forward this is our truth--our very very own as the children' say, for which we are responsible and with whichl let any man meddle at his peril !" " Foster children ' are usually baptized in another name I believe " said Eusebius. "Yes," said my father," the name of truth seems to be too sacred to be used at the naming of every squalling brat, it would take the keen edge of our self-appreciation did it become too common." "And yet there be exceptions " began my ercle—"That proves the rule, "inter- rupted my father—"But now let us look at England things through Atreiican spectacles. In a book named England within and without '— an American has favoured us with some very candid, and, on the whole, very fair criticism on English things and English folk. "Hear weat he has to say on jerry bailding :—'lt is the custom there (in England) to put up shells of l'ouses, usually three or four together, and to leave them to be furnished according to the wishes of an intending tenant or purchaser. They are called carcases. I examined many of these without find- ing even one tolerably well built. The walls brought to mind the scoff of Tobiah the A morite against the newly btiilt wall of Jerusalem—‘ If a fox go up he shall break down their stcne wall'—and Panurge's declaration that a cow could destroy, in a not very quotable manner, six fathoms of the wall of old Paris. The mortar, although it had been set for years, would crumble under the touch of my stick, or even my thumb nail. And walls of the modern VIM villa houses that I visited were rarely more substantial, while the joiner's work was both slight and course. I also remarked that where recent a& ditions had been made to the height of garden walla the mortar in the new part, although in general it was plainly ten or twenty years old was more like mud than mortar. Indeed I did not see in England, in a new private building of moderate pretention, any mortar worthy of the name. This attracted my attention, I need hardly say, because of the notion generally prevailing, and sedulously encouraged by British writers, that all British work is distin- guished from work of its kind by excellence of material and thoroughness of workmanship, that although it might not have elegance, it is sure to be substantial, That such was once the character of the work of English artizans and manufacturers, I believe is not to be disputed; but during the last 50 years this glory of England seems to have de- parted.' " P. 146. "Such," said. my father, "is Bri- tish workmanship as seen through American spec- tacles." "A heavy indictment surely," said Buse- bins, "if it be true.' " Too near the truth, I am afraid, to be easily disproved," said Mr. Shandy, "the very excellence of old British work serves as a divaraging contrast to the slight and slovenly modern kind. The work of our forefathers, like the British oak, was of slow growth, sturdy, substantial and durable. Each house in those days had to , have its own knowledge—one clock would not then serve for a row of nine houses, nor could a whis- ; pared conversation be overheard in the next house but one!. "Then again, this writer turns his spectacles full glare upon the social life of our little island, with this result—' The god of English social life next to Mammon'—is Propriety. Now propriety, rightly worshippea,is a very good god; his rites are sweet- ness, order, decency ; and in their practice they involve that consideration for others which is the highest form-of morality, and even justice. But your average Briton makes propriety a Moloch, before whom he prostrates himself, and before whom he often makes his children sacrifice some of the beauty of their youthful lives, the highest socialism, the greatest social law,. to this sort of Englishman,.is to do' the correct thing.' Having this, he feels that he has clothed his soul in a panoply of proof. Whether the 'correct thing' be really the right thing he does not know, does not seek to know. That so it is, and so it has been are to him both Yogic and religion. In his mouth the greatest reproach is unprecedented ' ; the mere statement of the fact that an act has not been done before,- that a word has not been spoken before, :brings to him its condemnation. Wherefore he lives his life surrounded by dead, shrivelled forms, eye- less, brainless, bloodless, whose only voice is from the grave of: a dead past. If he breaks away from this oppression he is likely to run into ex- tremes which. violate all decency, all decorum, all propriety. Freed from his accustomed restraint,he is apt to a grossness to vice which makes it more hideous, if not more harmful.' And again . . co-existent, however, with this strong indivi- duality, and the license accorded to it, is a disposi- tion to resent any attempt to introdue social changes, particularly if the attempt seems to imply any reproach. The sensitiveness on this point is very great, so great that it becomes touchousness. Naumus lege antiquas Anglice mutare express.es the spirit of the rulers of society now aa much as it did that of the State centuries ago. It is not the general custom to use napkins at luncheon in Eng- land, although at 'great houses' luncheon is really a small dinner; as it may well be when' ta muckle dinner hersel 'is at eight o'clock, and on great oc- casions at nine. An American lady was visiting at one of these houses, where she found the usual absence of neekins at midday. She knew her hostess so welll that she could venture to ask her why it was that napkins were not used at luncheon. Her grace (for she was a duchess) replied simply that it was not the custom, with an air that that settled the cenestion. But her guest had taken lun- cheon with die Queen more than once at Balmoral and there she found napkins. This she told her friend as a sort of justification of her inquiry. Indeed,' replied the duchess, 'the Queen had better be careful. She will make herself unpopular if she undertakes to change the customs of the country.' "What a,momentcus question,' said Slawkenber- gius. "Truly the fate of Empires hang upon a ; thread." "-Aye or may be wrapped in the table queth my father. "Is it not an evidence of how very little it requires to fill the average mind ? The to be or not to be 'napkin question would have been relegated to its proper sphere had her grace been possessed of bet ter and worthier subjects for discussion," remarked Eusebius, " there are graver cniestions awaiting solution than the presence or absence of a clout." " Did'ea' ever miss napkins at luncheon, Trim," said my Uncle Toby. " I have often missed the lunch, your lionour, but never felt the want of the ' napkin,' replied Trim," they might do te staunch a wound, but are of little use to staunch the appetite of a soldier on the field." " Why whet a heretic the man must be "exclaimed Yorick,who had been looking into the book during the progress of this dialogue "listen"—' the truth seems to be that the thoughtful and scholarly divines of the English Church, those whose acquirements and mental in- dependence fit them to be critical are sorely per- plexed by their position. For the Church of Eng- land is a political institution so interwoven with the structure of English society that, should it be sh al en, the whole social fabric might go to ruin. The feeling is prevalent (as I gathered although I did not hear -it attested), and it is reasonable that doing away with bishops wouH be the first step to dispensing with dukes. And what would England be without her dukes? An English- man might lead a godless life ; hut could he lead a dukeless one I was surprised at the free-thought and the free-speaking which I met with among English clergymen. Opinions as to the inspiration and authoeship of the Bible, which not many years ago would have created horror among all decent people, were expressed in private conver- sation by some of these gentlemen with an aston- ishing absende of reserve. And the freedom of the thinking and of the speech seemed to me just in proportion to the intelligence and scholarship of the speaker." " Whet is the world coming to?" exclaimed Yorick as ge finished rending this. "Possibly to that time when the old order giveth place to the new," replied my father. " But what will be the consequence of such teaching ?"rejoined Yoricle. "That," said my father—, But " that " we will deal with another time.
BRUNNER. MOND, AND CO., LIMITED.
HALF YEARLY MEETING.

The 26th half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, was held yes- terday afternoon at the Law rooms, Cook-street, Liverpool. In the absence through indisposition, at Cannes, of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., chairman of the company, the chair was occupied by Mr. Harry Coghill, and there was a crowded attendance of shareholders.

The balance-sheet and profit and loss account showed a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half year ended on the 31st December, 1893, of £150,550 11s. Bd., which, with the amount of £89,400 12s. 11d. hrought forward from the previous- half year, made a total of £239,951 4s. 7d. The direc tors proposed to deal with the above balance as follows: —Dividend on the preference capital, at 7 per cent. pet' annum, £15,290 12s. 6d.; dividend on the ordinary capi- tal, at 30 par cent, per annum, £ll9 24. 6d.; amount to be written of patents account, £2,500; amount to be placed to suspense account, £20,000 ; and balance to be carried forward, £82,429 94. 7(1.; total, £239,951 4s. 7d. The directors proposed to place to the suspense ac- count the above sum of £20,000 in continuation ot a policy which had been found to be of great benefit to the company. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report and accounts and the declaration of divident as men- tioned therein, said that he was sorry that the results of the six months had not been so satisfactory as they might desire, owing to the sixteen weeks' coal strike and the depression of business ia America. They had had a difficult half year, and the present outlook was not very brilliant.

Mr. Henry Brunner seconded the report. Mr. Watson, a shareholder, protested against the bald- ness of both the report and the chiirman's remarks, and thought they were entitled to fuller information as to the causes of the falling off in their returns. He also called attention to the fact that last year the directors had called up .C 165,000 of which they had accounted in the report for only £74,000, and that they further proposed this year to call up £67,000 and had decreased the in- vestments by £25,000. He would like some information respecting the nature of the investments and considered there was no reason why the shareholders should be kept absolutely in the dark. Dr. Hewitt, a director, replied that the balance sheet was made up to the 31st December, 180, and the capi- tal called up on the Ist January, 1894, could not have been included in it. With respect to the so called cal- ling up of capital,' what Mr. Watson said was quite wrong. They had paid out of the profits over to the shareholders a sum of money which was represented of course by the £166,000, and that was necessary for the purpose of the business. It was really a distribution of profits, and not calling up capital. (Hear, hear.) In 2i years the capital of the company had been returned to the shareholders, and that was better than a boasting report with very little money to be distributed. As regards the report and balance sheet, they were in exactly the same form as they had been since the forma- tion of the conspany,and the figures spoke for themselves. The coal strike had cost them a lot of money, and this with the diminished sales showed a loss of profit of £105,000 as compared with the previous half year. Trade all over the world had been affected, and in America and Australia there had been such a disturb- ance as they had not seen for 20 years. Mr. Watson repeated his request that more informa- tion should in future be put in the report. He had heard it remarked that the company had no investment at all.

The Chairman: Whoever told you that knew nothing about it. We ha % consols, preferred shares, and other equally good secuntios. The motion was passed unanimously. On the motion of Mr. George Jones, seconded by Mr. John Harding, £5OO was voted to each directors, other than the managing directors, for their services during toe past half year. Messrs. Harry Coghill, David Basil Hewitt, and Gus- tav Jarmay were unanimously re-elected on the Beard of directors ; and it was resolved to elect Mr. John Fowler Leece Brunner (eldest son of the chairmen) as director at _a remuneration of £6OO per annum.
Messrs. T. W. Read and Co. were elected auditors at £5OO a year.
A-vote ot thanks to the Chairman closed the meeting.
CO-OPF,ItATIVE SOCIETY TEA MEETING AT RUNCORN.

The annual tea party and concert in connection with the Runcorn Co-operative Society, was held in the Assembly Room, above the stores, on Wednes- day evening. A large number of members and their families were- present. Tile tables were presided over by Mesdames Richardson (senior), Richardson (junr.), Bowyer, Rodgers, Watson (jour.), Rushton, Paton, Sillitoe, Peters, Evans, Ackerley, Lea, Cousins, Rawlinson, and the Misses B. Nickson, Rhodes, Massey, Hill, Leach, Dykes, Holt, Betney, Davies, and Worthington. After tea the entertain- ment was held under the presidency of Mr. Riley, wlio was supported by Messrs. Betney, Rogerson, Cropper, Holt, Watson, Royle , Rhodes, Upton, (sec.), Morris (assistant manager), and Messrs. Briers and Pyke dele- gates from St.. Helens. In opening the proceedings The Chairman said that as they had come there that evening Co enjoy themselves he should not occupy much of their time by his remarks. They had enjoyed a very palatable repast and now he thought they were inclined to a little agreeable delectation. (Applause.) Referring for a moment to their institution, he might say that it was 31 years since they commenced with a small shop under Forester's Hall. A few years afterwards they removed to Regent-st. and then they came to their pre- sent premises and commenced to open branches, the first of which was in Widnes. Since then they had gene on growing and now,their total membership amounted to 4,000. In conclusion he expressed the hope that the mernlars of their institution would remain. and come to them ,t nd do their shopping at their stores below and be satisfiA with their dividend, and not heed outside offers of reductions. (Applause.) Mr. Upton, secretary, said that in accordance with custom he would submit a resume .of the year's work. The return upon the sale of provisions was £89,102 10's. 5d., being an increase of £4,495 ss. 10-d. over that of the previous year. They were also in the proud posi- tion of having returned to their members a dividend of 20 per cent., and he could assure them that there were many companies like theirs; who were not returning more than 10 per cent.or 15 per cent. The company,too, was managed by working men, o hich was all the more creditable to them. (Applause.) Their share capital now atneunted to £42,755 12s, 9d., against £12,710 us. Bd. last year, showing a slight decrease which they could only expect after the depressed state of trade. Many towns had in this respect also suffered much more than Runcorn. They had in connection with the p?nny bank ne less a sum than £2,330 us. 6d. from the 3 oung people of Runcorn and Widnes. Then there was that excellent friend—which was a grand safeguard for them • —the reserve WO, which amounted to £2,808 Bs. 10d. Then there was the building fund. Now this was a matter which he thought the Runcorn people ought to educate themselves more upon. The Society was lending money at five per cent. interest, and thus enabled members to buy their own houses. This they could do easily enough in most cases by using their dividend to pay the interest with, and he urged them to take advantage of such a highly commend- able fund. The amount lent on this fund during the year was £11,75765. 11d. They had invested at inter- ests of four and five per cent, no less a sum than £13,726 ss. 2d.,.and altogether they had paid in capital no less a sum than £15,427 6s. (Hear hear,) Had any- one of their tradesmen given so much to them he would have been deemed a noble philanthrop- ist. (Applause.) Yet that Company did it and no one seemed to think anything of it. (Hear, hear.) The meeting was aftewards addressed by the two delegates. from St. Helens, and during the evening tle: following persons contributed to the entertainment : Mrs. Timperley and Messrs. Fox, Mason, Leathwoed, Worrall, Lacy, Wallington. The glee party also ren- dered several glees.

div.head: BOATING.
div.p: BOATING.

Another meeting was held on Monday in connection with the Warrington Sailing Club race. The question of allowing non-members from Widnes and Runcorn to join in the race was considered, but no decision was arrived at. Some" set speeches," I hear, were delivered on the subject, but to no avail. The Club is not going to have brought against it the charge of introducing any- thing knew—i.e. if some members can help it.

A number of the Widnrs and Runcorn boatmen have been interviewed on the point, but they will only enter when it is agreed t. run the race from Widnes to War- rington on the flood and back to Widnes on the ebb. Some of them too. I hear are in favour of having a cup among the prizes, but this the club will not agree to be- causeof the expense. What I should like to ask is,why honorary members are not invited to join the club, and a fund large enough for the purchase of a cup, thus main- tained.

div.head: GYbiNASITTAI.
div.p: GYbiNASITTAI.

In the third round of the National Shield Competition, Liverpool Gymnasium met the Dublin Gymnasium on Saturday at Dublin. The clritest aroused great interest in the Irish capital, and the result was that Liverpool were declared victors by 449 points to 4181. The vic- torious eight included a Warrington„maa viz., D. Walsh who scored 54- points. The visit was very much en- joyed by the Liverpool men. It is the rule that the home eight should entertain the visiting: eight, and right royally did the "Shamrock men" perform this pleasant duty.

Durisg. an exciting part of the contest, a loud voice was suddenly heard exclaiming "Go it, Warrington," and Walsh the next moment was surprised on turning round to catch sight of Herbert Webster, the lengthy Warringtonian who has done such good service for the Warrington Rugby Football Club. For a.few moments, the whole andience was convulsed with laughter at the enthusiastic way in which the two Warrin3tonians wel- comed each other.

div.head: CRUELTY TO CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: CRUELTY TO CHILDREN AT WARRING- TON.
SIISCEING CONDITIoN OF A HOUSE.
A MOTHER SENT TO GAUL,

On Tuesday morning at the Warrington Borough Court, Mrs.. Eliza Williams, wife of M. Williams, of 6e Back Stamford-sr., was chargel with having neglected her three children, Joseph aged 14,Arthur aged 7, and Sarah G. Mr. Buckton prosecuted on behalf of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty; to Children. lie said the prisoner and family occupied one bedroom, and had the partial use of the kitchen downstairs, at the house 6, Back Stam- ford-st. The three children had been fairly well nour- ished, but they were in a filthy state, and not properly clothed. rho two boys simply had on a ragged piece of shirt, and a ragged pair of trousers and jacket each. ll.Totither of them wore boots and their bodies were very dirty. The girl was wearing three dirty garments, ver- min was on her body, and also in her head. The back of her head was covered with sores, and this had not been attended to. At the time when the house was visited, on the 145t1i of the present month, there was no food in the houe ex(rept a quarter of a pound of bread. The bedroom CMC a ined one bedstead with two mattresses which were very dirty and stinking. Thfp husband had been on night duty 'and was sleeping on the bed at the time. "SVhen he was not on night duty two of the child- ren slept downs,tairs in a, box with no bedding and no clothing whatever. Thet stench in the bedroom was almost unbeara 0-le, and the cause of the negligence, as •was usual in such-cases, was drink. The husband in the ,presence of the prisoner told the officer that his wife was in the habit of getting drunk constantly. He earned about 255, per week regularly and be gave his ,wife 16s. and pa d the rent. - - -

Ins.pector Uphiti N.S.P.C.C. said on the pnvious Wed- nesday haviied the prisoner's house. The woman was out. He n•mained -in the house about a, quarter of an hour when the prisoner came in. She th3r; appeared the worse for think. He examined the three children, and the vermin had completely eaten into the girl's head He was unable to stand in the bedroom long owing to the stench. The mattresses were saturated, and rotting away. The husband told him that he worked at Dal- lam Forge, and earned 255. per week.. His wife got drunk on Sakurdav and two or three times during time week. The prisoner was in the room at the time and did not deny the statement. _ .
Constable-Smith corroborated Inspector Uphill's state- ment.

Mrs. Charlotte Willia'als mother of the•prisener's hus- band gave evidence as to the prisoner's drunken habits, and her neglect of the children. Mr. Jones. school attendance officer.. said the children ran about the streets without boots and were exceedingly dirty. They attended school very badly indeed. The parents had paid £7 in fines for the citildren's irregular attendance at school. One boy was in Father Nugent's school at Liverpool. Theirs was the most troublesome case they had had to deal with: The.children had been sent home from school for being dirty. D. S. Monagham gave evidence as to taking the pris- oner into Custody. The husband was a hard-working decent fellow. .
The magistrates committed the prisoner to ganl for three months with hard lab,,or.

div.head: SENSIBLE ARRANGEMENT.
div.p: A SENSIBLE ARRANGEMENT.

At a specially"convened meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Coal Sales-Association held in Manchester on Tuesday, the best Means of preventing excessive competition in tendering, for the forthcoming gas-c.)al contracts was "discussed ; and it was decided to 'appoint a fommittee representing gas-Coal produeing colheries in. Lancashire to meet in conference with Yorkshire r- presentaties with a view to coming to some. mutual • agrement with regard to the prices t e quoted.

div.head: EXPLORATIONS IN THE FAR NORTH,
div.p: EXPLORATIONS IN THE FAR NORTH,

Lieutenant J. B. Tyrrell, of the Governor General's Foot Guards, and a member of the staff: of the Canadian Geolcgicad Survey, has just accomplished a brilliant piece of work in exploring the hitherto unknown barren lands of Canada to the west of Hudson's Bay. Lieutenant Tyrrell„ who was acaompanied by his brother and six Indians, left Edmonton about the end of last May, and travelled by way of the Athabasca river to the lake of the same name. Tne barren lands are bounded on the south by a wooded belt some hundred miles across, which is the hunting ground of some of the Indian tribes. Afraid lest the explorers should rob than' of their hunting 'grounds, the local Indians left tha party in the lurch,. and they had to push on alone. The object of their journey was to ascertain if the vast unknown area of the , barren lands was rich in either minerals or fur-bearing animals. The party had canoes with them, and followed the Doobaunt river to the large lake of that name,thence making their way by Chesterfield Inlet into Hudson's Bay, and coasting southwards to York Factory, whence they proceeded to Winnipeg, having travelled 2,200 miles in canoes, of which 850 was through new country 650 miles were travelled on snow-shoes and 350 on dog sledges, so that the total distance covered was about ' 3,200 miles. The time occupied was about seven months, and the result of the expedition is to establish that the barren lands are a rolling track of land speckled over with swamps and occasional rocky hills. The country is entirely destitute of wood, and swamps with reindeer. Another result of Lieutenant Ty-rrell's ]ourney is to verc. considerably modify the western shore of Hudson's Bay, which he followed closely in his canoes. The party suffered intensely from cold, and during the passage through the barren lands were obliged to eat such meat as they had raw, since there was not a. stick of wood with which to make a fire.
ANARCHIST THREATS AT BLACKBURN.

EXTRAORDIAARY LETTER. A Blackburn evening newspaper on Thursday receiv- ed the following extraordinary letter : Sir,—We who have wrote this letter are AnarchistS from London, and we let you know to warn the public we have a plan on hand of blowing up a big mill in Blackburn. We will not give name. We only write to warn the public. We are doing it to let the public know that we are trying to get right for the poor. We are going to keep Vaillant's word up for ever—" Vive la Anarchie." We have got exactly the same bombs that Bourdin lost his life with. They were manufactured in the same shop. Bourdin was our leader, and soon after we heard of his death, we came northward. We have got the names of the richest manufacturers in this town such as Hornby's, Birtvvistle's, and Dugdale's. Their residences will have to be shattered, too, if we get to know where they live.

(Signed) The Anarchists. A rude fuse of lueifer matches was enclosed in the letter, with a label bearing the words, " These matches have first to be lighted, and when we put them into the mouth of the h-nrib, the bomb will explode and blow ihe whole buildings down." The letter and fuse were handed to the police.

THE LOCAL VETO BILL. MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S VIEWS. Mr. J. Chamberlain, M.P.,received a small deputation - of working men on Wednesday at the Liberal Unionist offices, Westminster. They objected to the Local Veto Bill, and urged the right hon. gentleman to oppose it. In reply, he said he could not take the bill seriously. It was meant for show and not for work. It was brought in to get popularity for the Government,and Sir William. Harcourt and Sir Wilfrid Lawson had come tc agree- ment upon it, laughing meanwhile like the augurs in Roman history. But if the bill did come before the House he readily promised to oppose it. He objected to the principle of the bill, for it was unjust to destroy any trade which had been carried on under the sanction of the law without givinc, compensation. Yet if compen- sation were granted he doubted whether the ratepayer s would allow millions upon millions of money to be flung away in order to gratify the strong prejudices of com- paratively a very small section of the community. There was, he contended, great .1 ieonsistency in respnt to the provisions for Sunday closing. Why should it majority of twfs-thirds be needed in all matters of social interest, whereas only a bare majority was necessary for Sunday closing? The bill, if passed into law, would be practically inoperative. It would lead to wholesale evasion and worse forms of drinking. He had no faith in compulsory prohibition, but he was in favour of measures that would improve the condition and increase the self-respect of the working classes. Education, for instance, had done much ta foster sobriety, and St. Monday and the tipsy workman were not so common as formerly.

"0 VUM . " CLICHONT HOUSE, LITTLE SANGHOLL, NEAR CHESTER. 2nd January, 1894. Mr. Jos. THORLEY, King's Cross, London. SIR, It may be of interest to you to know the follow- ing On the 2nd October last, I purchased 13 Hens and a Cock—all cross-bred—and a very miserable lot they looked; in fact, they had been half famished. I gave them hot food in the morning—boiled potatoes and meal, with dripping. bacon. liquor, or such like stuff in it—and every other day about a teaspoonful of OVUM well mixed up. NATEEKLY CHAT.—The Pantheon is. filled to overflowing with real genuine good SECOND-HAND FURNITURE, at Prices that simply bewilder and demoralise competition. The resources of The Pantheon are simply un- exhaustible. We reproduce a letter written on the 15th of January last which aptly describes the advantages of The Pantheon:— [Copy.) January 15th, 1894, Southport. Dear Mrs. E.—l have delightful news to tell you, Jack has bought the furniture, and we feel gratified that we belie.'e we have done well in our purchases. We have secured every thing we require from " The Pantheon," and though we never expected to reach our ambition on the limited amount we agreed to expend, we are quite satisfied. Truly some of th- heavy furniture is second-hand, but renovating and re- upholstering has made them quite equal, to new. We bought the Dining-room Furniture, which was made by Ogden and cost £l2O for £45. It consists of a massive suite, a most lovely sLie board with Dining Table and Overmantel to match, it lain old Spanish mahogany, matured to a dark rich colour ; we can have our money returned if not satisfactory. I may say that I saw a large number of suites that would have suited at. £2O to £3O, but we feel in love with the one £45. You would hardly credit the enormous variety in dining room suites they have at" The Pantheon." I believe there are always over 100 on view. The Drawingroom, Showroom is really charming, and I should like to have pur- chased several pieces of Chippendale Furniture, but for economy, we bought a Sheraton Suite with a dear little settee, two odd Lounge chairs, and a set of occa- sional chairs, all different designs, hut harmonising in colour. The cabinet is just what I desired, and must have cost three times as much as we paid for it. Two Occasional Tables, Overmantel, and Coal Vase completed the lot for £3B. I must tell you about the bedrooms. We furnished only two for the present, one in American walnut and the other in lancewood. The' walnut cost £4O, we paid £22. The lance- wood, we paid 16 gulneas for, and I think it is worth double. I won't tell you about the bedsteads, bedding, carpets, cur- tains, ornaments, and all the sundries You must come when the I ouse is finished and see everything for yourself, which Is promised within a week, We must thank Jack's cousin for recommending us to 'The Pantheon," and I cannot do better than suggest that you should pay them a visit at the earliest op ortnnity, With love, and hoping to see you the moment we are ready to receive visitors.—Yours sincerely, FLORRIE.
